Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.
Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The external elastic membrane is a fenestrated elastic membrane that constitutes the innermost component of the tunica externa of arteries (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The external elastic membrane (or lamina) is considered to be part of the tunica externa, separating it from the tunica media. The external elastic membrane is composed of sheets of fenestrated elastic connective tissue. The fenestrations allow nutrients to pass to the cells buried deep within the arteries walls.

The external elastic membrane is most prominent in muscular arteries, thin in elastic arteries (if present), and absent in arterioles and veins.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The external elastic membrane lies between the tunica media and the tunica externa.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The external elastic lamina serves to provide a readily deformable, compliant structure surrounding the lumen of the vessel to enable diameter changes when needed.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The tunica externa of a blood vessel is the outer, fibroelastic coat of vessels, usually in contact with surrounding tissues (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The walls of blood vessels consist of three main layers:
•	the inner layer, the tunica interna (or intima)
•	the middle layer, the tunica media
•	the outer layer, the tunica externa (or adventitia).

Recent studies have suggested that the tissue arrangement of tunica externa is not a densely packed wall-like structure, commonly seen in alcohol fixed tissue. In fact, it is composed of a collagen lattice surrounded by fluid filled interstitial spaces (Benias et al., 2018). This has also been described in other tissues, such as lung, renal, dermis, and fascia.

The tunica externa possesses its own network of smaller blood vessels, known as the vasa vasorum, which provide the blood vessel with the molecules and nutrients necessary for cellular activity (Pawlina, 2016). Along with this small network of supportive blood vessels, the tunica externa is innervated by unmyelinated autonomic nerve fibers, the nervi vasorum (Mescher, 2013). The nervi vasorum are efferent autonomic fibers that play a role in vasodilation and vasoconstriction. 

The tunica externa of elastic arteries is relatively thin and usually less than half the thickness of the tunica media. It is primarily composed of thick bundles of collagen running in a circular manner. Elastin in this layer forms a loose network and is not well organized like that seen in the tunica media.

In muscular arteries, the tunica externa is a relatively thick (about the same thickness as the tunica media) collagenous tissue and often separated from the tunica media by a discernable external elastic membrane. 

In arterioles, the tunica externa is thin and poorly defined with loosely arranged elastin and collagen. It blends with the surrounding connective tissue the vessels travel within.
 
The tunica externa is the most prominent part of veins. In medium veins, the externa is almost entirely collagenous, but also contains longitudinally arranged smooth muscle. In large veins, the tunica externa is the thickest layer and is composed mainly of longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle surrounded by collagenous connective tissue. The tunica externa of postcapillary venules is absent but is thicker than the media in typical (muscular) venules,

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The tunica externa is the outermost layer of the blood vessel. It surrounds the tunica media.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The tunica externa acts as an anchor, securing the blood vessel to the surrounding body tissue.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The vasa vasorum are the small nutrient arteries and the veins in the walls of the larger blood vessels (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The vasa vasorum are a network of small blood and lymphatic vessels surrounding arteries and veins (Phillippi, 2022). Veins tend to have more extensive and well-developed vasa vasorum compared to arteries (Ovalle and Nahirney, 2021).

The vessels of the vasa vasorum are composed of a single layer of endothelium surrounded by a very thin basement membrane.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The vasa vasorum are located within the tunica externa and extend into the tunica media of arteries and veins.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The vasa vasorum delivers oxygen and nutrients and removes metabolites, waste, and extracellular fluid from the tunica externa and media of larger blood vessels (Mulligan-Kehoe and Simons, 2014). The inner parts of blood vessels receive their nutrient supply from the lumen.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: •	Syphilitic aortitis

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nervi vasorum are the nerve branches that supply the adventitia of the blood vessels (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: Efferent autonomic fibers innervate blood vessels via the nervi vasorum (Mescher, 2013). These nervi vasorum are composed of unmyelinated axons in little parcels. These axons are predominantly postganglionic fibers originating from sympathetic ganglionic neurons.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nervi vasorum branch and connect within the tunica externa of vessels, forming a meshwork around it. The density of innervation varies in different vessels and in different areas of the body.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nervi vasorum regulate muscular tone, and therefore, blood vessel diameter.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The basement membrane is a layer within the vessel wall on which the endothelium lies, dividing the endothelium from the connective tissue in the vessel wall. The basement membrane is made up of two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina. These two laminae are comprised of different matrices. The basal lamina is a matrix of collagen formed by the endothelial cells. The reticular lamina is deep to the basal lamina and composed of reticular fibers produced by fibroblasts.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The basement membrane separates the endothelium from the connective tissue in the vessel walls.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The basement membrane contributes to physical support of the vessel, holding the endothelium to connective tissue. This membrane also functions as a defense against harmful cells infiltrating the deeper tissue levels (Liotta et al., 1980). It also plays a role in angiogenesis through the release of peptide fragments.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
•	Alport syndrome
•	Formation of tumors (Figg and Folkman, 2008)

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Vascular endothelium is the layer of epithelial cells that lines the lumina of blood vessels; it originates from the mesoderm (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The vascular endothelium is a key component of the tunica interna of a blood vessel. It forms the innermost layer surrounding the lumen, which separates the various cells and molecules within the blood from the surrounding tissue. The endothelium is therefore in direct contact with the bloodstream.

The endothelium is composed of a single layer of simple squamous endothelial cells. These cells form a continuous and uninterrupted sheet, or lining, around the lumen of the artery.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The endothelium lies on the basement membrane of the blood vessel. This membrane affixes the endothelium to the connective tissue as well as providing the vessel wall with strength. The basement membrane is attached to the subendothelial connective tissue layer of the tunica interna.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The vascular endothelium presides over the movement of cells in and out the blood as well as the exchange of molecules between the blood and surrounding tissues. Endothelium also influences blood flow by acting as a mechanoreceptor when shear stress is applied to the vessel and transmitting the signal to intracellular organelles resulting in an alteration in vascular tone (Akira and Joji, 1993).

sections.text:
•	Atherosclerosis 
•	Thrombosis

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The subendothelial layer is a middle, fibrous layer of the tunica intima of typical blood vessels, located between the endothelium and internal elastic membrane; it also comprises the bulk of the endocardium, where it lies deep to the lining endothelium. It is composed of varying amounts of collagen and elastic fibers and smooth muscle cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The subendothelial layer is a thin layer consisting of a single layer of loose connective tissue. This layer also contains some elastic fibers, collagen type I fibrils, fibroblasts, and small smooth muscle cells.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The subendothelial layer lies between the endothelium and internal elastic lamina in the tunica interna of blood vessels.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Cells of the subendothelial layer are contractile, but they also secrete ground substance (an amorphous jelly-like material containing proteoglycans), collagen, and elastic fibers, which assists in compliance of the vessel wall. In addition, macrophages are occasionally present in this layer, scavenging for foreign material and dead cells (Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A venous valve is any of the small cusps or folds found in the tunica intima of many veins, serving to prevent backflow of blood (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
Venous valves are unidirectional, i.e., they open in one direction only, projections found inside veins. When blood flows along a vein it pushes the valve open, the valve then closes to prevent the backflow of the blood. 

Intravenous valves are formed by an inward projection of the tunica interna which is strengthened by collagen and elastic fibers and covered by endothelial cells.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The number of valves in a vein differs depending on the size of the blood vessel, one, two, or occasionally three valves are seen to lie opposite one another.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Venous valves play a vital role in keeping blood moving in one direction, while working against gravity, to ensure venous return.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
•	Peripheral Venous Disease
•	Varicose Veins

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The tunica externa of a blood vessel is the outer, fibroelastic coat of vessels, usually in contact with surrounding tissues (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The walls of blood vessels consist of three main layers:
•	the inner layer, the tunica interna (or intima)
•	the middle layer, the tunica media
•	the outer layer, the tunica externa (or adventitia).

Recent studies have suggested that the tissue arrangement of tunica externa is not a densely packed wall-like structure, commonly seen in alcohol fixed tissue. In fact, it is composed of a collagen lattice surrounded by fluid filled interstitial spaces (Benias et al., 2018). This has also been described in other tissues, such as lung, renal, dermis, and fascia.

The tunica externa possesses its own network of smaller blood vessels, known as the vasa vasorum, which provide the blood vessel with the molecules and nutrients necessary for cellular activity (Pawlina, 2016). Along with this small network of supportive blood vessels, the tunica externa is innervated by unmyelinated autonomic nerve fibers, the nervi vasorum (Mescher, 2013). The nervi vasorum are efferent autonomic fibers that play a role in vasodilation and vasoconstriction. 

The tunica externa of elastic arteries is relatively thin and usually less than half the thickness of the tunica media. It is primarily composed of thick bundles of collagen running in a circular manner. Elastin in this layer forms a loose network and is not well organized like that seen in the tunica media.

In muscular arteries, the tunica externa is a relatively thick (about the same thickness as the tunica media) collagenous tissue and often separated from the tunica media by a discernable external elastic membrane. 

In arterioles, the tunica externa is thin and poorly defined with loosely arranged elastin and collagen. It blends with the surrounding connective tissue the vessels travel within.
 
The tunica externa is the most prominent part of veins. In medium veins, the externa is almost entirely collagenous, but also contains longitudinally arranged smooth muscle. In large veins, the tunica externa is the thickest layer and is composed mainly of longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle surrounded by collagenous connective tissue. The tunica externa of postcapillary venules is absent but is thicker than the media in typical (muscular) venules,

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The tunica externa is the outermost layer of the blood vessel. It surrounds the tunica media.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The tunica externa acts as an anchor, securing the blood vessel to the surrounding body tissue.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The tunica media a blood vessel is made up of transverse elastic fibers and smooth muscle cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The walls of blood vessels consist of three main layers:
•	the inner layer, the tunica interna (or intima)
•	the middle layer, the tunica media
•	the outer layer, the tunica externa (or adventitia).

The tunica media is generally the largest layer within arteries and much thinner in corresponding veins.

The tunica media of elastic arteries is modified by having multiple concentric, fenestrated elastic laminae wrapped around the vessel. The fenestrations allow nutrients to pass to the cells buried deep within the arteries walls. Smooth muscle cells are interspersed between the elastic laminae and synthesize and secrete collagen and elastin. 

The tunica media is the thickest layer of muscular arteries and is dominated by concentric layers of smooth muscle, with a small number of thin elastic sheets and collagen fibers between them. 

The tunica media of arterioles and venules contain one or two layers of helically arranged smooth muscle. 

The tunica media of the good-sized medium veins (such as the brachial or basilic veins) has significant amounts of smooth muscle separated by sheets of collagen, although it’s much thinner than a corresponding muscular artery.

The tunica media of large veins is not well developed and is relatively narrow. The presence of circumferentially arranged smooth muscle in this layer depends on the location of the vein, e.g., uterine veins have several layers of smooth muscle, while retinal veins have none (Ovalle and Nahirney, 2021).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The tunica media separates the tunica interna from the tunica externa. In arteries, the external elastic membrane separates the tunica media from the tunica externa, while the internal elastic membrane divides the tunica media from the tunica interna.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The mechanical strength of the tunica media comes from structural collagen and smooth muscle. The smooth muscle coiled around the vessel can contract or relax, altering the diameter of the vessel’s lumen, which causes the lumen to decrease or increase. This is known as vasoconstriction and vasodilation, respectively.

The function of the tunica media of veins is distinctly different from that of arteries. Veins maintain the tone in their walls to regulate the volume of blood that is held in them. Veins can hold approximately 70% of the blood volume and can alter this reserve by contraction.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A capillary network is any of the minute vessels that connect the arterioles and venules, forming a network in nearly all parts of the body. Their walls act as semipermeable membranes for the interchange of various substances, including fluids, between the blood and tissue fluid. The two principal types are continuous and fenestrated capillaries (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
Capillary vessels form a vascular network known as capillary beds. These capillary networks supply all the body's organs and tissues in the form of an interlacing web of capillaries. Capillaries have only one layer, the tunica intima, consisting of endothelial cells and their basal lamina.

The tunica intima is made up of a single layer of endothelial cells, a very thin basal lamina, and scattered pericytes. The basal lamina provides support to the endothelial cells, while the pericytes provide contractility.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Extensive branching of capillary beds enables capillaries to be in contact with every cell. The rate of blood flow within a capillary bed is slow due to its highly branched nature. This slow blood flow, along with their very thin walls means that capillary beds are the ideal site for exchange of molecules.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The thin walls of capillaries allow for the exchange of gases, nutrients, hormones, and waste products between blood and tissue cells:

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates

- Age-related macular degeneration

- Coronary heart disease

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A venule is any of the small vessels that collect blood from the capillary plexuses and join to form veins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Venules have extremely thin walls, similar to that of capillaries, which give them a misshapen or flattened appearance in a cross-sectional view. 

There are two types of venules.
•	Postcapillary venules, which are found directly after capillary beds, are typically 10–30 μm in diameter, only slightly larger than that of capillaries (Standring, 2016). Postcapillary venules are composed of an endothelial layer and a basal lamina surrounded by a thin connective tissue layer in place of the tunica externa. 
•	True venules, also known as muscular venules, are typically distinguished from postcapillary venules where their diameter exceeds 50 μm and smooth muscle cells are found in their walls (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Venules receive blood from capillaries and deliver blood to medium veins. They often accompany arterioles.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
All venous vessels carry blood from body organs and tissues back to the heart. They typically transport deoxygenated blood, with the exception of the venules within the pulmonary circulation. These vessels are involved in the transportation oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart. 

As the postcapillary venules have a composition similar to that of capillaries, they may be involved in gas and solute exchange with surrounding tissues. The movement of leukocytes into extravascular spaces, also known as leukocyte migration, also occurs in postcapillary venules (Standring, 2016). 

Muscular venules are not involved in gas and solute exchange due to their more substantial wall thickness. Muscular venules will eventually merge and form veins, which will continue to carry blood back towards the heart. 

Because of the low levels of elastin fibers, lower mass of smooth muscle (in comparison to arteries), and relatively large lumen, venules and veins can be stretched and expanded (distensible). The distensibility of veins enables them to act as a blood reservoir, allowing storage of large volumes of blood. This can occur when blood returning to the heart is disrupted due to low pressure or compression.

sections.text:
•	Venous insufficiency
•	Deep vein thrombosis
•	Portal hypertension
•	Varicose veins

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The white matter is the nervous tissue of the brain and spinal cord composed mostly of myelinated nerve fibers arranged in bundles (fasciculi) (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The outer layer of each cerebral hemisphere is composed of a thin (2–4 mm) gray matter, or cerebral cortex, which overlies a thick mass of white matter, or cerebral medulla. Additionally, confined regions of gray matter are distributed between the white matter. These are known as the basal ganglia or basal nuclei. The white matter is devoid of neuronal cell bodies and consists of myelinated axons, non-myelinated axons and oligodendrocytes. The myelinated nerve fibers of the white matter differ, and can be classified into association, commissural, and projection fibers. 

Association fibers are either short or long nerve fibers that connect different cortical regions within the same hemisphere. 

Commissural fibers cross from one side of the central nervous system to the other, therefore, connecting corresponding gray matter areas of the right and left cerebral hemispheres. The largest commissural fiber is the corpus callosum which connects the right and left cerebral hemispheres. 

Projection fibers are nerve fibers that either ascend from caudal regions of the central nervous system towards the cerebral cortex or descend from the cerebral cortex to lower regions. The projection fibers deep to the cerebral white matter form a compact band which is known as the internal capsule. As these projection fibers emerge superior to the internal capsule, they run towards the cerebral cortex or away from it forming a bundle known as corona radiata.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The organization of white matter allows several areas of the cerebral cortex to communicate with the brainstem and the spinal cord. Commissural fibers connect corresponding gray matter areas of the right and left hemispheres and allows them to function together as a unit. Association fibers are responsible for connecting different parts of the same. Projection fibers are thought to be responsible for sensory information reaching the cerebral cortex.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Multiple Sclerosis

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The gray matter is the nervous tissue of the brain and spinal cord composed of nerve cell bodies, unmyelinated nerve processes, and glia (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The outer layer of each cerebral hemisphere is composed of a thin (2–4 mm) gray matter, or cerebral cortex, which overlies a thick mass of white matter, or cerebral medulla. Additionally, confined regions of gray matter are distributed between the white matter. These are known as the basal ganglia or basal nuclei. The gray matter consists of neuronal cell bodies, neuronal dendrites, axons, and neuroglia (neuronal supporting cells). Synapses between neurons occur in the gray matter (Pawlina, 2016).

The gray matter of the cerebral cortex consists of different cell types and it is therefore divided in six layers. 

—The first and most superficial layer of the gray matter of the cerebral cortex is the molecular layer (or plexiform layer). It contains predominantly of neuroglial cells which maintain homeostasis, protect and support neurons, and form myelin. Additionally, Cajal cells are found in this layer. A great number of synapses between different neurons occur in this layer. 

—The second layer is the external granular layer, which contains various types of neuroglial cells and small pyramidal cells. 

—The third layer is the external pyramidal layer which constitutes mainly of medium-sized pyramidal cells. 

—The fourth layer is the internal granular layer. This layer is thin and consists of small granule cells, pyramidal cells, and neuroglia. 

—The fifth layer is the internal pyramidal layer and consists of neuroglia and large pyramidal cells. 

—The sixth and deepest layer is the multiform layer, or polymorphic layer, and consists of intermixed cells that vary in size and shape. The cells that make up this layer are the fusiform cells, stellate cells, and cells of Martinotti (Eroschenko, 2008).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The gray matter possesses most of the cell bodies of the neurons in the brain; therefore, the gray matter is involved in sensory perception and voluntary motor function, as well as integrating diverse information and allowing purposeful action.

—Alzheimer’s disease

—Dementia

—Parkinson’s disease

sections.text: The falx cerebri is the sickle-shaped fold of dura mater that extends downward in the longitudinal cerebral fissure and separates the two cerebral hemispheres (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: The falx cerebri is a large fold of the meningeal cranial dura mater that projects down into the longitudinal fissure, separating the left and right cerebral hemispheres.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The falx cerebri is the largest fold of meningeal dura mater in the cranium. It runs from the crista galli of the ethmoid bone anteriorly, back to the straight sinus and tentorium cerebelli posteriorly. Its superior margin forms the superior sagittal sinus while its inferior margin lie just above the corpus callosum and contains the inferior sagittal sinus.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cranial dura matter has a deep meningeal layer adjacent to the arachnoid and a superficial periosteal layer adjacent to the cranium. The periosteal dura is firmly adhered to the meningeal dura in most places, except when they come apart at the dural venous sinuses.

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The periosteal cranial dura mater is the superficial layer of cranial dura. It is superficial to the meningeal dura and deep to the inner compact layer of bone making up the cranium. The internal surface of the cranium does not exhibit a periosteum, instead the outer layer of dura acts as this periosteum, hence the name. 

The periosteal dura is firmly adhered to the meningeal dura in most places, except when they come apart at the dural venous sinuses. This thick fibrous material blends with the bone at the foramina on the basal surface of the skull and is firmly adhered to the sutures between bones. 

A number of small vessels exist within the dura, the meningeal vessels. If these vessels rupture due to trauma, blood will accumulate in the space between the periosteal dura and the calvaria, the epidural space. The accumulation of blood during epidural hemorrhage is limited to the spaces between the sutures, as the periosteal dura is firmly adhered to the bone here, thus on CT and MRI it presents as a convex lesion.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The periosteal cranial dura mater is adherent to the inner surface of the cranial bones, especially along the sutures and foramina. It is continuous with the pericranium, covering the outer surfaces of the cranial bones, through the cranial sutures and the foramina. Additionally, it is continuous with the periosteum of the orbit via the superior orbital fissure.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cranial dura matter has a deep meningeal layer adjacent to the arachnoid and a superficial periosteal layer adjacent to the cranium. The periosteal dura is firmly adhered to the meningeal dura in most places, except when they come apart at the dural venous sinuses.

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The meningeal cranial dura mater is the deep layer of cranial dura mater. It lies superficial to the arachnoid, to which it has a close anatomical relationship. It is firmly adhered to the periosteal layer of dura mater in most places within the cranium, except surrounding the dural venous sinuses, where they diverge to enclose the vessel. 

The meningeal dura mater is penetrated by arachnoid granulations and cerebral vessels, both of reach into the venous sinuses allowing for the movement of CSF and blood respectively.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The meningeal cranial dura mater is closely applied to the arachnoid. Additionally, it surrounds and fuses with the epineurium of each cranial nerve as they exit their designated cranial foramen. The meningeal cranial dura also fuses with the outer adventitia of major vessels, e.g., the internal carotid artery, when it enters the cranial cavity.

Even though the meningeal cranial dura mater is not in close contact with the brain, it reflects inward at certain points known as dural folds. The first is the falx cerebri in which the meningeal dura runs within the longitudinal fissure separating the two cerebral hemispheres. The second is the tentorium cerebelli, a dural fold that separates the cerebellum below from the cerebrum above. A third fold, the falx cerebelli, runs perpendicular to the tentorium cerebelli and separates the two cerebellar hemispheres. Lastly, the diaphragma sellae surrounds the pituitary stalk.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cranial arachnoid is the arachnoid covering the brain; it is a delicate membrane interposed between the dura mater and the pia mater, separated from the pia mater by the subarachnoid space (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: The arachnoid mater is the middle of the three meningeal layers. It is a thin opaque layer that sends wispy fibers, or trabeculations, inward to the pia mater, forming the spider web appearance that gives the arachnoid mater its name. Where it overlies a dural venous sinus, the arachnoid mater can develop arachnoid granulations, extensions of the arachnoid that pierce the dura and allow cerebrospinal fluid to be absorbed into the venous sinuses from the subarachnoid space. The cranial arachnoid mater is similar in function and appearance to the spinal arachnoid mater.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The arachnoid mater lies against the dura mater, being held away from the brain and pia mater by the presence of cerebrospinal fluid. This space found between the pia and the arachnoid mater is the subarachnoid space and contains cerebrospinal fluid.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cerebrospinal fluid is the fluid contained within the four ventricles of the brain, the subarachnoid space, and the central canal of the spinal cord; formed by choroid plexuses, it circulates through the ventricles into the subarachnoid space and is absorbed into the venous system (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Composition
sections.text:
The cerebrospinal fluid is a colorless fluid that contains little protein and a few cells and is different from the electrolyte composition of the blood plasma. The cerebrospinal fluid is produced by choroidal epithelial cells, which are modified ependymal cells found in the choroid plexuses. The choroid plexus is formed by small vascular extensions of dilated, fenestrated capillaries that penetrate the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles of the brain (Eroschenko, 2008). The choroidal epithelial cells bear cilia which facilitate the circulation of the cerebrospinal fluid (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

The cerebrospinal fluid flows from the lateral ventricles to the third ventricle, passing through the interventricular foramina. It then passes through the cerebral aqueduct and enters the fourth ventricle. Some of the cerebrospinal fluid exits the fourth ventricle via median and lateral apertures to reach the subarachnoid space between the pia and arachnoid mater.

The cerebrospinal fluid is continuously reabsorbed from the subarachnoid space into the venous system via the arachnoid granulations, which are knob-like prolongations of the arachnoid. Arachnoid granulations protruding into the superior sagittal sinus and its lateral lacunae are the main sites of absorption of the cerebrospinal fluid. The cerebrospinal fluid enters the venous system either by being transported by cells of the arachnoid granulations or by moving between the cells that make up the arachnoid granulations (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

The total volume of the cerebrospinal fluid in an adult ranges from 140 to 270 ml, with around 0.2-0.7 ml added per minute (Standring, 2016). With this rapid production rate, cerebrospinal fluid is replaced around four times a day.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The cerebrospinal fluid protects the brain by acting as a cushion to blows that are applied to the head. Cerebrospinal fluid in the subarachnoid space also prevents the weight of the brain compressing the roots of the cranial nerves and the internal surface of the cranium compressing the blood vessels (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012; Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

The cerebrospinal fluid is important for homeostasis and brain metabolism. It provides the brain with nutrients and removes metabolites. It also provides the appropriate chemical environment for neurons to function properly and nerve impulses to conduct efficiently (Eroschenko, 2008).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The arachnoid granulations are small elevations, visible to the naked eye, which project into the superior sagittal sinus and associated venous lacunae and create slight depressions on the inner surface of the cranium; these granulations are the structures through which cerebrospinal fluid is reabsorbed into the venous system (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: Arachnoid villi or granulations are out pockets of the arachnoid that protrude into the dura mater and into the dural venous sinuses. They are commonly found in the superior sagittal sinus and lateral lacunae; however, they are also found in the transverse, straight, and superior petrosal sinuses (Standring, 2016). Large accumulations of granulations may cause an impression on the overlying bone, forming indentations on the internal surface of the calvaria, known as granular foveolae (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Arachnoid granulations allow transport of cerebrospinal fluid from the subarachnoid space into the venous system.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The epicranial aponeurosis is the aponeurotic layer of the scalp; the central tendon of the epicranius muscle, connecting the frontal and occipital bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle, and the temporoparietalis muscles (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The epicranial aponeurosis is the third layer of the scalp and the strongest. It is a thin (approximately 0.5 mm), broad, and strong tendinous sheet that serves as an intermediate tendon between the occipital and frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2015). 

The epicranial aponeurosis is tightly bound to the overlying skin via a fibrous subcutaneous tissue. However, it is loosely connected to the underlying pericranium, thus allowing it to move freely, while carrying the skin with it.

Deep lacerations, or cuts, to the scalp can result in continuous bleeding. This is because the underlying epicranial aponeurosis is abundant in elastic fibers, which prevents the vessels in the overlying superficial fascia from retracting.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The epicranial aponeurosis is internal to the dense superficial fascia of the scalp and external to the loose connective tissue of the scalp. 

Posteriorly, it blends with the occipital belly of the occipitofrontalis to insert into the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone. Anteriorly, it is continuous with the frontal portion of the occipitofrontalis muscle and blends with the eyebrows. Laterally, it blends with the temporalis fascia, as well as the anterior and superior auricular muscles and the temporoparietalis muscle. 

The subaponeurotic space, or “danger space,” is a potential space deep to the epicranial aponeurosis. This space contains the loose connective tissue and the emissary veins that link the intracranial dural sinuses with the extracranial veins. Thus, localized infections within this space have the potential to spread intracranially. The subaponeurotic space is limited anteriorly by the frontal belly and posteriorly by the occipital belly of the occipitofrontalis muscle.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The epicranial aponeurosis serves as a site of origin for the frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle and a site of insertion for the occipital muscles of the occipitofrontalis muscle. Additionally, it is loosely connected to the underlying loose connective tissue; thus it can move over it freely, carrying the skin and subcutaneous tissue.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The subcutaneous tissue is the layer of loose connective tissue situated just beneath the skin (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The subcutaneous tissue, or superficial fascia, of the scalp is composed of a dense connective tissue. It contains adipose tissue that is separated by fibrous septae. The thickness of the superficial fascia decreases with age (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2015). 

The subcutaneous tissue is the most vascularized region of the scalp and contains many anastomosing arteries, veins, and lymphatic vessels. The vessels are attached to the fibrous connective tissue, thus, if a vessel is cut, the ends become retracted between the fibrous septae and may lead to profuse bleeding (Ellis and Mahadevan, 2014).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The subcutaneous tissue of the scalp lies below the skin to which it is firmly attached. It also attaches to the occipitofrontalis muscle and epicranial aponeurosis internally. Posteriorly, it is continuous with the subcutaneous tissue that covers the back of the neck. Laterally, the subcutaneous tissue of the scalp is continuous with the subcutaneous tissue overlying the temporal region.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The subcutaneous tissue possesses fibers that join the skin of the scalp with the epicranial aponeurosis.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The pericranium is the external periosteum of the skull (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The pericranium, also known as the periosteum of the skull, is the fifth and deepest layer of the scalp. The pericranium is a dense fibrous membrane covering the neurocranium. The outer surface of the pericranium is loosely attached to the epicranial aponeurosis via the loose connective tissue. The inner surface of the pericranium firmly attaches to the calvaria. Due to its elasticity, it can be easily removed from the calvaria except at the location of the suture lines where it is firmly attached. The pericranium is generally thin at the frontal area and thicker at the posterior aspect of the skull (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2015). 

The pericranium is supplied by the supraorbital and supratrochlear (arising from the internal carotid artery) and the superficial temporal artery (arising from the external carotid artery) (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2014).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The pericranium is the deepest layer of the scalp. It is deep to the loose connective tissue of the scalp and superficial to the cranial bone. It is continuous with the deep temporal fascia at the superior temporal line (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2015).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The pericranium provides structural support and a minimal blood supply to the underlying cranium (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2015). It is also important during bone growth and remodeling following fracture as it supplies cells with nutrients required for bone formation (Kierszenbaum, 2007).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Loose connective tissue is a type of connective tissue in which the interlacing collagen and elastin fibers are not tightly packed; it provides connections between adjacent structures but allows them to move independently; it also has a greater density of cells and vessels than dense connective tissue (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The loose connective tissue is the fourth layer of the scalp. It is composed of a thin layer of loose fibroareolar tissue that contains a network of reticular and elastic fibers and collagen. It is loosely bound to the overlying epicranial aponeurosis, which accounts for the mobility of the scalp over the underlying calvaria.

Emissary veins traverse the loose connective tissue layer of the scalp and, along with the diploic veins, connect the intracranial dural sinuses with the extracranial veins. The loose connective tissue is often called the subaponeurotic space, or “danger space,” since localized infections within this layer have the potential to spread intracranially (Thompson and Yeung, 2016). The subaponeurotic space is limited anteriorly by the frontal belly and posteriorly by the occipital belly of the occipitofrontalis muscle.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The loose connective tissue of the scalp separated the epicranial aponeurosis from the pericranium of the calvaria.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The loose connective tissue of the scalp allows the scalp proper (the skin, superficial fascia, and epicranial aponeurosis) to glide over the calvaria.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Scalp lacerations

—Scalp infections

—Subgaleal hemorrhage

—Osteomyelitis

—Brain abscess

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The skin is the outer integument or covering of the body, consisting of the dermis and epidermis, and resting upon the subcutaneous tissue (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The skin forms the outermost layer of the scalp and is relatively thick, measuring approximately 3 mm (vertex) to 8 mm (occiput) in thickness (Brennan, Mahadevan and Evans, 2015).

The skin of the scalp resembles skin covering the rest of the body and is composed of an epidermis and dermis, with an underlying superficial fascia. The epidermis is the outermost layer of the skin and is composed of a stratified squamous keratinized epithelium. The dermis is the layer of skin found deep to the epidermis and contains the skin appendages, such as hair follicles, sweat glands, and sebaceous glands. 

The superficial fascia that lies beneath the dermis and forms the second layer of the scalp is often considered part of the skin, since they are difficult to separate during surgery.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The skin is the most superficial layer of the scalp. It is adjacent to the dense connective tissue of the superficial fascia.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
In general, the skin functions as a barrier against the external environment, such as harmful microbial organisms and damage from mechanical, chemical, thermal, and UV stimuli. The skin also performs an important endocrine function, such as Vitamin D formation and synthesis of cytokines and growth factors. The skin is also involved in excretion, through the secretion of sweat and sebum. 

The skin is important in maintaining homeostasis by controlling the body's temperature and water loss. During thermoregulation, sweating first occurs on the forehead and scalp (Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cranium is the large round superior part of the skull; it encloses the brain, forms the skeleton of the midface, and is made up of the cranial bones held together by sutures, synchondroses, and bony unions (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The bones that make up the neurocranium, the portion of the cranium that houses the brain, are the frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, ethmoid, and sphenoid bones. The cranial bones are considered flat bones derived from the mesenchyme and develop by intramembranous and endochondral ossification. The bones contain a thin inner and outer layer of compact bone, separated by cancellous bone, known as diploë. The inner layer of compact bone is thinner and more brittle than its external layer (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013; Snell, 2011).

The frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital bones make up the calvaria, which is covered by the scalp. The scalp attaches to the calvaria via the pericranium. The outer surface of the pericranium is loosely fused with the epicranial aponeurosis of the scalp via a loose connective tissue. The inner surface of the pericranium firmly attaches to the calvaria. Due to its elasticity, the pericranium can be easily removed from the calvaria, except at the location of the suture lines where it is firmly attached.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The cranial bone is located deep to the scalp and superficial to the meninges and brain parenchyma.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The cranial bones protect the brain within the cranial vault.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Skull fracture

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The lateral lacunae are venous meshworks within the dura mater on either side of, and continuous with, the superior sagittal sinus; arachnoidal granulations project into them (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Description
sections.text:
There are usually three irregularly shaped venous spaces, or lacunae, present inside the dura mater, on either side of the superior sagittal sinus. They can be considered as the lateral extensions of the sinus. These include a small frontal, large parietal, and intermediate occipital lacunae. The venous lacunae could potentially become confluent with age and form large single spaces on either side of the superior sagittal sinus. 

Most of the cerebral veins open into the venous lacunae and numerous arachnoid granulations project into them from below. The venous lacunae also drain diploid, emissary, and meningeal veins.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text:
Origin: Formed by union of tiny meningeal veins at the crista galli.

Course: Runs backwards within the attached upper margin of the falx cerebrum, from crista galli (anteriorly) to the confluence of sinuses (posteriorly).

Tributaries: Communications with the veins of the frontal sinus, veins of the nose (via foramen cecum), the superior cerebral veins, parietal emissary veins, and venous lacunae. 

Drainage: Anterior cerebral hemispheres.

sections.name: Origin
sections.text: The superior sagittal sinus begins at the crista galli, formed by the union of small meningeal veins.

sections.name: Course
sections.text: The superior sagittal sinus lies within the upper fixed convex margin of the falx cerebrum. It courses in the midline in a shallow groove on the inner aspect of the cranium and grows in caliber as it continues posteriorly. The sinus extends backwards from the crista galli to the confluence of sinuses where it usually turns to the right side to become continuous with the right transverse sinus (Pamir, Black and Fahlbusch, 2010).

sections.name: Tributaries
sections.text: The superior sagittal sinus communicates anteriorly at the crista galli with the veins of the frontal sinus and nose (via foramen cecum). The sinus has additional connections with the superior cerebral veins, parietal emissary veins, and venous lacunae.

sections.name: Structures Drained
sections.text: Lying along the sagittal groove, the superior sagittal sinus drains lateral aspects of the anterior cerebrum into the confluence of the sinuses.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The diploic veins are veins of the skull, including the frontal, occipital, anterior temporal, and posterior temporal diploic veins, that form sinuses in the cancellous tissue between the laminae of the cranial bones. They send branches to the external and the internal lamina, the periosteum, and the dura mater, and empty in part inside and in part outside the skull, communicating with meningeal veins, dural sinuses, pericranial veins, and each other (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cerebral arteries are the arteries supplying the cerebral hemispheres, derived from the internal carotid artery (anterior choroid, anterior cerebral, middle cerebral, and posterior communicating arteries and the circle of Willis) or from the basilar artery (posterior cerebral artery) (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The anterior and middle cerebral arteries are terminal branches of the internal carotid arteries and supply more than 80% of the cerebrum. 

The anterior cerebral arteries anastomose via the anterior communicating artery and supply the superior and medial surfaces of the frontal and parietal lobes. 

The middle cerebral artery is the largest branch of the internal carotid artery. It passes through the lateral sulcus of each hemisphere to supply lateral parts of the parietal and temporal lobes. 

The basilar artery, formed by the union of the right and left vertebral arteries, divides into posterior cerebral arteries. They supply the occipital lobes and the inferomedial temporal lobes. They are connected to the middle cerebral arteries by two short posterior communicating arteries (Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The cerebral arteries provide blood to the brain.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Ischemic or hemorrhagic Stroke

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The arteries that supply the scalp are located in the subcutaneous tissue and form an anastomosing network.

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: The scalp has a particularly rich blood supply, with vessels located in the dense subcutaneous tissue. Branches of the external carotid artery supplying the scalp include the occipital, posterior auricular, and superficial temporal arteries. Branches of the internal carotid artery include the supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The arteries of the scalp course through the subcutaneous tissue. These arteries form an anastomosing network with adjacent and contralateral arteries. The arteries are attached to the fibrous connective tissue of the subcutaneous tissue, thus, if a vessel is cut, the ends become retracted between the fibrous septae which may lead to profuse bleeding (Ellis and Mahadevan, 2014).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The arteries of the scalp provide blood to the five layers of the scalp.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The emissary vein is one of the small, valveless veins that pass through foramina of the skull, connecting the dural venous sinuses with scalp veins or with deep veins below the base of the skull (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cerebral veins are veins that drain the surfaces or inner regions of the cerebral hemispheres; they are divided into superficial and deep groups (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
The cerebral veins that drain venous blood from the brain are classified into superficial and deep veins. They are valveless, possess thin walls, and lack muscular tissue. Cerebral veins and venules in the cerebral cortex or white matter have a larger lumen and thin walls compared to the cerebral arterioles which are surrounded by smooth muscle (Standring, 2016; Snell, 2010).

Cerebral veins pierce the arachnoid and meningeal layer of dura and terminate in the nearest dural venous sinus.

The superficial cerebral veins have thin walls and their external surface area is covered by a single layer of meningeal cells. They are divided into three groups which are the superior, middle, and inferior cerebral veins.

The superior cerebral veins drain the superolateral and medial surfaces of each hemisphere of the brain and eventually open into the superior sagittal sinus. The lateral portion of each hemisphere is drained by the middle cerebral vein which ends in the cavernous sinus.

The inferior cerebral veins on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe join the superior cerebral veins and drain into the superior sagittal sinus. The inferior cerebral veins on the temporal lobe anastomose with the middle cerebral veins and drain into the transverse, superior petrosal, and cavernous sinuses (Standring, 2016).

Deep structures of the brain, such as the thalamus, are drained by internal cerebral veins. These veins unite, forming the great cerebral vein, which drains into the straight sinus.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Cerebral veins end in the nearest dural venous sinuses.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The cerebral veins drain the cerebrum.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The veins of the scalp are located in the subcutaneous tissue and largely follow the course of the arteries.

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: The scalp has a particularly rich blood supply, with vessels located in the dense subcutaneous tissue. The venous drainage of the anterior scalp is via the supraorbital and supratrochlear veins. The scalp anterior to the auricles is drained by the superficial temporal veins, while the scalp posterior to the auricles is drained by the posterior auricular veins. The occipital region of the scalp is drained by the occipital veins. The deep parts of the scalp in the temporal region are drained by the deep temporal veins (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The veins that drain the scalp generally accompany the arteries. The supraorbital and supratrochlear veins terminate by forming the angular vein at the root of the nose. The superficial temporal veins terminate by joining the maxillary veins to form the retromandibular veins. The posterior auricular veins descend behind the auricle and unite with the posterior division of the retromandibular vein, thus forming the external jugular vein. The deep temporal veins are tributaries of the pterygoid venous plexus which is drained by the deep facial vein. Tributaries of the external jugular veins drain the scalp posteriorly and laterally.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The veins of the scalp drain blood from the scalp.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries supply the suprarenal gland.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features:
sections.text: Despite their small size, the suprarenal glands are one of the most extensively vascularized organs. They have a well-established arterial supply via the superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries. These arteries arise from the inferior phrenic artery, abdominal aorta, and renal artery, respectively.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries provide the main vascular supply to the suprarenal gland.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The medullary venous sinus is formed by the convergence of medullary cortical sinusoids and the medullary artery. They merge with the central veins.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features:
sections.text: The medullary venous sinus is formed by the convergence of medullary cortical sinusoids and the medullary artery. The venous sinuses pass among the chromaffin cells in the medullary tissue. They go on to merge with the central veins, carrying the secreted hormones in the blood from the various suprarenal regions. At the hilum, the central veins emerge as the left and right suprarenal veins, which empty into the left renal vein on the left, and the inferior vena cava on the right (Inomata and Sasano, 2015).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The medullary venous sinus transports the secreted hormones of the suprarenal gland to the systemic circulation.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Inomata, A. & Sasano, H. (2015) Practical approaches for evaluating adrenal toxicity in nonclinical safety assessment. J Toxicol Pathol, 28(3), 125-32.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The medullary arteries are arteries that arise from the subcapsular arterial plexus. They pass through the cortex to reach the medulla, without providing any branches to the cortex. They join the medullary venous sinus.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features:
sections.text: The medullary arteries are one set of arteries that arise from the subcapsular arterial plexus. They are longitudinal vessels that pass through the zones of the cortex, with the trabeculae, or the inward projections of the capsule, to reach the medulla, without providing any branches to the cortex. They join the medullary venous sinus in the medulla of the suprarenal gland. Therefore, the medullary arteries, together with the cortical sinusoids, provide a dual blood supply to the medulla (Inomata & Sasano, 2015).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The dual blood supply to the medulla of the suprarenal gland is vital for the rapid transport of both glucocorticoids and enriched blood to the medulla, required in response to stress (Inomata & Sasano, 2015).

sections.name: References
sections.text: Inomata, A. & Sasano, H. (2015) Practical approaches for evaluating adrenal toxicity in nonclinical safety assessment. J Toxicol Pathol, 28(3), 125-32.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features:
sections.text: The cortical sinusoids are one set of arteries that arise from the subcapsular arterial plexus. They form an established, convoluted network among the cortex, which ensures a rich arterial supply to the tissue. As the capillaries penetrate deeper, they begin to coalesce and form an arterial plexus deep within the zona reticularis and medullary tissue.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The cortical sinusoids ensure adequate perfusion of blood to the cortex and medulla of the suprarenal glands.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The suprarenal arteries give rise to the subcapsular arterial plexus, which supplies the cortical and medullary tissue.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
Despite their small size, the suprarenal glands are one of the most extensively vascularized organs. They have a well-established arterial supply via the superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries, which emerge from the inferior phrenic artery, the abdominal aorta, and the renal artery, respectively. 

The suprarenal arteries give rise to the subcapsular arterial plexus, which supplies the cortical and medullary tissue. In fact, three sets of arteries arise from the subcapsular plexus. 

—One set directly supplies the fibrous capsule surrounding the suprarenal gland. 

—The second set of arteries are the cortical sinusoids, which project into the zona glomerulosa and fasciculata and form a dense capillary network as they reach the zona reticularis before entering the medulla. 

—The third set of arteries are the medullary arteries. These do not supply the zones of the cortex. Instead, they travel with the trabeculae, or the inward projections of the capsule, to supply blood to the medulla only (Inomata and Sasano, 2015).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The subcapsular arterial plexus ensures adequate perfusion of blood to the fibrous tissue, cortex, and medulla of the suprarenal glands.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Inomata, A. & Sasano, H. (2015) Practical approaches for evaluating adrenal toxicity in nonclinical safety assessment. J Toxicol Pathol, 28(3), 125-32.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The central vein is the large single vein into which the various veins within the substance of the gland empty, and which continues at the hilum as the suprarenal vein (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features:
sections.text: The central veins travel to the hilum, carrying the secreted hormones from the various suprarenal regions. At the hilum, the medullary vein emerges as the left and right suprarenal veins, which empty into the left renal vein on the left, and the inferior vena cava on the right.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The central veins transport the secreted hormones of the suprarenal gland to the systemic circulation.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The perirenal fat capsule is the investment of fat surrounding the fibrous capsule of the kidney and continuous at the hilum with the fat in the renal sinus (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The perirenal fat is composed of adipose tissue that surrounds the kidneys and the suprarenal glands. It envelopes the fibrous capsules and is held tight around the organs via the renal fascia (Gerota’s fascia). This fat is typically more solid than normal fat.

In neonates, the perirenal fat capsule has a brown appearance due to the number of iron-containing mitochondria. However, the brown adipose tissue is thought to diminish gradually over the first ten years of life (Cantisani et al, 2003).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The perirenal fat capsule is superjacent to the capsule of the suprarenal gland and kidney and is subjacent to the renal fascia (Gerota’s fascia) which tightly wraps it around the organs.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The perirenal fat capsule serves numerous functions. It provides both protection and structural support to the kidneys and suprarenal glands, by stabilizing their anatomical position. Its primary function is yet to be fully elucidated but is thought to play a role in thermoregulation; generating heat via non-shivering thermogenesis due to its rich vascular supply.

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Nephroptosis

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A suprarenal capsule encloses the suprarenal gland.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The capsule of the suprarenal gland is composed of a single layer of thick fibrous tissue which envelopes the whole gland, providing numerous supportive and protective features. It is derived from mesenchymal cells (Vidal et al, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The capsule of the suprarenal gland is covered with perirenal fat, which is enclosed within the renal fascia. These capsulated glands lie on the anterior superomedial aspect of the kidneys. The capsule of the suprarenal gland is separated from the kidney via a thin fibrous layer along the inferior aspect of the capsule.

Superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries approach and branch out over the capsule. They form a subcapsular meshwork of vessels which provide an arterial supply to the gland.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
While the capsule of the suprarenal gland offers structural and protective support to the glands, it also houses a dense arterial plexus within it. Projections of the capsule, called trabeculae, penetrate throughout the gland, and provide passage of the long sinusoids of the arterial plexus deep into gland tissue, providing a plentiful blood supply. The glands require this dense bloody supply due to the production of important hormones.

Another important role of the capsule is to aid the upkeep and repair of the cells throughout the gland. There is a reserve pool of progenitor stem cells within the capsule. These can differentiate to restore senescent cells, and to maintain or expand the three different zones of the cortex (Pihlajoki et al, 2015).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The medulla of suprarenal gland is the inner, reddish brown, soft part of the suprarenal gland; it synthesizes, stores, and releases catecholamines (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The medulla of the suprarenal gland forms the inner layer of the gland. There are no different morphological zones within the tissue, unlike the cortex of the suprarenal gland. The medulla is dark red/gray and is derived from neuroectoderm.

The medulla comprised of small assemblies and pillars of chromaffin cells (pheochromocytes) which line the venous sinuses. These chromaffin cells are part of the neuroendocrine system and are comparable to postganglionic sympathetic neurons. They synthesize, store, and secrete catecholamines into the bloodstream. Storage occurs by packing the catecholamines into granules by chromogranin proteins. Essentially, the medulla is a large sympathetic ganglion, which releases catecholamines into circulation. Secretion of medullary catecholamines occurs largely in response to sympathetic stimulation via splanchnic nerve activity, and a variety of physiological and emotional stresses.

The medulla has a dual blood supply. It is supplied by arterial sinusoids which perfuse the suprarenal cortex. It is also supplied by direct branches from the capsular plexus, the medullary arteries, penetrating deep into the medullary tissue without branching. The medulla is drained by medullary veins, which form the suprarenal veins at the hilum of the suprarenal gland. Lymph is drained to the hilum, where lymph vessels transport lymph to the lateral aortic lymph nodes.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations:
sections.text: The suprarenal medulla forms the inner part of the suprarenal gland. It is subjacent to the suprarenal cortex.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The primary function of the suprarenal medulla is the secretion of catecholamines into the venous sinuses. They have a variety of bodily functions, including increasing heart rate and blood pressure. Of note, norepinephrine increases diastolic pressure, while epinephrine reduces the diastolic pressure on account of its vasodilatory effects within skeletal muscle.

The mechanism of releases is exocytosis of granule-containing catecholamines in response to depolarization of the chromaffin cells via sympathetic activation. Epinephrine is the majority of secretions (around 80%), with norepinephrine being the minority (around 20%). The release of the catecholamines is mediated by splanchnic nerve activity. They are also secreted in response to physiological stresses such as hypoglycemia, hypotension, hemorrhage, and to emotional stresses including fear, anger, and sexual arousal.

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Pheochromocytoma

—Von Hippel-Lindau disease

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The zona fasciculata is the thick middle layer of the suprarenal cortex; it is the major source of glucocorticoids (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The cortex of the suprarenal gland is comprised of three distinct morphological zones, the zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and the zona reticularis. These lie above the medulla of the suprarenal gland. The zona fasciculata is the large zone of the suprarenal cortex and composes nearly 75% of the cortical mass. 

The zona fasciculata is made of cells which are large and polyhedral. These are aligned together to form linear columns, which run the depth of the zona fasciculata. Long sinusoids from the capsular plexus travel alongside these cellular columns, supplying the cortex throughout. The sinusoidal paths end as they come together in the zona reticularis to form a vascular network.

Inside the cells of the zona fasciculata, prominent organelles include a large amount of smooth endoplasmic reticulum present in the basophilic cytoplasm, as well as a large number of lipid droplets. These store cholesterol, the main precursor of steroid biosynthesis. These are important organelles as they relate to the cell’s primary function (Pocock, Richards and Richards, 2013).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The zona fasciculata is the intermediate layer of the suprarenal cortex, surrounding by the zona glomerulosa on the outside and the zona reticularis on the inside.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The primary function of the cortex is to produce steroid hormones. In particular, the zona fasciculata secretes glucocorticoids, such as cortisol. These glucocorticoids are involved in, anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive processes. They also have a physiological role in the metabolism of carbohydrates and proteins.

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Cushing’s syndrome

sections.name: References
sections.text:

Pocock, G., Richards, C. D. & Richards, D. A. (2013) Human Physiology, 4 edition. OUP Oxford.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The zona reticularis is the inner layer of the suprarenal cortex, consisting of cells arranged as clearly anastomosing cords, and abutting the medulla (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features:
sections.text:
The cortex of the suprarenal gland is comprised of three distinct morphological zones, the zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and the zona reticularis. The zona reticularis is the innermost section of the suprarenal cortex. Unlike the other cortical regions, it does not differentiate completely until childhood. 

The zona reticularis is made of a network of cellular pillars interconnected with each other. The cells of this region contain numerous lysosomes to generate a cholesterol-rich supply. This lysosomal digestion process results in speckles of yellow-brown pigments within the cell (Pocock, Richards and Richards, 2013).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations:
sections.text:
The zona reticularis is the innermost layer of the suprarenal cortex and is contained between the zona fasciculata on the outside and the suprarenal medulla on the inside.

The long arterial sinusoids from the zona fasciculata form a fenestrated network of vessels to supply the zona reticularis tissue.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The primary function of the cortex is to produce steroid hormones. In particular, the zona reticularis secretes androgens, such as dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), its sulfated form DHEAS, and androstenedione. These are prohormones which must be converted to sex hormones in the gonads. In females, they are thought to contribute to the development of secondary sexual characteristics (Lois et al, 2014).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Precocious puberty

—Congenital suprarenal hyperplasia

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The zona glomerulosa is the thin outer layer of the suprarenal cortex, contiguous with the capsule; it is the source of aldosterone (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The cortex of the suprarenal gland is comprised of three distinct morphological zones, the zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and the zona reticularis. These lie above the medulla of the suprarenal gland. 

The zona glomerulosa is the outer zone of the cortex and comprises nearly 10% of the cortical mass. It consists of a thin area of small, polyhedral cells which are clumped together in groups. Inside each cell, prominent organelles include a large amount of smooth endoplasmic reticulum present in the basophilic cytoplasm, as well as a small number of lipid droplets. These store cholesterol, the main precursor of steroid biosynthesis. These are important organelles as they relate to the cell’s primary function (Pocock, Richards and Richards, 2013).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The zona glomerulosa is situated between the capsule and the zona fasciculata of the suprarenal gland. Numerous branches of the capsular plexus, situated just below the capsule, enter the zona glomerulosa to form an arterial network that extends through the cortex.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The primary function of the cortex is to produce steroid hormones. In particular, the zona glomerulosa secretes mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone, a component of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system (RAAS). These play a crucial role in maintaining blood pressure, blood volume, and electrolyte homeostasis (Bollag, 2014).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s syndrome, bilateral suprarenal hyperplasia)
