sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The transverse mesocolon is the fold of peritoneum attaching the transverse colon to the posterior abdominal wall (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The mesentery is an expansive double fold of visceral peritoneum, which is a continuation of the parietal peritoneum lining the posterior abdominal wall. The mesentery extends anteriorly in the abdomen to reach the organs. The part of the mesentery that extends to the transverse colon is referred to as the transverse mesocolon. It envelopes the transverse colon as the serosa, therefore, suspending the transverse colon for the posterior abdominal wall. 

The transverse mesocolon houses the vessels which supply the transverse colon. These vessels travel in the transverse mesocolon, spreading and branching out as they get closer to the transverse colon. The arteries form supportive anastomosis as the mesentery envelopes the colon. The proximal two thirds of the transverse colon is a midgut derivative; therefore, it is supplied and drained by colic branches of the superior mesenteric vessel, while the distal third of the transverse colon is a hindgut derivative and is supplied and drained by colic branches of the inferior mesenteric vessels. 

Innervation follows a model of distribution similar to the arterial blood supply. The celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses supply sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon, while the inferior mesenteric and hypogastric plexuses provide a sympathetic and parasympathetic supply to the distal transverse colon.

The mesentery houses a lymphatic system along and the drainage is distributed amongst various lymph nodes group within the mesentery such as the epicolic, paracolic, intermediate colic, and preterminal colic node groups. This distribution is based on the arterial supply to the various aspects of the colon.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The transverse mesocolon suspends the transverse colon from the posterior abdominal wall and protects the passage of the vessels, nerves, and lymphatics from the posterior abdominal wall.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Mesenteric lymphadenitis

—Vascular mesenteropathies

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The omental appendices are peritoneum-covered tabs of fat, 2 to 10 cm long, attached in rows along the taeniae of the colon (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Omental appendices are pouches of peritoneum that are filled with fat (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013). They are attached to the external surface of the colon, opposite the side that the mesentery arising from the posterior abdominal wall attaches to.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The appendices are absent or sparse on the cecum and the ascending colon. However, they increase in frequency along the distal colon, particularly on the surface of the sigmoid colon (Standring, 2016). In contrast, the rectum does not have omental appendices. The omental appendices receive vascular supply from the vessels that enter the wall of the colon.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Moore, K. L., Dalley, A. F. and Agur, A. M. R. (2013) Clinically Oriented Anatomy. Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series: Elsevier Limited.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The greater omentum is a prominent peritoneal fold suspended from the greater curvature of the stomach and passing laterally and inferiorly a variable distance in front of the intestines; it is attached to the anterior surface of the transverse colon; a remnant of the dorsal mesogastrium, it comprises the omental apron and several peritoneal ligaments connecting abdominal organs (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Description
sections.text:
The greater omentum is a large double sheet of visceral peritoneum that drapes inferiorly from the greater curvature of the stomach. It hangs over the upper abdominal organs and then folds back on itself to attach to the transverse colon.

The greater omentum contains a significant amount of adipose tissue, and it also plays a role in immune function.

The left and right gastroepiploic arteries, which run along the inferior border of the stomach, supply the greater omentum, and an anastomosis of these vessels, called the epiploic arterial arc, lies along its inferior peritoneal fold.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The serosa is the membrane lining the walls of various body cavities, reflected over the surfaces of protruding organs; it consists of mesothelium lying upon a subserosal connective tissue layer, and it secretes a watery exudate (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The serosa (or visceral peritoneum) is a membrane that lines the outer wall of the transverse colon. It is continuous with the transverse mesocolon, the mesentery that suspends the transverse colon. 

The serosa is composed of two layers. It is a continuous sheet of squamous epithelial cells (mesothelium), which are supported by an underlying layer of thin loose connective tissue. The loose connective tissue separates the mesothelium from the muscular layer.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The serosa forms the outermost layer of the transverse colon.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The serosa acts as a protective layer by forming a barrier against potential inflammatory and malignant spread.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Iatrogenic serosal tear

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The crypts of small intestines are the straight tubular invaginations of the surface epithelium of the small intestine (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Intestinal glands or crypts of Lieberkühn are simple tubular invaginations of the epithelium deep into the lamina propria that extend as far down as the muscularis mucosae. They open at the bases of villi and are composed of simple columnar epithelium that is continuous with the epithelial surface of the villi. 

Cells of the intestinal epithelium (enterocytes) are found within the crypts as well as on the surface of the villi. Goblet cells are scattered throughout the epithelial surface of the villi and within the intestinal glands. Paneth cells are located at the very base of the crypts and appear with reddish granules within their cytoplasm in routine H&E stained sections. Enteroendocrine cells tend to concentrate more in the crypts, while a population of stem cells is also located here.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The enterocytes’ primary function is absorption. Goblet cells are unicellular mucin secreting glands. Paneth cells secrete antimicrobial substances. Enteroendocrine cells produce various paracrine and endocrine hormones.

The population of stem cells found in the intestinal crypts are responsible for the constant renewal of the mucosal epithelium. The stem cells are capable or differentiating into enterocytes or the secretory cells mentioned above.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The intestinal villi are the multitudinous threadlike projections that cover the surface of the mucosa of the small intestine and serve as the sites of absorption (by active transport and diffusion) of fluids and nutrients (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Intestinal villi are 0.5-1.5 mm long, fingerlike or leaf-like extensions of the mucosa into the lumen of the small intestine (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). The central core of each villus is the lamina propria.

In the duodenum, they are leaf-shaped but gradually adopt a more finger-like shape as they appear in the ileum. Between each villus is the opening of the mucosal and submucosal glands. These are mainly intestinal glands inappropriately referred to as crypts or glands of Lieberkühn.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Villi magnify the surface area of the intestinal epithelium to maximize secretion and absorption capacity.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The muscularis mucosa is the thin layer of smooth muscle fibers usually found as a part of the tunica mucosa deep to the lamina propria mucosae (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The muscularis mucosa is similar in the three components of the small intestine. It is the deepest part of the mucosa and consists of a very thin inner circular layer of smooth muscle and an equally thin outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle.

Some small smooth muscle cells travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The muscularis mucosa is the deepest part of the mucosa and adjacent to the submucosa.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Contraction of the muscularis mucosa (independent of the peristaltic movement of the entire gut wall) moves the mucosa and form ridges and depressions that facilitate absorption and secretion.

Rhythmic movement of villi is due to the contractions of the smooth muscle cells that travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi. These contractions occur several times per minute and serve to pump lymph from lacteals into mesenteric lymphatics (Eroschenko, 2008).

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. 11th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Transit amplifying cells are the daughter cells of the intestinal stem cells found in the lower half of the intestinal glands (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Intermediate cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands. This population of cells is known as the amplifying compartment as these cells are actively undergoing mitosis and will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Intermediate cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: This population of cells will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to surfaces of the villi.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: An enterocyte is an epithelial cell of the intestinal wall (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Enterocytes are simple, tall columnar epithelial cells with a nucleus positioned in the basal domain of the cell. Microvilli extend from the apical surface. Collectively, the microvilli of enterocytes are called a “striated border.”

Apical borders of adjacent enterocytes are joined by tight junctions and permit selective absorption of substances from the intestinal lumen. The lateral surfaces of the enterocytes exhibit cytoplasmic processes that interdigitate with those of adjacent cells thus increasing the amount of the plasmalemma housing transport enzymes.

The cytoplasm of enterocytes also exhibits specializations of an absorptive cell. Elongated mitochondria and smooth/agranular endoplasmic reticulum (sER) are concentrated in the apical cytoplasm.

The cytoplasm of enterocytes also exhibits specializations of a secretory cell. Stacks of Golgi cisternae are near the nucleus accompanied by free ribosomes and rough/granular endoplasmic reticulum (rER). Small secretory vesicles congregate at the apical border of the cell.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The primary function of the enterocytes is absorption. The striated border increases the surface area for absorption as much as 600 times. 

Lateral interdigitations of the plasmalemma of adjacent enterocytes expand and enlarge the intercellular compartment during absorption of solutes, water and lipids.

Mitochondria provide the energy required for transport processes and the sER are involved in the absorption of fatty acids and glycerol.

Enterocytes are also secretory cells, primarily producing glycoprotein enzymes that will be reinserted into the apical membrane. They also secrete water and electrolytes (mainly those enterocytes in the intestinal glands to balance water absorption across the enterocytes lining the villi), which maintains a constant liquified intestinal chyme.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Microfold cells are specialized cells of the epithelium, overlying the lymphoid nodules of the intestines, that bind antigens and transport them to the underlying lymphocytes; they may provide a continuous sampling of the intestinal contents to the immune system (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: At the luminal surface of the ileum, a Peyer’s patch appears as a dome-shaped region devoid of villi and the epithelial surface consists of low cuboidal microfold (or M) cells rather than absorptive cells (enterocytes).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: M cells are antigen-transporting cells and carry antigens from the intestinal lumen to reach immune cells within the lamina propria of the digestive tract or gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT).

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A goblet cell is a unicellular mucous gland found in the epithelium of various mucous membranes, especially that of the respiratory passages and intestines. Droplets of mucinogen collect in the upper part of the cell and distend it, while the basal end remains slender, and the cell assumes the shape of a goblet (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Goblet cells are dispersed between enterocytes. They are more numerous in the ileum than in the jejunum or the duodenum. Their unique shape with the apical aggregations of mucinogen granules distending the apical domain of the cell and the narrow basal domain which houses the nucleus is responsible for the name of the cell i.e., it resembles a wine goblet.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: A goblet cell is a unicellular mucous gland dispersed between enterocytes in the epithelium lining the small and large intestine.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Goblet cells secrete mucus. Their main function is to produce mucus which protects and lubricates the surface of the intestines.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Enteroendocrine cells are a group of APUD cells (amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation cells), which may be divided into several populations based on polypeptide hormone and biogenic amine production, found scattered throughout the gastrointestinal epithelium, mainly at the base of the epithelium; their numerous small secretory granules are concentrated chiefly between the nucleus and the cell base. Their secretions affect gastrointestinal motility, pancreatic and biliary secretions, and gastrointestinal epithelial growth, as well as being regulators of other enteroendocrine products (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The enteroendocrine cells in the small intestine are like those in the stomach mucosa and form part of the diffuse neuroendocrine system (DNS). They tend to occupy the lower part of the intestinal glands.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The activity of the small intestine includes some modulation by a complex system of locally produced peptide hormones from enteroendocrine cells.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Paneth cells are narrow, pyramidal, or columnar epithelial cells with a round or oval nucleus close to the base, occurring in the fundus of the crypts of Lieberkühn; they contain large granules that secrete antimicrobial substances such as defensins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Paneth cells are very prominent at the base of the intestinal glands as, when using traditional H&E histological staining, they have acidophilic, apical secretory vesicles.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Granules in Paneth cells contain lysozyme, an enzyme which digests the cell wall of some bacteria, so Paneth cells have a role in regulating the natural bacterial flora of the small intestine.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Stem cells are undifferentiated cells with the ability to divide and proliferate to provide precursor cells that can differentiate into specialized cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Stem cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands. This population of cells is referred to as the amplifying compartment as these cells are actively undergoing mitosis and will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi and replace epithelial cells as they are “sloughed off” the surface during normal intestinal mobility.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: This population of cells will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The lamina propria is the connective tissue coat of a mucous membrane (tunica mucosa) just deep to the epithelium and basement membrane (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The lamina propria forms the core of each villus and surrounds each intestinal gland. It is loose connective tissue and contains blood vessels and lymphatic vessels (lacteals). 

The lamina propria contains aggregations of lymphocytes and associated immune cells e.g., eosinophils, macrophages, and neutrophils particularly within each villus. This aggregation is referred to as diffuse lymphatic tissue. It also contains many nodules/follicles of lymphatic tissue that represent the GALT (gut associated lymphatic tissue). They are particularly large and numerous in the ileum and are referred to as “Peyer’s patches.” They can extend from the lamina propria to occupy the submucosa.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lamina propria is immediately underlying the surface epithelium and forms the core of each villus and surrounds each intestinal gland. Its deepest boundary is the muscularis mucosa.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The lamina propria is the supporting connective tissue of the surface epithelium and underlying intestinal glands. It also supports blood vessels and lymphatic vessels (lacteals) involved in absorption of digested products as well as accommodating cells of the gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT) that can identify antigens and initiate the immune response.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The central lymphatic vessel, or lacteal, are any of the intestinal lymphatic vessels that transport chyle; so called because during absorption they are white from absorbed fat (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Lymph vessels of the intestine begin as blind-ended or closed tubes near the tip of each villus. These vessels are called lacteals and although they are larger in diameter than neighboring blood vessels, they tend to collapse which makes them difficult to observe in routine histological sections.

Lacteals extend deep to the muscularis mucosa where they form a plexus. From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa then unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine. Smooth muscle cells accompany these lacteals.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Lacteals are important for the absorption of lipids. It is thought that the rhythmic movement of villi is due to the contractions of the smooth muscle cells that travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi. These contractions occur several times per minute and serve to pump lymph from lacteals into mesenteric lymphatics (Eroschenko, 2008).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The longitudinal muscular layer of small intestine is the outer layer of the muscular coat (tunica muscularis or muscularis externa) of the small intestine, consisting of longitudinally coursing fibers (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The cross-sectional microarchitecture of the small intestine demonstrates mucosa, submucosa, and muscular (inner circular and outer longitudinal) layers with a thin outer serosal covering.

The longitudinal muscular layer forms the outer muscle fibers of the muscular layer and its fibers are smooth muscle cells which are oriented roughly parallel to the long axis of the digestive canal.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The outer longitudinal muscular layer, together with the circular muscle layer, act to create rhythmic peristaltic contractions. This mixes chyme and pushes contents distally.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The myenteric plexus is a nerve plexus that is part of the enteric plexus and is within the tunica muscularis (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus is a network of thin bundles of axons and neurons, which may be grouped as small ganglionic clusters. It lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscular layer (muscularis externa) of the small intestine. The myenteric plexus arises from the periarterial plexus that follows the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and their terminal branches. All components of the myenteric plexus are continuous with the inner circular muscle nerve fiber bundles, which go on to synapse with the ganglionated and non-ganglionated plexuses of the submucosa. Both the myenteric and the submucosal plexuses make up the enteric (or intrinsic) nervous system.

The enteric nervous system is unique to the digestive system and is autonomic in nature. It extends the entire length of the gastrointestinal tract and is composed of three types of neurons (Standring, 2016).

—Sensory neurons transmit information from receptors in the mucosa and muscle of the gut wall, which respond to mechanical, chemical, thermal, and osmotic stimuli. They project information to the interneurons.

—Motor neurons control the motility and secretions in the gut and may be inhibitory or excitatory.

—Interneurons go between the sensory and motor neurons, thus integrating the information between the two.

The enteric nervous system may function autonomously; however, it does communicate with the central nervous system via parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers. Cross connections between the two allow information from the gut to be relayed to the CNS, and vice versa. Generally, sympathetic inputs cause inhibition of secretions and motor activity and contraction of sphincters and blood vessels (fight or flight response). Parasympathetic stimulation of the enteric nervous system promotes secretions and motor activity and dilation of the sphincters and blood vessels (rest and digest response) (Standring, 2016; Costa, Brookes and Hennig, 2000).

The interstitial cells of Cajal are flat, thin, branched cells are linked to the smooth muscle cells via gap junctions. They overlap with the myenteric plexus, and they are believed to act as pacemakers for myogenic contraction of the muscular layer, modulating the electrical slow wave activity to alter the rhythm of intestine contractions.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The myenteric plexus is situated between the two muscular layers; superjacent to the inner circular smooth muscle layer and subjacent to the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The myenteric plexus houses most of the enteric neurons with motor function. These act on the different effector cells within the intestinal system. In conjunction with the interstitial cells of Cajal, this enables the coordinated muscular movements of the intestines, and contributes to immune and endocrine functions (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The circular muscular layer of small intestine is the inner layer of circularly coursing fibers in the muscular coat (tunica muscularis or muscularis externa) of the small intestine (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The cross-sectional microarchitecture of the small intestine demonstrates mucosa, submucosa, and muscular (inner circular and outer longitudinal) layers with a thin outer serosal covering.

The circular muscular layer forms the inner muscle fibers of the muscular (muscularis externa) layer and contains smooth muscle cells which are usually oriented roughly perpendicular to the long axis of the digestive canal. However, they can also adopt a spiral arrangement.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The circular muscular contracts and reduce the diameter of the small intestine. Together with the outer longitudinal muscular layer, these fibers act to create rhythmic peristaltic contractions, mixing chyme and pushing contents distally.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The serosa is the membrane lining the walls of various body cavities, reflected over the surfaces of protruding organs; it consists of mesothelium lying upon a subserosal connective tissue layer, and it secretes a watery exudate (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The first 2.5 cm of the duodenum is intraperitoneal, thus is covered by a serosa (i.e., visceral peritoneum). As it becomes retroperitoneal, only the anterior surface of the duodenum is covered by a serosa, with the remaining covered by adventitia. The jejunum and ileum are covered by a serosa. 

Serosa is a serous membrane made of simple squamous epithelium or mesothelium supported by a basement membrane and a small amount of connective tissue.

Adventitia is only connective tissue that binds the gut to surrounding connective tissue of adjoining structures.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The serosa of the small intestine is the outermost layer of the small intestine. It encloses the jejunum and ileum, except at the mesenteric borders, where the serosa is reflected onto the mesentery.

The deep surface of the serosa adheres to the longitudinal muscular layer of the small intestine. The superficial surface of the serosa is an epithelium or mesothelium, which is in contact with surrounding organs or the parietal peritoneum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The serosa of the small intestine secretes a serosal fluid. This fluid allows the small intestine to slide across neighboring tissues without creating friction and damage.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The submucosal vascular plexus is a network of intercommunicating blood vessels found in the submucosa.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Blood vessels (small arteries and veins) form large plexuses in the submucosa.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The submucosal vascular plexus nourishes the layers of the intestinal wall as well as removing absorbed products of digestion.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The submucosal plexus is a nerve plexus that is part of the enteric plexus and is situated in the submucosa (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The submucosal plexus is formed from branches of the myenteric plexus, which arise from the periarterial plexus that follows the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and their terminal branches. Both the myenteric and the submucosal plexuses make up the enteric (or intrinsic) nervous system. The submucosal plexus itself may be subdivided into inner (or Meissner’s) and outer (or Schabadasch’s) submucosal plexuses (Brehmer, Rupprecht and Neuhuber, 2010). 

The enteric nervous system is unique to the digestive system and is autonomic in nature. It extends the entire length of the gastrointestinal tract and is composed of three types of neurons (Standring, 2016).

—Sensory neurons transmit information from receptors in the mucosa and muscle of the gut wall, which respond to mechanical, chemical, thermal, and osmotic stimuli. They project information to the interneurons.

—Motor neurons control the motility and secretions in the gut and may be inhibitory or excitatory.

—Interneurons go between the sensory and motor neurons, thus integrating the information between the two.

The enteric nervous system may function autonomously; however, it does communicate with the central nervous system via parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers. Cross connections between the two allow for information from the gut to be relayed to the CNS, and vice versa. Generally, sympathetic inputs cause inhibition of secretions and motor activity and contraction of sphincters and blood vessels (fight or flight response). Parasympathetic stimulation of the enteric nervous system promotes secretions and motor activity and dilation of the sphincters and blood vessels (rest and digest response) (Standring, 2016; Costa, Brookes and Hennig, 2000). 

In histological sections, the submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus is only visible as scattered ganglion cell bodies with satellite cells lying within the submucosal elements.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The submucosal plexus is superficial to the muscularis mucosae of the mucosa, and deep to the inner circular muscular layer.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The submucosal plexus innervates the mucosal epithelium and the smooth muscle of the muscularis mucosa, which facilitate their respective functions of water and ion absorption and interstitial crypt emptying.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The aggregated lymphoid nodules of small intestine are the oval elevated areas of lymphoid tissue on the mucosa of the small intestine, composed of many lymphoid follicles closely packed together (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Diffuse lymphatic tissue and lymphatic nodules occur as single entities along the alimentary tract; however, in the ileum, the submucosa (and the lamina propria) contains aggregations of lymphoid nodules known as “Peyer’s patches.” They are an important component of the gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT). In humans, there are about 30 patches, with each patch may contain 10–200 lymph nodules. They contain T cells and B lymphocytes. At the luminal surface, a Peyer’s patch appears as a dome-shaped region devoid of villi and the epithelial surface consists of low cuboidal M (microfold) cells rather than absorptive cells (enterocytes).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Aggregations of lymphoid nodules known as “Peyer’s patches” dominate the submucosa (and the lamina propria) mostly in the ileum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Lymphocytes and associated immune cells, e.g., eosinophils, macrophages, and neutrophils, are in the ideal location to recognize antigens and initiate the immune response.

The germinal center indicates that the lymphatic tissue is responding to an antigen resulting in the proliferation of lymphocytes, the differentiation of plasma cells and the production of antibodies.

M cells are antigen-transporting cells and carry antigens from the intestinal lumen to reach immune cells within the lamina propria of the digestive tract or gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT).

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The submucosa is the layer of dense connective tissue between the mucosa and the muscularis externa in most parts of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and genital tracts (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The submucosa is essentially a dense, irregular connective tissue layer found deep than the mucosa. It contains blood and lymphatic vessels. Blood vessels form large plexuses in the submucosa. Lacteals originating in the lamina propria of villi form a plexus near the muscularis mucosa (the outermost layer of the mucosa). From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa and unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) nerve plexus is only visible as scattered ganglion cell bodies with satellite cells lying within the submucosal elements.

Glandular tissue is prominent in the duodenum (as “Brunner’s” or submucosal glands) where they dominate the lamina propria and the submucosa. These compound tubular glands have both serous (zymogen) and mucous secreting components.

The submucosa (and the lamina propria) in the ileum contains aggregations of lymphoid nodules known as “Peyer’s patches.” They are an important component of the gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT). In humans there are about 30 patches. Each patch may contain 10–200 lymph nodules. At the luminal surface, they appear as a dome-shaped region devoid of villi. The epithelial surface consists of low cuboidal “M” (microfold) cells rather than absorptive cells (enterocytes) (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Plicae circulares are circular transverse folds that extend up to two thirds the circumference of the lumen. They contain a core of the submucosa. They begin about 5–6 cm beyond the pylorus and are most numerous towards the end or distal part of the duodenum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The blood vessels within the submucosa nourish the layers of the intestinal wall as well as removing absorbed products of digestion.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus is mainly responsible for innervating the smooth muscle layers of the muscularis mucosae.

Brunner’s glands secretions are between a pH of 8.1 and 9.3 and contain alkaline glycoproteins and bicarbonate which neutralizes the acidic containing chyme entering the duodenum from the stomach. Another function of these secretions is to create a pH ideal for the actions of pancreatic enzymes delivered to the duodenum.

M cells are antigen-transporting cells and carry antigens from the intestinal lumen to reach immune cells within the lamina propria of the digestive tract or gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT).

Lacteals and the lymphatic vessels are important for the absorption of lipids.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The submucosal lymphatic plexus is an interconnecting network of lymph vessels, i.e., the lymphocapillary vessels, collecting vessels, and trunks, which provides drainage of lymph in a one-way flow (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Lacteals originate in the lamina propria of villi and form a plexus near the muscular layer (muscularis mucosa) of the small intestine. From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa and unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Lacteals and the lymphatic vessels are important for the absorption of lipids.

sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The intestinal villi are the multitudinous threadlike projections that cover the surface of the mucosa of the small intestine and serve as the sites of absorption (by active transport and diffusion) of fluids and nutrients (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Intestinal villi are 0.5-1.5 mm long, fingerlike or leaf-like extensions of the mucosa into the lumen of the small intestine (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). The central core of each villus is the lamina propria.

In the duodenum, they are leaf-shaped but gradually adopt a more finger-like shape as they appear in the ileum. Between each villus is the opening of the mucosal and submucosal glands. These are mainly intestinal glands inappropriately referred to as crypts or glands of Lieberkühn.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Villi magnify the surface area of the intestinal epithelium to maximize secretion and absorption capacity.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The crypts of small intestines are the straight tubular invaginations of the surface epithelium of the small intestine (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Intestinal glands or crypts of Lieberkühn are simple tubular invaginations of the epithelium deep into the lamina propria that extend as far down as the muscularis mucosae. They open at the bases of villi and are composed of simple columnar epithelium that is continuous with the epithelial surface of the villi. 

Cells of the intestinal epithelium (enterocytes) are found within the crypts as well as on the surface of the villi. Goblet cells are scattered throughout the epithelial surface of the villi and within the intestinal glands. Paneth cells are located at the very base of the crypts and appear with reddish granules within their cytoplasm in routine H&E stained sections. Enteroendocrine cells tend to concentrate more in the crypts, while a population of stem cells is also located here.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The enterocytes’ primary function is absorption. Goblet cells are unicellular mucin secreting glands. Paneth cells secrete antimicrobial substances. Enteroendocrine cells produce various paracrine and endocrine hormones.

The population of stem cells found in the intestinal crypts are responsible for the constant renewal of the mucosal epithelium. The stem cells are capable or differentiating into enterocytes or the secretory cells mentioned above.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A goblet cell is a unicellular mucous gland found in the epithelium of various mucous membranes, especially that of the respiratory passages and intestines. Droplets of mucinogen collect in the upper part of the cell and distend it, while the basal end remains slender, and the cell assumes the shape of a goblet (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Goblet cells are dispersed between enterocytes. They are more numerous in the ileum than in the jejunum or the duodenum. Their unique shape with the apical aggregations of mucinogen granules distending the apical domain of the cell and the narrow basal domain which houses the nucleus is responsible for the name of the cell i.e., it resembles a wine goblet.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: A goblet cell is a unicellular mucous gland dispersed between enterocytes in the epithelium lining the small and large intestine.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Goblet cells secrete mucus. Their main function is to produce mucus which protects and lubricates the surface of the intestines.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: An enterocyte is an epithelial cell of the intestinal wall (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Enterocytes are simple, tall columnar epithelial cells with a nucleus positioned in the basal domain of the cell. Microvilli extend from the apical surface. Collectively, the microvilli of enterocytes are called a “striated border.”

Apical borders of adjacent enterocytes are joined by tight junctions and permit selective absorption of substances from the intestinal lumen. The lateral surfaces of the enterocytes exhibit cytoplasmic processes that interdigitate with those of adjacent cells thus increasing the amount of the plasmalemma housing transport enzymes.

The cytoplasm of enterocytes also exhibits specializations of an absorptive cell. Elongated mitochondria and smooth/agranular endoplasmic reticulum (sER) are concentrated in the apical cytoplasm.

The cytoplasm of enterocytes also exhibits specializations of a secretory cell. Stacks of Golgi cisternae are near the nucleus accompanied by free ribosomes and rough/granular endoplasmic reticulum (rER). Small secretory vesicles congregate at the apical border of the cell.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The primary function of the enterocytes is absorption. The striated border increases the surface area for absorption as much as 600 times. 

Lateral interdigitations of the plasmalemma of adjacent enterocytes expand and enlarge the intercellular compartment during absorption of solutes, water and lipids.

Mitochondria provide the energy required for transport processes and the sER are involved in the absorption of fatty acids and glycerol.

Enterocytes are also secretory cells, primarily producing glycoprotein enzymes that will be reinserted into the apical membrane. They also secrete water and electrolytes (mainly those enterocytes in the intestinal glands to balance water absorption across the enterocytes lining the villi), which maintains a constant liquified intestinal chyme.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Transit amplifying cells are the daughter cells of the intestinal stem cells found in the lower half of the intestinal glands (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Intermediate cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands. This population of cells is known as the amplifying compartment as these cells are actively undergoing mitosis and will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Intermediate cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: This population of cells will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to surfaces of the villi.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Stem cells are undifferentiated cells with the ability to divide and proliferate to provide precursor cells that can differentiate into specialized cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Stem cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands. This population of cells is referred to as the amplifying compartment as these cells are actively undergoing mitosis and will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi and replace epithelial cells as they are “sloughed off” the surface during normal intestinal mobility.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Stem cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: This population of cells will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Enteroendocrine cells are a group of APUD cells (amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation cells), which may be divided into several populations based on polypeptide hormone and biogenic amine production, found scattered throughout the gastrointestinal epithelium, mainly at the base of the epithelium; their numerous small secretory granules are concentrated chiefly between the nucleus and the cell base. Their secretions affect gastrointestinal motility, pancreatic and biliary secretions, and gastrointestinal epithelial growth, as well as being regulators of other enteroendocrine products (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The enteroendocrine cells in the small intestine are like those in the stomach mucosa and form part of the diffuse neuroendocrine system (DNS). They tend to occupy the lower part of the intestinal glands.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The activity of the small intestine includes some modulation by a complex system of locally produced peptide hormones from enteroendocrine cells.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Paneth cells are narrow, pyramidal, or columnar epithelial cells with a round or oval nucleus close to the base, occurring in the fundus of the crypts of Lieberkühn; they contain large granules that secrete antimicrobial substances such as defensins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Paneth cells are very prominent at the base of the intestinal glands as, when using traditional H&E histological staining, they have acidophilic, apical secretory vesicles.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Granules in Paneth cells contain lysozyme, an enzyme which digests the cell wall of some bacteria, so Paneth cells have a role in regulating the natural bacterial flora of the small intestine.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The muscularis mucosa is the thin layer of smooth muscle fibers usually found as a part of the tunica mucosa deep to the lamina propria mucosae (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The muscularis mucosa is similar in the three components of the small intestine. It is the deepest part of the mucosa and consists of a very thin inner circular layer of smooth muscle and an equally thin outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle.

Some small smooth muscle cells travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The muscularis mucosa is the deepest part of the mucosa and adjacent to the submucosa.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Contraction of the muscularis mucosa (independent of the peristaltic movement of the entire gut wall) moves the mucosa and form ridges and depressions that facilitate absorption and secretion.

Rhythmic movement of villi is due to the contractions of the smooth muscle cells that travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi. These contractions occur several times per minute and serve to pump lymph from lacteals into mesenteric lymphatics (Eroschenko, 2008).

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. 11th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The central lymphatic vessel, or lacteal, are any of the intestinal lymphatic vessels that transport chyle; so called because during absorption they are white from absorbed fat (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Lymph vessels of the intestine begin as blind-ended or closed tubes near the tip of each villus. These vessels are called lacteals and although they are larger in diameter than neighboring blood vessels, they tend to collapse which makes them difficult to observe in routine histological sections.

Lacteals extend deep to the muscularis mucosa where they form a plexus. From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa then unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine. Smooth muscle cells accompany these lacteals.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Lacteals are important for the absorption of lipids. It is thought that the rhythmic movement of villi is due to the contractions of the smooth muscle cells that travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi. These contractions occur several times per minute and serve to pump lymph from lacteals into mesenteric lymphatics (Eroschenko, 2008).

sections.text:

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The submucosal lymphatic plexus is an interconnecting network of lymph vessels, i.e., the lymphocapillary vessels, collecting vessels, and trunks, which provides drainage of lymph in a one-way flow (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Lacteals originate in the lamina propria of villi and form a plexus near the muscular layer (muscularis mucosa) of the small intestine. From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa and unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Lacteals and the lymphatic vessels are important for the absorption of lipids.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The submucosa is the layer of dense connective tissue between the mucosa and the muscularis externa in most parts of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and genital tracts (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The submucosa is essentially a dense, irregular connective tissue layer found deep than the mucosa. It contains blood and lymphatic vessels. Blood vessels form large plexuses in the submucosa. Lacteals originating in the lamina propria of villi form a plexus near the muscularis mucosa (the outermost layer of the mucosa). From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa and unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) nerve plexus is only visible as scattered ganglion cell bodies with satellite cells lying within the submucosal elements.

Glandular tissue is prominent in the duodenum (as “Brunner’s” or submucosal glands) where they dominate the lamina propria and the submucosa. These compound tubular glands have both serous (zymogen) and mucous secreting components.

The submucosa (and the lamina propria) in the ileum contains aggregations of lymphoid nodules known as “Peyer’s patches.” They are an important component of the gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT). In humans there are about 30 patches. Each patch may contain 10–200 lymph nodules. At the luminal surface, they appear as a dome-shaped region devoid of villi. The epithelial surface consists of low cuboidal “M” (microfold) cells rather than absorptive cells (enterocytes) (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Plicae circulares are circular transverse folds that extend up to two thirds the circumference of the lumen. They contain a core of the submucosa. They begin about 5–6 cm beyond the pylorus and are most numerous towards the end or distal part of the duodenum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The blood vessels within the submucosa nourish the layers of the intestinal wall as well as removing absorbed products of digestion.

The submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus is mainly responsible for innervating the smooth muscle layers of the muscularis mucosae.

Brunner’s glands secretions are between a pH of 8.1 and 9.3 and contain alkaline glycoproteins and bicarbonate which neutralizes the acidic containing chyme entering the duodenum from the stomach. Another function of these secretions is to create a pH ideal for the actions of pancreatic enzymes delivered to the duodenum.

M cells are antigen-transporting cells and carry antigens from the intestinal lumen to reach immune cells within the lamina propria of the digestive tract or gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT).

Lacteals and the lymphatic vessels are important for the absorption of lipids.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The submucosal vascular plexus is a network of intercommunicating blood vessels found in the submucosa.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Blood vessels (small arteries and veins) form large plexuses in the submucosa.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The submucosal vascular plexus nourishes the layers of the intestinal wall as well as removing absorbed products of digestion.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The submucosal plexus is a nerve plexus that is part of the enteric plexus and is situated in the submucosa (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The submucosal plexus is formed from branches of the myenteric plexus, which arise from the periarterial plexus that follows the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and their terminal branches. Both the myenteric and the submucosal plexuses make up the enteric (or intrinsic) nervous system. The submucosal plexus itself may be subdivided into inner (or Meissner’s) and outer (or Schabadasch’s) submucosal plexuses (Brehmer, Rupprecht and Neuhuber, 2010). 

The enteric nervous system is unique to the digestive system and is autonomic in nature. It extends the entire length of the gastrointestinal tract and is composed of three types of neurons (Standring, 2016).

—Sensory neurons transmit information from receptors in the mucosa and muscle of the gut wall, which respond to mechanical, chemical, thermal, and osmotic stimuli. They project information to the interneurons.

—Motor neurons control the motility and secretions in the gut and may be inhibitory or excitatory.

—Interneurons go between the sensory and motor neurons, thus integrating the information between the two.

The enteric nervous system may function autonomously; however, it does communicate with the central nervous system via parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers. Cross connections between the two allow for information from the gut to be relayed to the CNS, and vice versa. Generally, sympathetic inputs cause inhibition of secretions and motor activity and contraction of sphincters and blood vessels (fight or flight response). Parasympathetic stimulation of the enteric nervous system promotes secretions and motor activity and dilation of the sphincters and blood vessels (rest and digest response) (Standring, 2016; Costa, Brookes and Hennig, 2000). 

In histological sections, the submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus is only visible as scattered ganglion cell bodies with satellite cells lying within the submucosal elements.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The submucosal plexus is superficial to the muscularis mucosae of the mucosa, and deep to the inner circular muscular layer.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The submucosal plexus innervates the mucosal epithelium and the smooth muscle of the muscularis mucosa, which facilitate their respective functions of water and ion absorption and interstitial crypt emptying.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The duodenal glands are tubuloacinar glands in the submucous layer of the duodenum that open into the crypts of Lieberkühn; they secrete urogastrone (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Duodenal glands, or “Brunner’s glands,” dominate the lamina propria and the submucosa. These compound tubular glands have both serous (zymogen) and mucous secreting components.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Secretion is carried out by the duodenal glands. The products of secretion include mucus for lubrication as well as enzymes, hydrochloric acid, peptide hormones and water for digestion.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The serosa is the membrane lining the walls of various body cavities, reflected over the surfaces of protruding organs; it consists of mesothelium lying upon a subserosal connective tissue layer, and it secretes a watery exudate (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The first 2.5 cm of the duodenum is intraperitoneal, thus is covered by a serosa (i.e., visceral peritoneum). As it becomes retroperitoneal, only the anterior surface of the duodenum is covered by a serosa, with the remaining covered by adventitia. The jejunum and ileum are covered by a serosa. 

Serosa is a serous membrane made of simple squamous epithelium or mesothelium supported by a basement membrane and a small amount of connective tissue.

Adventitia is only connective tissue that binds the gut to surrounding connective tissue of adjoining structures.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The serosa of the small intestine is the outermost layer of the small intestine. It encloses the jejunum and ileum, except at the mesenteric borders, where the serosa is reflected onto the mesentery.

The deep surface of the serosa adheres to the longitudinal muscular layer of the small intestine. The superficial surface of the serosa is an epithelium or mesothelium, which is in contact with surrounding organs or the parietal peritoneum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The serosa of the small intestine secretes a serosal fluid. This fluid allows the small intestine to slide across neighboring tissues without creating friction and damage.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The myenteric plexus is a nerve plexus that is part of the enteric plexus and is within the tunica muscularis (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus is a network of thin bundles of axons and neurons, which may be grouped as small ganglionic clusters. It lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscular layer (muscularis externa) of the small intestine. The myenteric plexus arises from the periarterial plexus that follows the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and their terminal branches. All components of the myenteric plexus are continuous with the inner circular muscle nerve fiber bundles, which go on to synapse with the ganglionated and non-ganglionated plexuses of the submucosa. Both the myenteric and the submucosal plexuses make up the enteric (or intrinsic) nervous system.

The enteric nervous system is unique to the digestive system and is autonomic in nature. It extends the entire length of the gastrointestinal tract and is composed of three types of neurons (Standring, 2016).

—Sensory neurons transmit information from receptors in the mucosa and muscle of the gut wall, which respond to mechanical, chemical, thermal, and osmotic stimuli. They project information to the interneurons.

—Motor neurons control the motility and secretions in the gut and may be inhibitory or excitatory.

—Interneurons go between the sensory and motor neurons, thus integrating the information between the two.

The enteric nervous system may function autonomously; however, it does communicate with the central nervous system via parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers. Cross connections between the two allow information from the gut to be relayed to the CNS, and vice versa. Generally, sympathetic inputs cause inhibition of secretions and motor activity and contraction of sphincters and blood vessels (fight or flight response). Parasympathetic stimulation of the enteric nervous system promotes secretions and motor activity and dilation of the sphincters and blood vessels (rest and digest response) (Standring, 2016; Costa, Brookes and Hennig, 2000).

The interstitial cells of Cajal are flat, thin, branched cells are linked to the smooth muscle cells via gap junctions. They overlap with the myenteric plexus, and they are believed to act as pacemakers for myogenic contraction of the muscular layer, modulating the electrical slow wave activity to alter the rhythm of intestine contractions.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The myenteric plexus is situated between the two muscular layers; superjacent to the inner circular smooth muscle layer and subjacent to the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The myenteric plexus houses most of the enteric neurons with motor function. These act on the different effector cells within the intestinal system. In conjunction with the interstitial cells of Cajal, this enables the coordinated muscular movements of the intestines, and contributes to immune and endocrine functions (Standring, 2016).
