3075ec341df738cf09ae10d466a8a3e2.name: Longitudinal Muscular Layer of Small Intestine (Jejunum)

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The longitudinal muscular layer of small intestine is the outer layer of the muscular coat (tunica muscularis or muscularis externa) of the small intestine, consisting of longitudinally coursing fibers (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The cross-sectional microarchitecture of the small intestine demonstrates mucosa, submucosa, and muscular (inner circular and outer longitudinal) layers with a thin outer serosal covering.

The longitudinal muscular layer forms the outer muscle fibers of the muscular layer and its fibers are smooth muscle cells which are oriented roughly parallel to the long axis of the digestive canal.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The outer longitudinal muscular layer, together with the circular muscle layer, act to create rhythmic peristaltic contractions. This mixes chyme and pushes contents distally.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

4f5b07b461eaf1e6dfc03e1ce914e165.name: Circular Muscular Layer of Small Intestine (Jejunum)

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The circular muscular layer of small intestine is the inner layer of circularly coursing fibers in the muscular coat (tunica muscularis or muscularis externa) of the small intestine (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The cross-sectional microarchitecture of the small intestine demonstrates mucosa, submucosa, and muscular (inner circular and outer longitudinal) layers with a thin outer serosal covering.

The circular muscular layer forms the inner muscle fibers of the muscular (muscularis externa) layer and contains smooth muscle cells which are usually oriented roughly perpendicular to the long axis of the digestive canal. However, they can also adopt a spiral arrangement.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The circular muscular contracts and reduce the diameter of the small intestine. Together with the outer longitudinal muscular layer, these fibers act to create rhythmic peristaltic contractions, mixing chyme and pushing contents distally.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The intestinal villi are the multitudinous threadlike projections that cover the surface of the mucosa of the small intestine and serve as the sites of absorption (by active transport and diffusion) of fluids and nutrients (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Intestinal villi are 0.5-1.5 mm long, fingerlike or leaf-like extensions of the mucosa into the lumen of the small intestine (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). The central core of each villus is the lamina propria.

In the duodenum, they are leaf-shaped but gradually adopt a more finger-like shape as they appear in the ileum. Between each villus is the opening of the mucosal and submucosal glands. These are mainly intestinal glands inappropriately referred to as crypts or glands of Lieberkühn.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Villi magnify the surface area of the intestinal epithelium to maximize secretion and absorption capacity.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The muscularis mucosa is the thin layer of smooth muscle fibers usually found as a part of the tunica mucosa deep to the lamina propria mucosae (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The muscularis mucosa is similar in the three components of the small intestine. It is the deepest part of the mucosa and consists of a very thin inner circular layer of smooth muscle and an equally thin outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle.

Some small smooth muscle cells travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The muscularis mucosa is the deepest part of the mucosa and adjacent to the submucosa.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Contraction of the muscularis mucosa (independent of the peristaltic movement of the entire gut wall) moves the mucosa and form ridges and depressions that facilitate absorption and secretion.

Rhythmic movement of villi is due to the contractions of the smooth muscle cells that travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi. These contractions occur several times per minute and serve to pump lymph from lacteals into mesenteric lymphatics (Eroschenko, 2008).

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. 11th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The lamina propria is the connective tissue coat of a mucous membrane (tunica mucosa) just deep to the epithelium and basement membrane (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The lamina propria forms the core of each villus and surrounds each intestinal gland. It is loose connective tissue and contains blood vessels and lymphatic vessels (lacteals). 

The lamina propria contains aggregations of lymphocytes and associated immune cells e.g., eosinophils, macrophages, and neutrophils particularly within each villus. This aggregation is referred to as diffuse lymphatic tissue. It also contains many nodules/follicles of lymphatic tissue that represent the GALT (gut associated lymphatic tissue). They are particularly large and numerous in the ileum and are referred to as “Peyer’s patches.” They can extend from the lamina propria to occupy the submucosa.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lamina propria is immediately underlying the surface epithelium and forms the core of each villus and surrounds each intestinal gland. Its deepest boundary is the muscularis mucosa.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The lamina propria is the supporting connective tissue of the surface epithelium and underlying intestinal glands. It also supports blood vessels and lymphatic vessels (lacteals) involved in absorption of digested products as well as accommodating cells of the gut associated lymphatic tissue (GALT) that can identify antigens and initiate the immune response.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: An enterocyte is an epithelial cell of the intestinal wall (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Enterocytes are simple, tall columnar epithelial cells with a nucleus positioned in the basal domain of the cell. Microvilli extend from the apical surface. Collectively, the microvilli of enterocytes are called a “striated border.”

Apical borders of adjacent enterocytes are joined by tight junctions and permit selective absorption of substances from the intestinal lumen. The lateral surfaces of the enterocytes exhibit cytoplasmic processes that interdigitate with those of adjacent cells thus increasing the amount of the plasmalemma housing transport enzymes.

The cytoplasm of enterocytes also exhibits specializations of an absorptive cell. Elongated mitochondria and smooth/agranular endoplasmic reticulum (sER) are concentrated in the apical cytoplasm.

The cytoplasm of enterocytes also exhibits specializations of a secretory cell. Stacks of Golgi cisternae are near the nucleus accompanied by free ribosomes and rough/granular endoplasmic reticulum (rER). Small secretory vesicles congregate at the apical border of the cell.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The primary function of the enterocytes is absorption. The striated border increases the surface area for absorption as much as 600 times. 

Lateral interdigitations of the plasmalemma of adjacent enterocytes expand and enlarge the intercellular compartment during absorption of solutes, water and lipids.

Mitochondria provide the energy required for transport processes and the sER are involved in the absorption of fatty acids and glycerol.

Enterocytes are also secretory cells, primarily producing glycoprotein enzymes that will be reinserted into the apical membrane. They also secrete water and electrolytes (mainly those enterocytes in the intestinal glands to balance water absorption across the enterocytes lining the villi), which maintains a constant liquified intestinal chyme.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Stem cells are undifferentiated cells with the ability to divide and proliferate to provide precursor cells that can differentiate into specialized cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Stem cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands. This population of cells is referred to as the amplifying compartment as these cells are actively undergoing mitosis and will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi and replace epithelial cells as they are “sloughed off” the surface during normal intestinal mobility.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Stem cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: This population of cells will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Enteroendocrine cells are a group of APUD cells (amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation cells), which may be divided into several populations based on polypeptide hormone and biogenic amine production, found scattered throughout the gastrointestinal epithelium, mainly at the base of the epithelium; their numerous small secretory granules are concentrated chiefly between the nucleus and the cell base. Their secretions affect gastrointestinal motility, pancreatic and biliary secretions, and gastrointestinal epithelial growth, as well as being regulators of other enteroendocrine products (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The enteroendocrine cells in the small intestine are like those in the stomach mucosa and form part of the diffuse neuroendocrine system (DNS). They tend to occupy the lower part of the intestinal glands.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The activity of the small intestine includes some modulation by a complex system of locally produced peptide hormones from enteroendocrine cells.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Paneth cells are narrow, pyramidal, or columnar epithelial cells with a round or oval nucleus close to the base, occurring in the fundus of the crypts of Lieberkühn; they contain large granules that secrete antimicrobial substances such as defensins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Paneth cells are very prominent at the base of the intestinal glands as, when using traditional H&E histological staining, they have acidophilic, apical secretory vesicles.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Granules in Paneth cells contain lysozyme, an enzyme which digests the cell wall of some bacteria, so Paneth cells have a role in regulating the natural bacterial flora of the small intestine.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Transit amplifying cells are the daughter cells of the intestinal stem cells found in the lower half of the intestinal glands (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Intermediate cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands. This population of cells is known as the amplifying compartment as these cells are actively undergoing mitosis and will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to the surfaces of the villi.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Intermediate cells occupy much of the basal regions of the intestinal glands.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: This population of cells will differentiate into absorptive cells or goblet cells as they migrate up the epithelium to surfaces of the villi.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A goblet cell is a unicellular mucous gland found in the epithelium of various mucous membranes, especially that of the respiratory passages and intestines. Droplets of mucinogen collect in the upper part of the cell and distend it, while the basal end remains slender, and the cell assumes the shape of a goblet (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Goblet cells are dispersed between enterocytes. They are more numerous in the ileum than in the jejunum or the duodenum. Their unique shape with the apical aggregations of mucinogen granules distending the apical domain of the cell and the narrow basal domain which houses the nucleus is responsible for the name of the cell i.e., it resembles a wine goblet.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: A goblet cell is a unicellular mucous gland dispersed between enterocytes in the epithelium lining the small and large intestine.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Goblet cells secrete mucus. Their main function is to produce mucus which protects and lubricates the surface of the intestines.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The crypts of small intestines are the straight tubular invaginations of the surface epithelium of the small intestine (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Intestinal glands or crypts of Lieberkühn are simple tubular invaginations of the epithelium deep into the lamina propria that extend as far down as the muscularis mucosae. They open at the bases of villi and are composed of simple columnar epithelium that is continuous with the epithelial surface of the villi. 

Cells of the intestinal epithelium (enterocytes) are found within the crypts as well as on the surface of the villi. Goblet cells are scattered throughout the epithelial surface of the villi and within the intestinal glands. Paneth cells are located at the very base of the crypts and appear with reddish granules within their cytoplasm in routine H&E stained sections. Enteroendocrine cells tend to concentrate more in the crypts, while a population of stem cells is also located here.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The enterocytes’ primary function is absorption. Goblet cells are unicellular mucin secreting glands. Paneth cells secrete antimicrobial substances. Enteroendocrine cells produce various paracrine and endocrine hormones.

The population of stem cells found in the intestinal crypts are responsible for the constant renewal of the mucosal epithelium. The stem cells are capable or differentiating into enterocytes or the secretory cells mentioned above.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The central lymphatic vessel, or lacteal, are any of the intestinal lymphatic vessels that transport chyle; so called because during absorption they are white from absorbed fat (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Lymph vessels of the intestine begin as blind-ended or closed tubes near the tip of each villus. These vessels are called lacteals and although they are larger in diameter than neighboring blood vessels, they tend to collapse which makes them difficult to observe in routine histological sections.

Lacteals extend deep to the muscularis mucosa where they form a plexus. From there, they flow to lymph nodules in the submucosa then unite to accompany blood vessels out of the intestine. Smooth muscle cells accompany these lacteals.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Lacteals are important for the absorption of lipids. It is thought that the rhythmic movement of villi is due to the contractions of the smooth muscle cells that travel vertically from the muscularis mucosa to the tips of villi. These contractions occur several times per minute and serve to pump lymph from lacteals into mesenteric lymphatics (Eroschenko, 2008).

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Eroschenko, V. P. (2008) DiFiore's Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations. 11th edn.: Wolters Kluwer Health/Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Interstitial endocrine cells, or Leydig cells, are epithelioid cells of the interstitium of the testis, which elaborate androgens, chiefly testosterone (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Interstitial endocrine cells, or Leydig cells, are located in the interstitial tissue between seminiferous tubules. They are large, polyhedral cells with eccentric nuclei containing 1–3 nucleoli. Their cytoplasm contains smooth endoplasmic reticulum, lipid droplets, mitochondria with tubulovesicular cristae and characteristic needle-shaped crystalloid inclusions (crystals of Reinke; approximately 3 x 20 μm) (Standring, 2020).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The interstitial tissue is located between the seminiferous tubules. It houses myoid cells, neurovasculature, and interstitial endocrine (Leydig) cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Interstitial cells of the testis (Leydig cells) are active during the first five months of male fetal life but then are inactive until responding to stimulation by pituitary gonadotropins at puberty and again synthesize and secrete testosterone. They remain active throughout adult life.

Secretion of testosterone is essential in the embryo for the normal development of the male gonads.

Interstitial cells (Leydig cells) also secrete insulin-like protein 3 that stimulates the descent of the testis during development. Insulin-like protein 3 promotes meiotic divisions in the seminiferous tubules.

Sperm production begins at puberty as well as secretions from accessory glands due to testosterone secretion. Secondary sex characteristics are dependent on testosterone secretion from the Leydig cells.

Leydig cells also produce and secrete oxytocin which stimulates contraction of the myoid cells so moving the spermatozoa along the seminiferous tubules towards the rete testis and excurrent ductal system (Standring, 2020).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Leydig cell tumors are mostly benign and are apparent in childhood then again between the age of 20 and 60 years old. They are related to abnormal levels of testosterone production and may lead to unexpected pubertal changes early in childhood (prepubertal boys) or in adults it may lead to feminization and gynecomastia (development of breasts).

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A capillary is any of the minute vessels that connect the arterioles and venules, forming a network in nearly all parts of the body. Their walls act as semipermeable membranes for the interchange of various substances, including fluids, between the blood and tissue fluid. The three principal types are continuous, discontinuous or sinusoidal, and fenestrated capillaries (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Capillaries are blood vessels with the smallest diameter and are classified into three types. 

—Continuous capillaries have a continuous endothelial lining. 

—Discontinuous, or sinusoidal, capillaries have the largest diameter and have large openings and intercellular spaces with a discontinuous supporting basal lamina. 

—Fenestrated capillaries have a continuous supporting basal lamina but have numerous small openings or windows (i.e., fenestrae) in the capillary wall.

Many capillaries have undifferentiated mesenchymal cells close by called pericytes.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Blood capillaries are located in the interstitial tissue compartment between seminiferous tubules.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Capillaries act as semipermeable vessels, which allow for the exchange of various substances between the blood and tissue.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Sperm is a mature male germ cell, the specific output of the testes. It is the generative element of the semen that serves to fertilize the oocyte and contains the genetic information to be transmitted to the zygote by the male. It consists of a head (or nucleus), a neck, a middle piece, and a tail with an end piece. Spermatozoa, formed in the seminiferous tubules, are derived from spermatogonia, which first develop into spermatocytes, which, in turn, undergo meiosis to produce spermatids; the spermatids then differentiate into spermatozoa (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The mature sperm, or spermatozoon, is a highly differentiated and motile haploid cell. It is composed of a head, neck, and tail (flagellum) and measures about 60 μm in length (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014). The sperm is entirely encapsulated in a plasma membrane, which undergoes regional modifications necessary for fertilization to occur.

The sperm head is flattened and pointed in shape and measures approximately 4.5 μm long, 3 μm wide, and 1 μm thick. It is made up of the nucleus, of which the anterior two thirds is covered by the acrosomal cap and a scanty cytoplasm. The nucleus contains tightly packed chromatin that is enveloped anteriorly by the acrosomal cap. The sperm head is connected to the tail via a short neck, or connecting piece, which spans approximately 0.3 μm in length (Standring, 2020).

The tail makes up most of the sperm’s length, measuring about 55 μm. It is made up of three distinct parts: the middle piece, principal piece, and the end piece. The sperm tail contains several structural components including the axoneme, mitochondrial sheath, outer dense fibers, and the fibrous sheath. The function of the tail is to propel the sperm forward in a whiplash-like fashion and to generate the energy required for this movement.

Sperm is an end product of a process called spermatogenesis. Sperm in the seminiferous tubules are highly differentiated, but are still relatively non-motile. They acquire their motility as they pass through the epididymis. 

Fertilization cannot be completed without a process known as capacitation. Capacitation is essentially the functional maturation of a sperm cell and is completed after the sperm has made its journey to the uterine tube (oviduct or fallopian tube). Various structural and biochemical changes occur during capacitation in which sperm change their behavior, including the acrosome reaction. Following capacitation, sperm develop the ability to penetrate the cumulus of the egg and bind to the zona pellucida. This stimulates the release of digestive enzymes from the acrosome to aid in the dissolution of the zona pellucida in the vicinity of the sperm head, allowing it to access the perivitelline space (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014; Standring, 2020).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The principal function of the sperm is to move through the female genital tract, fuse and penetrate the ovum and deliver the male pronucleus containing the genetic material. It also contributes centrioles that help to organize the cytoskeleton of the zygote.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Infertility

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Sustentocytes, or Sertoli cells, are cells elongated cells in the seminiferous tubules, to which the spermatids become attached; they provide support, protection, and possibly nutrition until the spermatids become transformed into mature spermatozoa (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Sustentocytes, more commonly known as Sertoli cells, are non-dividing, support cells found in the seminiferous tubules and may occupy 25% of epithelial volume. Each Sertoli cell partly or completely surrounds several dozen germ cells (Standring, 2020).

Adjacent Sertoli cells have long cytoplasmic processes that extend above the basal spermatogonia and interface with each other, forming specialized tight cell junctions. This organization essentially creates the blood testis barrier, which creates basal and adluminal compartments within the seminiferous tubules and prevents intercellular transport of substances. The tight junctions can disassemble, enabling spermatogonia that lose their connection with the basement membrane to migrate to the adluminal compartment.

Sertoli cells are variable in shape although mostly appear as a pyramidal cell. Their basal ends sit on the basement membrane, while their apical ends extend into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: In the adult testis, Sertoli cells occupy up to 25% of the volume of the seminiferous epithelium.

sections.name: Function
List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: The blood testis barrier can be disrupted by trauma or inflammatory events, leading to subfertility.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
Most epithelia attach to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basal lamina. The basal lamina is a thin sheet of extracellular proteins and fibrils. Additionally, carbohydrate-rich material is appended to the lower face of the basal lamina. If the accumulation is sufficient, the basal lamina is referred to as a basement membrane.

The basement membrane is synthesized by the epithelium and the additional material by the underlying connective tissue cells. Some epithelia do not have a basement membrane but most have a basal lamina (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Most epithelia are attached to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basal lamina.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The basement membrane separates the seminiferous epithelium from the underlying connective tissue within the interstitial compartment of the testis.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ovalle, W. K., Nahirney, P. C. and Netter, F. H. (2013) Netter's Essential Histology. ClinicalKey 2012: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A primary spermatocyte is a diploid cell that has derived from a spermatogonium and can subsequently begin meiosis and divide into two haploid secondary spermatocytes (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Progenitor cells (type B spermatogonia) differentiate into primary spermatocytes. Primary spermatocytes are diploid cells, i.e., they have 46 chromosomes and 4N of DNA. When a primary spermatocyte is formed, it quickly enters the 1st meiotic division and these cells are viewed in more numbers in the prophase of this 1st meiotic division as this stage of meiosis takes about 22 days (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

Primary spermatocytes are the largest spermatogenic cell and are easily identified by the presence of coiled chromosomes in their nuclei.

Primary spermatocytes undergo two meiotic cell divisions so that the resultant haploid cells, called spermatids, contain half the original chromosome number and amount of DNA. Small cells, called secondary spermatocytes, arise from the first meiotic division.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Primary spermatocytes are confined to the basal epithelial compartment of the seminiferous epithelium.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Primary spermatocytes undergo two meiotic cell divisions so that the resultant haploid cells called spermatids contain half the original chromosome number and amount of DNA. 

Small cells, called secondary spermatocytes, arise from the first meiotic division.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A spermatogonium is an undifferentiated germ cell of a male, originating in a seminiferous tubule and dividing into two primary spermatocytes (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Spermatogonia are the germ cells of spermatozoa. They arise from primordial germ cells that migrate to the genital cords during development of the testes. 

Spermatogonia are only small cells, about 12 μm in diameter, and are located adjacent to the basement membrane of the seminiferous epithelium. At puberty they undergo mitotic divisions producing a renewing population of stem cells, type A dark (Ad) spermatogonia, or type A pale (Ap) spermatogonia. Type A pale (Ap) spermatogonia continue through many mitotic divisions and establish a population of renewing stem cells that will differentiate into progenitor cells (Type B spermatogonia) which will differentiate into primary spermatocytes (Standring, 2020).

When a type B spermatogonium divides and subsequent populations of cells differentiate, these cells do not completely separate but maintain a connection through small cytoplasmic bridges. This intercellular bridge permits communication between the primary and secondary spermatocytes and the spermatids.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: In the fully differentiated testis, spermatogonia are located adjacent to the basement membrane of the seminiferous epithelium.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Spermatogonia are the germ cells for all spermatozoa.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Myoid cells are the cells found in the seminiferous tubules of common laboratory rodents, which cytologically resemble smooth muscle and are presumed to be contractile and to be responsible for the rhythmic shallow contractions of the seminiferous tubules of these species (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The myoid layer of the convoluted seminiferous tubules consists of three to five layers of thin contractile cells, called myoid cells, and collagen fibrils.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The myoid layer is located between the basal compartment and the interstitial connective tissue of the testis.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Myoid cells are contractile. Leydig cells in the adjacent interstitial tissue produce and secrete oxytocin which stimulates contraction of the myoid cells, thus moving the spermatozoa along the seminiferous tubules towards the rete testis and excurrent ductal system.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A secondary spermatocyte is one of the two haploid cells into which a primary spermatocyte divides and which in turn gives origin to spermatids (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Primary spermatocytes undergo two meiotic cell divisions so that the resultant haploid cells, called spermatids, contain half the original chromosome number and amount of DNA. 

Small cells, called secondary spermatocytes, arise from the first meiotic division. Each cell contains only 23 chromosomes and either an X or a Y chromosome. There is also a reduction from 4N to 2N of DNA in each secondary spermatocyte. These cells are very sparse in the seminiferous epithelium because they rapidly enter the second meiotic division and give rise to spermatids.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Secondary spermatocytes occupy the adluminal compartment of the seminiferous epithelium.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Secondary spermatocytes give rise to spermatids.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A spermatid is a cell derived from a secondary spermatocyte by fission, and capable of undergoing spermiogenesis to develop into a spermatozoon (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The younger generation of spermatids are small round cells (7–8 μm in diameter), with condensed chromatin in their round nuclei, and are located adjacent to the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. Quickly the round spermatids will enter the differentiation process called spermiogenesis with the end of the process characterized by more elongated spermatids.

Spermiogenesis involves the development of the acrosome, condensation and elongation of the nucleus, development of the flagellum, and loss of the majority of the cytoplasm. The spermatozoon is then released into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. This morphological transformation enables the spermatozoon to be highly specialized to deliver the male DNA to the ovum.

There are three phases in spermiogenesis including the Golgi, acrosomal, and maturation phase.

—During the Golgi phase, spermatids contain free ribosomes, tubules of smooth endoplasmic reticulum, and very prominent Golgi complexes adjacent to the nucleus. Small pro-acrosomal granules (rich in glycoproteins) accumulate in the Golgi complex and rapidly coalesce into acrosomal granules housed within a membrane-bound acrosomal vesicle. The location of the vesicle defines the anterior pole of the developing sperm. A flagellar axoneme begins forming as the centrioles move to a location opposite the site of the future acrosomal cap.

—During the acrosomal phase, the acrosomal vesicle extends over the anterior portion of the condensed nucleus to become the acrosome. It is a specialized lysosome containing hydrolytic enzymes, in particular hyaluronidase, neuraminidase, acid phosphatase and a protease with trypsin-like activity. These enzymes will disperse the cells of the corona radiata and digest the zona pellucida. Also during this phase, the spermatid becomes oriented so that the condensed nucleus elongates and faces the seminiferous epithelium and the axoneme extends into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. One centriole forms the flagellum and mitochondria begin to collect around its proximal portion, forming a region called the middle piece.

—The maturation phase is characterized by shedding of the cytoplasm and the cytoplasmic bridges as residual bodies which are phagocytosed by sustentocytes (Sertoli cells). Spermatozoa are then released into the seminiferous tubule lumen.

A proportion of spermatids degenerate during maturation, reducing the expected yield (Standring, 2020).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Spermatids undergo spermiogenesis and differentiate into spermatozoa.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Some pharmacological treatments, toxic agents and any decrease in gonadotrophins can prevent spermiation and so the spermatids are phagocytized by Sertoli cells.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A spermatid is a cell derived from a secondary spermatocyte by fission, and capable of undergoing spermiogenesis to develop into a spermatozoon (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Secondary spermatocytes rapidly enter the second meiotic division and give rise to spermatids each having 23 chromosomes (a haploid number of chromosomes) and N amount of DNA since there is no DNA synthesis between the first and second meiotic divisions. Following the union of the spermatozoon with an ovum, the diploid number of chromosomes is achieved.

Spermiogenesis is the transformation of spermatids into spermatozoa. 

During spermatogenesis cell division occurs but there is no cell division during spermiogenesis.

The younger generation of spermatids are small round cells (7–8 μm in diameter), with condensed chromatin in their round nuclei, and are located adjacent to the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. Quickly the round spermatids will enter the differentiation process called spermiogenesis with the end of the process characterized by more elongated spermatids.

Spermiogenesis involves the development of the acrosome, condensation and elongation of the nucleus, development of the flagellum, and loss of the majority of the cytoplasm. The spermatozoon is then released into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. This morphological transformation enables the spermatozoon to be highly specialized to deliver the male DNA to the ovum.

There are three phases in spermiogenesis including the Golgi, acrosomal, and maturation phase.

—During the Golgi phase, spermatids contain free ribosomes, tubules of smooth endoplasmic reticulum, and very prominent Golgi complexes adjacent to the nucleus. Small pro-acrosomal granules (rich in glycoproteins) accumulate in the Golgi complex and rapidly coalesce into acrosomal granules housed within a membrane-bound acrosomal vesicle. The location of the vesicle defines the anterior pole of the developing sperm. A flagellar axoneme begins forming as the centrioles move to a location opposite the site of the future acrosomal cap.

— During the acrosomal phase, the acrosomal vesicle extends over the anterior portion of the condensed nucleus to become the acrosome. It is a specialized lysosome containing hydrolytic enzymes, in particular hyaluronidase, neuraminidase, acid phosphatase and a protease with trypsin-like activity. These enzymes will disperse the cells of the corona radiata and digest the zona pellucida. Also during this phase, the spermatid becomes oriented so that the condensed nucleus elongates and faces the seminiferous epithelium and the axoneme extends into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. One centriole forms the flagellum and mitochondria begin to collect around its proximal portion, forming a region called the middle piece.

—The maturation phase is characterized by shedding of the cytoplasm and the cytoplasmic bridges as residual bodies which are phagocytosed by sustentocytes (Sertoli cells). Spermatozoa are then released into the seminiferous tubule lumen.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The dura mater is the outermost, toughest, and most fibrous of the three membranes (meninges) covering the brain and spinal cord (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
There are three layers that make up the meninges, the dura, arachnoid, and pia mater. The meningeal layers can also be divided according to the stage of their development, including the leptomeninges (arachnoid and pia mater) and pachymeninx (dura mater).

The dura mater is a dense fibrous layer, composed mostly of tightly packed fascicles of collagen in a laminae configuration. It lies external to the arachnoid and is separated from the arachnoid by the subdural space. 

The cranial dura mater has two layers, the external endosteal layer and the internal meningeal layer. The endosteal layer of the cranial dura mater is adherent with the inner surface of the calvaria, particularly at the sutures, the cranial base, and in the vicinity of the foramen magnum. The endosteal layer is continuous with the periosteum on the outer aspect of the calvaria at the cranial foramina, while the meningeal layer is continuous with the spinal dura at the foramen magnum. The two layers are inseparable, except at points where the dural sinuses and dural reflections arise. The meningeal layer of the dura mater is closely associated with the arachnoid and both layers are fused at points where veins course from the brain into the venous sinuses (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013; Standring, 2016).

Dural reflections, or infoldings, are formed by the inner meningeal layer of the dura at points where it separates from the external endosteal layer. The dural reflections include the falx cerebri, falx cerebelli, tentorium cerebelli, and diaphragma sellae. These reflections divide the cranial cavity into various compartments (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013). 

The falx cerebri is shaped like a crescent. It narrows anteriorly towards the point where it attaches to the crista galli, and widens posteriorly to merge with the tentorium cerebelli. It is the largest of the four dural reflections and is inhabited in the longitudinal fissure between the left and right cerebral hemispheres. The inferior edge of the falx is free and houses the inferior sagittal sinus. The falx cerebri terminates by continuing as the tentorium cerebelli (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

The falx cerebelli is a small vertical dural reflection that is situated in the posterior cranial fossa, inferior to the tentorium cerebelli. It slightly separates the two cerebral hemispheres. Posteriorly, it is attached to the internal occipital crest and inhabits the occipital sinus (Standring, 2016)

The diaphragma sellae, the smallest of the four dural reflections, is a spherical horizontal sheet that hangs between the clinoid processes and forms a roof over the sella turcica, encircling the pituitary gland. 

The tentorium cerebelli is the second-largest dural reflection and shaped like a crescent. It is situated between the cerebellum and the occipital lobes. It separates the cranial cavity into supra- and infra-tentorial segments where the forebrain and hindbrain are situated, respectively. The falx cerebri affixes itself to the tentorium cerebelli and props it up, hence the similarity to a tent. It connects to the sphenoid bone (rostrally), the petrous portion of the temporal bone (rostrolaterally), the occipital bone, and the parietal bone (posterolaterally) (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The dura mater forms the external sheet of the meninges and is separated from the arachnoid by the subdural space.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The principal function of meningeal layers is to protect and provide support to the brain and spinal cord. The dura mater is thickest and most resilient of the three meningeal layers; hence it shields the brain and spinal cord from mechanical trauma.

The dura mater encircles and supports the dural venous sinuses that convey blood from the brain to the heart. It is also responsible for sealing the central nervous system to ensure cerebrospinal fluid is kept within.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: An odor is a volatile emanation that is perceived by the sense of smell (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Odor molecules are small, volatile, lipid-soluble molecules, contained within inhaled air, and are detected and processed by the olfactory system in order to facilitate the sense of smell. 

During the process of olfactory transduction by the olfactory sensory neurons, odor molecules are absorbed and bind to the odor-binding proteins present within the mucus layer of the olfactory epithelium. Odor molecules are then detected by the odorant receptors in the olfactory cilia (Longstaff, 2005). 

The olfactory epithelium contains bipolar olfactory sensory neurons, which have long dendrites that project to the epithelial surface forming olfactory cilia (Longstaff, 2005). 

Odorant receptors are a group of approximately 1,000 G-protein-coupled receptors, most of which are linked to the cAMP second messenger system. On binding of an odorant molecule to an odorant receptor, cAMP levels increase resulting in the opening of a cation channel and subsequently the generation of a depolarizing generator potential that corresponds to the concentration of various odorants (Longstaff, 2005). 

Each olfactory sensory neuron exhibits a single species of odorant receptor, while each odorant receptor binds a multitude of homologous molecules with varying affinities. As a result of the low specificity of odorant receptors, olfactory receptor neurons can detect a multitude of odors (Longstaff, 2005).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The odor molecules, which are contained within inhaled air, are identified by the olfactory system. This facilitates olfactory transduction and makes sense of smell possible.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The lamina propria is the connective tissue coat of a mucous membrane just deep to the epithelium and basement membrane (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The olfactory mucosa is composed of the olfactory epithelium and the lamina propria.

The lamina propria is approximately two to three times thicker than the olfactory epithelium. It is situated deep to the olfactory epithelium, separated from it by a basement membrane. 

The lamina propria is a highly vascularized layer made up of collagen, elastin, as well as a number of connective tissue elements including fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, and leukocytes. The lamina propria also contains lymphatic vessels, olfactory nerve fibers, and olfactory glands (Farbman et al., 1992; Krstic, 2013; Conn, 2008). A notable amount of olfactory ensheathing glia are situated within the lamina propria.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lamina propria is situated deep to the basement membrane of the olfactory epithelium, separating it from the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The lamina propria contains blood and lymph vessels through which the olfactory organ is nourished and drained. It also contains immune cells such as macrophages, mast cells, and leukocytes. In addition to this, the lamina propria houses the olfactory glands, which are responsible for secreting the serous component of the mucus layer that covers the olfactory epithelium.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The olfactory mucosa is composed of the olfactory epithelium and the lamina propria. The basement membrane essentially separates the lamina propria from the olfactory epithelium. The basal (stem) cells of the olfactory epithelium, through which olfactory cell regenerate, are situated along the basement membrane.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The basement membrane essentially separates the lamina propria from the olfactory epithelium.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The principal function of a basement membrane is to provide structural support for the epithelium. In this case, it is the olfactory epithelium.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Centrifugal nerve fibers are those that arise from the brain and act on the mitral and tufted cells as they respond to incoming stimuli.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
There are three neural pathways (aside from the primary olfactory fibers) through which efferent fibers are conveyed to the olfactory bulb. The centrifugal axons arise from the brain. The other two pathways are the commissural fibers and collaterals from the anterior olfactory nucleus (Masterton, 2013). 

The olfactory bulb receives a large number of centrifugal neural inputs from various higher processing parts of the brain, which potentially influence the neuronal activity of the mitral and tufted cells as they respond to incoming stimuli. The centrifugal fibers use a variety of neurotransmitters and neuromodulators and arise from the cerebral cortex. Their cortical inputs arise from areas including the cerulean nucleus (locus caeruleus), raphe nucleus, ipsilateral anterior olfactory nucleus, and the diagonal band of Broca’s area (Haines and Ard, 2006). Excitatory amino acids such as glutamate can be found within the centrifugal fibers that originate from structures in the cerebral cortex.

Fibers originating from the cerulean nucleus and raphe nucleus in the midbrain terminate in the glomeruli of the glomerular cell layer. Fibers originating from the anterior olfactory nucleus and Broca’s area terminate on periglomerular cells (Haines and Ard, 2006).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The centrifugal axons function as a feedback loop, which represents the afferent neural system (Arslan, 2014).

The olfactory bulb receives a large number of centrifugal neural inputs from various higher processing parts of the brain, which potentially influence the neuronal activity of the mitral and tufted cells as they respond to incoming stimuli (Masterton, 2013). 

The centrifugal axons have numerous sites of termination on the olfactory bulb. This suggests that their neuromodulatory influences are diverse and affect a substantial number of olfactory bulb neurons simultaneously. The neuromodulatory inputs of the centrifugal axons aid in the attainment of odor memory (Haines and Ard, 2006).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The olfactory glomerulus is one of the small globular masses of dense neuropil in the olfactory bulb; it contains the first synapse in the olfactory pathway, and the axons of olfactory cells synapse here with dendrites primarily of mitral cells and tufted cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The glomeruli are circular non-conspicuous areas, with diameters of about 150 μm, and are situated within the glomerular layer of the olfactory bulb (Barlow and Mollon, 1982). 

Each glomerulus is a composite site of synapses, where incoming olfactory nerve fibers split and synapse with the dendrites of mitral, tufted, and periglomerular cells (Standring, 2016; Longstaff, 2005). 

Glomeruli have odor specificity, since each of them receives nerve fibers from olfactory sensory cells that respond to the same category of odors. There are about 2000 glomeruli within each olfactory bulb, each of which receives the nerve fibers of up to 25,000 olfactory sensory cells (Longstaff, 2005). 

The glomeruli are surrounded by the cell bodies of periglomerular cells. The dendritic branches of these periglomerular cells extend into the glomerulus (Barlow and Mollon, 1982).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The glomeruli are situated within the glomerular layer of the olfactory bulb. The glomerular layer lies internal to the olfactory nerve layer and external to the external plexiform layer of the olfactory bulb (Barlow and Mollon, 1982).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Glomeruli play a key role in odor specification and identification as each glomerulus responds to specific groups of odors.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The periglomerular cells are nerve cells in the olfactory bulb that have synaptic connections with glomeruli, mitral cells, and tufted cells, and are thought to act as dampers (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The periglomerular cell is one of the two main types of interneurons in the olfactory bulb. The second type is the granular cell. They are contained almost exclusively within the glomerular layer, which contains the external tufted cells and the axons of other cells. The periglomerular cell synapses with the olfactory sensory neurons, the mitral/tufted cells, and the centrifugal efferent nerve fibers (Standring, 2016; Pignatelli and Belluzzi, 2017; Csillag, 2007). 

The periglomerular cells have axons that project laterally, all of which terminate in the extraglomerular parts of the olfactory bulb (Standring, 2016; Kosaka and Kosaka, 2009). 

The periglomerular cells are the only catecholaminergic neurons located within the olfactory bulb. They are significantly flexible and continuously regenerated throughout a person’s lifetime. Although most of the periglomerular cells are dopaminergic, some are GABAergic (Pignatelli and Belluzzi, 2017).

Some periglomerular cells receive minimal to no inputs from the olfactory sensory neurons and these particular types of periglomerular cells have been known to be located in specific areas within the glomerulus. Thus, the glomerulus essentially has two compartments, the olfactory neuron compartment and the non-olfactory neuron compartment. It is within the olfactory neuron compartment is where periglomerular neurons synapse with mitral/tufted cells and olfactory sensory cells (Kosaka and Kosaka, 2009).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The periglomerular cells are located in the periglomerular region, within the glomerular layer of the olfactory bulb.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The periglomerular cells are tactically located at the entry points of the olfactory bulb where they synapse with olfactory sensory neurons conveying incoming olfactory neural information. This unique positioning at the commencement point of the olfactory bulb circuitry means they play a major role in processing of odors and modification of the olfactory bulb neural interconnections to external stimuli (Pignatelli and Belluzzi, 2017).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Mitral cells are neurons with pyramidal bodies located in the olfactory bulb, being the second stage in the pathway to the cortex; they receive impulses in the olfactory glomeruli from the olfactory cells and transmit impulses through the olfactory tracts to various areas of the cortex (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The mitral cell is the principal neuron of the olfactory bulb, with a cell body diameter of 20–30 μm. Fibers of the olfactory nerve carrying sensory information synapse with the mitral cells. The axons of mitral cells coalesce to form the major output of the olfactory bulb to the cerebral cortex (Blass, 1988; Barlow and Mollon, 1982). 

The cell body of mitral cells is made up of a large circular nucleus and a cytoplasm. Within the nucleus, there are one or multiple apparent nucleoli as well as granular chromatin that are spread out around the nucleus. A large number of ribosomes, as well as prominent Golgi bodies are situated in the perikaryon of mitral cells. Dendrites and axons arise from the cell body. The point at which the axon arises from the cell body is referred to as the axon hillock. The cell bodies of mitral cells are arranged in a way that they form a mitral cell layer that is internal to the glomerular and external plexiform layers (Blass, 1988; Farbman et al., 1992). 

The dendrites of mitral cells arise from the apical aspect of the cell body. The dendrite travels superficially, and into a glomerulus (in the glomerular layer) via the external plexiform layer where it branches abundantly, forming a dendritic tree of thin dendritic processes (Farbman et al., 1992). 

The mitral cells have an additional group of dendrites called the basal dendrites, which are not involved with the glomeruli. These basal dendrites synapse with the dendrites of the granular cells. These synapses are referred to as dendrodendritic synapses (Brown, 2012).

The axons of the mitral cell travel caudally and eventually coalesce to form the lateral olfactory tract, which is the major output of the olfactory bulb to the cerebral cortex. The axons of mitral cells have collaterals that branch off them and terminate on the anterior olfactory nucleus. The cells of the anterior olfactory nucleus in turn project back to the dendritic spines of the granular cells which lie in close proximity to the dendrodendritic synapses with mitral cells (Brown, 2012; Barlow and Mollon, 1982).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The cell bodies of the mitral cells are situated in the mitral layer of the olfactory bulb. Their dendrites extend across the external plexiform and glomerular layers of the olfactory bulb.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Mitral cells are vital in the olfactory transduction. Their axons form the major output of the olfactory bulb to the cerebral cortex (Barlow and Mollon, 1982).

Neural impulses from the mitral cell travel to the cerebral cortex where it activates target neurons by releasing glutamate. The neural impulse also activates the granular cells through collaterals from axons, as well as by projecting back to the basal dendrites that lie in close proximity to the dendrodendritic synapses between the granular and mitral cells (Brown, 2012).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The olfactory bulb is the bulblike expansion of the olfactory tract on the undersurface of the frontal lobe of each cerebral hemisphere; the olfactory nerves enter it (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The olfactory bulb is a structure located on the inferior surface of the frontal lobe, on the undersurface of the frontal lobe. Each individual has two olfactory bulbs, one associated with each cerebral hemisphere. The olfactory bulb sits just intracranially to the cribriform plate. It receives input from olfactory nerve bundles located in the nasal epithelium.

The olfactory bulb is the point where olfactory nerve bundles terminate and their central processes coalesce. Their fibers synapse with the mitral cells located in the olfactory bulb.

The olfactory nerve fibers originate from the olfactory epithelium in the superior aspect of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. These nerves, encircled by dura and arachnoid mater, travel through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone via cribriform foramina, to reach the olfactory bulb in the anterior cranial fossa.

The olfactory bulb’s structure has a layered configuration. From external to the internal, the layers include the olfactory nerve layer, glomerular layer, external plexiform layer, mitral cell layer, internal plexiform layer, and the granular cell layer. 

The olfactory nerve layer is made up of unmyelinated axons of the olfactory neurons in various stages of development. The glomerular layer is essentially a thin layer of glomeruli, where the olfactory sensory axons entering the olfactory bulb divide and synapse with the dendrites of secondary olfactory neurons (the mitral, tufted, and periglomerular cells). The dendrites of the mitral and tufted cells make up the external plexiform layer, while the cell bodies of the mitral cells make up the thin mitral cell layer. Each of these cell bodies contains a number of granular cell bodies, which project:

—a solitary principal dendrite to a glomerulus;

—a number of secondary dendrites to the external plexiform layer;

—a solitary axon to the olfactory tract. 

The internal plexiform layer is composed of axons of mitral and tufted cells, as well as some granular cell bodies. The majority of granular cells are situated in the granule cell layer. The granular cell layer also contains centrifugal nerve fibers. This layer projects into the olfactory tract in the form of multipolar neurons with which the anterior olfactory nucleus is made up of (Standring, 2016). The axons from the anterior olfactory nucleus are continuous with the rest of the olfactory fibers that travel from the bulb to the striae (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013; Standring, 2016). 

The olfactory tract originates at the posterior margin of the olfactory bulb. It runs parallel to and on either side of the midline on the inferior surface of the brain. The tract runs posteriorly to the anterior perforated substance where it bifurcates and penetrates the brain as the medial and lateral olfactory striae. The medial olfactory stria runs medially, anterior to the anterior perforated substance. It penetrates the cortex and sends axons to the septal nuclei and through the anterior commissure to the contralateral olfactory cortex.

The lateral olfactory stria runs laterally, anterior to the anterior perforated substance. It penetrates the uncus where it sends axons to the primary olfactory cortex.

Afferent neural inputs to the olfactory bulb come from the anterior olfactory nucleus, collaterals of pyramidal neurons, Broca’s area of the forebrain (cholinergic neurons), cerulean nucleus (pontine locus caeruleus), and the mesencephalic raphe nucleus. These afferent inputs are to the granular and glomerular layers of the olfactory bulb. The efferent fibers of the olfactory bulb project to the amygdala, hippocampus, and the orbitofrontal cortex (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The olfactory bulb is fundamental in the process of olfactory transduction. It receives neural signals about odors (via odor molecules) detected by olfactory sensory neurons in the nasal cavity. Odor molecules are absorbed and bind to the odor-binding proteins present within the mucus layer of the olfactory epithelium. Odor molecules are then detected by the odorant receptors in the olfactory cilia. This information is subsequently transmitted to the olfactory bulb via the axons of the olfactory sensory neurons, where they are processed. The processing of odor molecules makes it possible to differentiate between various odors (Longstaff, 2005).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Granular cells are inhibitory interneurons located in the granular layer of the olfactory bulb.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Amacrine granular cells are neurons situated within the internal granular layer of the olfactory bulb. Granular cells are inhibitory interneurons with small cell bodies that are 5–10 μm in diameter, a number of short basal dendrites, long dendritic spines, and no axons. Because they have no axons, their action is totally reliant on dendrite-to-dendrite synapses. The granular cells can be classified into the light and dark subtypes based on how darkly or lightly their nuclei stain (Nieuwenhuys, Voogd and van Huijzen, 2007; Farbman et al., 1992). 

The dendrites of granular cells travel peripherally to the external plexiform layer. Here, the granular cell dendrites synapse with the secondary dendrites of the mitral and tufted cells. Excitation of the mitral and/or tufted cells in turn excites their secondary dendrites, which in turn excites the granular cells. The excited granular cells respond by inhibiting the mitral and tufted cells (Margolis and Getchell, 2013).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The olfactory bulb has a layered configuration. From external to internal, the layers include the olfactory nerve layer, glomerular layer, external plexiform layer, mitral cell layer, internal plexiform layer, and the (internal) granular cell layer (Standring, 2016).

The amacrine granular cells mostly lie within the internal granular layer of the olfactory bulb, deep to the mitral cells, although cells are situated in the internal plexiform and mitral cell layers. The granular cell layer is the most discernible layer in the olfactory bulb (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The inhibitory action of the granular cells plays a vital role in refining the sensory output of the olfactory bulb during olfactory transduction (Balu, Pressler and Strowbridge, 2007). The granular cells may also play a role in forming long-term memories associated with various scents.

sections.text: —Anosmia

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A tufted cell is a type of neuron in the olfactory bulb; smaller, more numerous, and more superficially located than a mitral cell but with similar functions and connections (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Tufted cells, to a lesser extent (in comparison to mitral cells), are principal neurons of the olfactory bulb. They form the minor output of the olfactory bulb to the cerebral cortex via the olfactory tract, while the mitral cells form the major output. Although tufted cells are smaller than mitral cells, their branching configuration and synapses are similar. 

Tufted cells are situated throughout the external plexiform layer of the olfactory bulb and at the border of the glomerular layer. The tufted cells extend to inter- and intrabulbar locations, as well as to the piriform cortex (Davis and Eichenbaum, 1991). 

Tufted cells can be grouped into three subtypes, the external, middle, and internal tufted cells. They are situated in close proximity to the boundary between the glomerular layer and the external plexiform layer. They have small cell bodies with a diameter of 10–15 μm. 

The middle tufted cells have medium-sized cell bodies (15–20 μm in diameter) and are situated within the intermediate and superficial aspects of the external plexiform layer. The internal tufted cells have large cell bodies with diameters greater than 20 μm. They are situated in the deep part of the external plexiform layer (Soiza-Reilly, Saggau and Arenkiel, 2015). 

The dendrites of tufted cells arise from the apical aspect of the cell body. They travel superficially to a glomerulus where they each branch (less abundantly in comparison to the mitral cells) forming a dendritic tree of thin dendritic processes (Farbman et al., 1992).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Tufted cells are situated throughout the external plexiform layer of the olfactory bulb, and at the border of the glomerular layer.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Tufted cells play a role in olfactory transduction and facilitate the sense of smell along with the mitral cells. The tufted cells activate other parts of the olfactory system using a number of inter- and intrabulbar interconnections (Arslan, 2014).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Mucus is the free slime of the mucous membranes, composed of secretion of the glands, along with various inorganic salts, desquamated cells, and leukocytes (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Mucus is a thin, transparent fluid produced by the epithelial lining of many body tissues. It is composed mainly of high molecular weight glycoproteins (Parke, 2013).

The nasal mucus is secreted by mucus and serous glands in the lamina propria and epithelial goblet cells. It can be grouped into two categories, neutral glycoprotein (fucomucin) and acidic glycoproteins (sialomucin and sulfomucin) (Liron et al., 1998).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: There is a mucus layer situated at the base of the olfactory epithelium. The olfactory epithelium is made up of olfactory bipolar olfactory sensory neurons and supporting cells. The dendrites of the olfactory sensory neurons project through the olfactory epithelium to form olfactory cilia, which in turn extends into the layer of mucus secreted by the supporting cells (Longstaff, 2005).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Mucus layer overlying olfactory epithelium acts as a medium onto which odor molecules are absorbed. The odor molecules bind the odor-binding proteins in the mucus. Within this mucus medium, the odor-binding proteins concentrate the odor molecules which are subsequently able to reach the olfactory cilia (Longstaff, 2005). 

The mucus also serves as a filter for inhaled air; trapping irritants such as dust, smoke particles, bacteria, etc. Furthermore, the mucus serves as a shield for the epithelial layer, protecting the layer from damage caused by drying, extreme temperatures, infectious organisms, and non-infectious particles (Farbman et al., 1992).

sections.text:
—Cystic fibrosis 

—Acute respiratory distress syndrome 

—Asthma 

—Fucosidosis

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Glial cells are the cells of the supportive tissue of the central nervous system (neuroglia); these nonneural cells are of three kinds: astrocytes, oligodendrocytes (collectively termed macroglia), and microglia (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Olfactory glia originate in the olfactory system, arising originally from neural crest cells. They ensheath the axons of the olfactory sensory neurons in an unusual way that differs from the rest of the nervous system. They follow the olfactory sensory neurons through the lamina propria and the cribriform plate, to their synaptic terminals in the glomerular layer of the olfactory bulb. This enables them to guide the olfactory axons to the accurate location in the olfactory bulb. This unique configuration, unlike the rest of the nervous system, blurs the distinction between the territories of the central and peripheral nervous systems transition zones (Standring, 2016) 

Although olfactory glia have similar morphological and antigenic characteristics with astrocytes and non-myelinating Schwann cells, they have clear-cut attributes that define them. However, just like Schwann cells, olfactory glia can myelinate axons (Standring, 2016).

The olfactory glia, along with astrocytes situated between the olfactory axons, contribute to the glia limitans at the pial aspect of the olfactory bulbs.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The olfactory glia are situated in the lamina propria of the olfactory mucosa and the outer nerve layer of the olfactory bulb (Zigova, Sanberg and Sanchez-Ramos, 2002).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Olfactory glia guide the olfactory axons to their accurate positions in the olfactory bulb. Because the olfactory system is unique as it is one of the only tissues in the central nervous system that supports neurogenesis throughout life, olfactory glia can be useful in transplant-mediated cell repair via stem cells (Standring, 2016).

sections.text: —Spinal cord injuries

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Pia mater is the innermost of the three membranes (meninges) covering the brain and spinal cord, investing them closely and extending into the depths of the fissures and sulci; it consists of reticular, elastic, and collagenous fibers (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
There are three layers that make up the meninges, the dura, arachnoid, and pia mater. The meningeal layers can also be divided according to the stage of their development, including the leptomeninges (arachnoid and pia mater) and pachymeninx (dura mater).

The pia mater is the innermost of the three meningeal layers that are present around the brain and spinal cord. The meninges, as well as the cerebrospinal fluid encircle and protect the central nervous system. 

The pia mater is a fine, transparent, shiny, vascularized membrane. It appears to be tightly adhered to the cerebral surface, including all gyri and sulci, and cannot be dissected away. It is separated from the brain surface by a subpial space, which cannot be seen with the naked eye. The pia mater also closely surrounds the spinal cord, including the roots of the spinal nerves and the spinal blood vessels.

The pia mater and the arachnoid mater have similar structures as they share an embryological origin. Together, the pia and arachnoid make up the leptomeninges.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The pia mater forms the innermost layer of the meninges and is situated between the subarachnoid space and the subpial space. The cerebrospinal fluid can be found in the subarachnoid space.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The principal function of meningeal layers is to protect and provide support to the central nervous system. The pia mater plays a regulatory role in the central nervous system as it is concerned with the blood-brain barrier. More specifically, the pia mater serves as a regulatory gateway between the subarachnoid space and the brain.

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Bacterial meningitis

—Viral meningitis

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Supporting cells are cells that serve to provide support and protection and perhaps contribute to the nutrition of principal or other cells of certain organs; included are cells in the membranous labyrinth of the internal ear, olfactory epithelium, taste buds, and seminiferous tubules (Sertoli cells) (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The olfactory epithelium is made up of various cell types such as basal cells, olfactory sensory neurons, and the supporting epithelial cells (Rao, Vemuri and Carpenter, 2007). 

The supporting cells in the olfactory epithelium can be likened to the glial cells in the nervous system. They are non-neural cells that are located in the apical layer of the olfactory epithelium (Cheok and Karunanayaka, 2018). There are two types of supporting cells, the sustentacular and microvillar cells. 

The microvillar cells take up a superficial location within the olfactory epithelium. They are electron-lucent and shaped like flasks. At the apex of microvillar cells, there are microvilli that extend into the mucus layer that overlies the olfactory epithelium. The thickness of microvillar cells are about one tenth that of olfactory sensory neurons (Standring, 2016). 

The sustentacular cells are columnar cells that divide and partly envelope the olfactory sensory neurons. There are many microvilli situated on the apical surface of the sustentacular cells. These apical microvilli extend into the mucus layer overlying the olfactory epithelium where they are interconnected with the cilia of the olfactory sensory neurons. Desmosomes connect adjacent sustentacular cells near the epithelial surface, while tight junctions connect sustentacular cells and olfactory sensory neurons at the epithelial surface. These bonds aid in the stability of the olfactory epithelium (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
There are two types of supporting cells, the sustentacular cells and microvillar cells. 

The sustentacular cells provide metabolic and physical support for the olfactory epithelium. The physical support is as a result of the bonds formed by desmosomes and tight junctions between adjacent sustentacular cells, as well as between sustentacular cells and olfactory sensory neurons (Cheok and Karunanayaka, 2018; Standring, 2016). 

The function of microvillar cells is not well known. However, their apical microvilli increase the surface area for absorption.
