sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Alveolar pores are the openings between adjacent pulmonary alveoli that permit passage of air from one to another (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Alveolar pores are openings in the interalveolar septa, the space filled with connective tissue and capillaries that separates adjacent alveoli.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The alveolar pores are found between adjacent alveoli.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The alveolar pores allow air to circulate between adjacent alveoli.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: In obstructive lung disease where there is a blockage in the passage of air to the alveoli, alveoli distal to the blockage can still be aerated via the pores from adjacent pulmonary acini and lobules (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: References
sections.text:

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The basal lamina is the layer of the basement membrane lying next to the basal surface of the adjoining cell layer, composed of an electron-dense lamina densa and an electron-lucent lamina lucida; sometimes used to denote the lamina densa alone (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: The basal lamina is made up of several different proteins and carbohydrates, such as collagen, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The alveolar basal lamina is found adjacent to the pneumocytes (alveolar epithelial cells) and the basal lamina of the pulmonary capillaries, the latter to which it’s fused.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The alveolar basal lamina supports the type I and II pneumocytes.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Type I pneumocytes are the flattened cells of the alveolar epithelium, distinguished by their greatly attenuated cytoplasm and paucity of organelles (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
95% of the surface area of the alveolar epithelium is occupied by thin, squamous type I pneumocytes (type I alveolar cells). They’re joined to each other by occluding junctions which seals the airspace from the interalveolar septum (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

Type I pneumocytes aren’t able to divide (by mitosis). Type II pneumocytes are the progenitor cells for type I pneumocytes.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Gas exchange occurs across the type I pneumocytes.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The lamellar body is any of the osmiophilic, lipid-rich, layered bodies found in the type II alveolar cells of the lung (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: The apical cytoplasm of the type II pneumocytes is filled with vesicles caused by parallel stacks of membrane lamellae called lamellar bodies about 100–400 nm in diameter (Mescher, 2013). In routine histological sections, they give the impression of a foamy cytoplasm.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The lamellar bodies contain phospholipids, neutral lipids, and proteins that are continually secreted onto the air surface space by exocytosis to form an extracellular coating of surfactant. Surfactant decreases the alveolar surface tension but is also involved with removing foreign materials.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Type II pneumocytes are pleomorphic cells of the pulmonary alveolar epithelium that secrete surfactant and are distinguished by abundant cytoplasm containing numerous lipid-rich multilamellar bodies (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
About 5% of the surface area of the alveolar epithelium is occupied by cuboidal type II pneumocytes (type II alveolar cells) that bulge into the air luminal space (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). They have a dome shaped apical surface with numbers of short microvilli. There is some overlap on their lateral margins by the type I pneumocytes which are joined to the type II pneumocytes by occluding junctions.

The apical cytoplasm of the type II pneumocytes is filled with vesicles caused by parallel stacks of membrane lamellae called lamellar bodies about 100–400 nm in diameter (Mescher, 2013). In routine histological sections, they give the impression of a foamy cytoplasm.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant. The lamellar bodies contain phospholipids, neutral lipids and proteins that are continually secreted onto the air surface space by exocytosis to form an extracellular coating of surfactant. Surfactant decreases the alveolar surface tension but is also involved with removing foreign materials.

Type II pneumocytes are the progenitor cells for type I pneumocytes.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: After lung injury, type II pneumocytes divide to provide populations of both type I and type II pneumocytes.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Mescher, A. (2013) Junqueira's Basic Histology: Text and Atlas. 13th edn.: McGraw-Hill Education.

Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Surfactant is a mixture of phospholipids (chiefly lecithin and sphingomyelin) secreted by the alveolar type II cells into the alveoli and respiratory air passages, which reduces the surface tension of pulmonary fluids and thus contributes to the elastic properties of pulmonary tissue (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
Surfactant is produced and secreted by the type II pneumocytes. The critical component of surfactant that reduces surface tension is the phospholipid called dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC).

Hydrophobic proteins Surfactant protein A, B, C and D are also necessary for the structure and function of surfactant.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Surfactant covers the entire inner alveolar surface.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Surfactant decreases the alveolar surface tension and is involved with removing foreign materials.

—Surfactant protein A maintains surfactant homeostasis i.e., regulating the synthesis and secretion by the type II alveolar cells and also modulating immune responses to fungi, bacteria and viruses.

—Surfactant protein B assists the transport of the lamellar body onto the thin surface of surfactant and is critical in spreading the surfactant across the surface epithelium.

—Surfactant protein C orientates the DPPC within the thin film of surfactant and maintenance of the thin layer of surfactant.

—Surfactant protein D is involved in defense as it can bind to some microorganisms and to lymphocytes. It’s also a participant in local inflammatory responses to acute lung injury (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Surfactant synthesis occurs after the 35th week of fetal life. If there aren’t adequate secretions of surfactant, as is the case with premature infants, the alveoli collapse on successive exhalations. This is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Alveolar ducts are the small passages connecting the respiratory bronchioles and the alveolar sacs (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The distal ends of the respiratory bronchioles give rise to alveolar ducts. Initially, the walls of the ducts have an interrupted cell wall with smooth muscle and elastic fibers which bulge into the lumen. However, this disappears at the distal ends of the alveolar ducts and the lining is primarily that of type I pneumocytes (Kierszenbaum and Tres, 2020).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The alveolar ducts are found between the distal ends of the respiratory bronchioles and the alveolar sacs.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The alveolar ducts conduct oxygen-rich air to the alveoli for gas exchange to occur.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The perifollicular lymphocapillary network is the numerous lymphatic vessels accompanying the perifollicular capillary network.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Blind-ended lymphatic capillaries are composed of very thin squamous endothelial cells anchored to surrounding connective tissue elements.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The perifollicular lymphocapillary network surrounds the thyroid follicles.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The lymphatic capillaries may provide an alternative route for the hormones secreted by the thyroid to enter the bloodstream (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: References
sections.text: Ross, M. H. and Pawlina, W. (2016) Histology: A Text and Atlas. Wolters Kluwer Health.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Each lobe is surrounded by a thin connective tissue capsule which penetrates the parenchyma of the lobe and divides it into small irregular units or lobules.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The thyroid gland is surrounded by a capsule which penetrates the parenchyma of the lobes of the thyroid gland, dividing it into small irregular units or lobules.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The connective tissue septum divides the thyroid gland into smaller irregular functional units or lobules.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Parafollicular cells, or C thyrocytes, are ovoid cells with an irregular nucleus and many brown or black cytoplasmic granules, located in the follicular epithelium and interfollicular spaces along with the principal cells of the thyroid follicles, in the follicular epithelium and interfollicular spaces, and which elaborate calcitonin. They arise during embryonic life from the fifth pharyngeal pouches and are incorporated in the thyroid gland in mammals, but form discrete epithelial cell masses (ultimobranchial bodies) in submammalian vertebrates (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The thyroid follicle has two cell types, follicular cells, or T thyrocytes, and parafollicular cells, or C thyrocytes. 

Parafollicular cells are located within the basement membrane that surrounds the thyroid follicle. They are either solitary cells or occur in small clusters and have a rather foamy vesicle dominated cytoplasm. At the electron microscope (ultrastructural) level, the vesicles are between 60 and 550 nm in diameter (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). The apex of the parafollicular cells does not reach the lumen of the thyroid follicle, thus they not in contact with the central colloid.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The parafollicular cells are found within the thyroid follicle, squeezed within the basement membrane around the follicular epithelium.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The parafollicular cells secrete calcitonin which is responsible for lowering calcium levels in the blood.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Calcitonin can be secreted by several endocrine tumors e.g., medullary carcinoma of the thyroid.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The basement membrane is a thin sheet of amorphous extracellular material upon which the basal surfaces of epithelial cells rest; other cells associated with basement membranes are muscle cells, Schwann cells, and fat cells. The membrane is interposed between the cellular elements and the underlying connective tissue. It usually comprises two layers, the basal lamina and the reticular lamina, and is composed of Type IV collagen (which is unique to basement membranes), laminin, fibronectin, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Most epithelia are attached to some form of underlying connective tissues by a basal lamina. They are sheets of extracellular proteins and fibrils and are so thin that they can be seen only with an electron microscope. Under many epithelia, additional carbohydrate-rich material is appended to the lower face of the basal lamina. If the accumulation is sufficient to be seen under the light microscope, it is called a basement membrane. 

The basal lamina is synthesized by the epithelial cells and the additional material by the underlying connective tissue cells. Some epithelia do not have a basement membrane but most have a basal lamina (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2016; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The thyroid follicular cells are attached to the underlying connective tissues by a very thin basement membrane.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The basement membrane can influence the functions of epithelial cells and adheres the epithelium to the underlying connective tissue as a supporting/strengthening component.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The thyroid colloid is the colloid in the thyroid follicles; it contains several proteins, including thyroglobulin and CA2 (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Within the lumen of the thyroid follicle is a gel-like component called colloid. It’s the stored product thyroglobulin that was synthesized and secreted by the follicular cells.

The thyroglobulin is reabsorbed by the follicular cells via endocytosis from that colloid, which is then broken down and transformed into the two thyroid hormones, T3 and T4. 

Iodide is absorbed into the cell and highly concentrated. It is then oxidized and passed into the colloid as iodine, which forms a complex with the thyroglobulin. This is a very important complex, as when it’s reabsorbed back into the cell, it contributes to the formation of the thyroid hormones. So, two very important functions of this cell, one, to produce the thyroglobulin, and one to concentrate and oxidize iodide that helps form this iodinated thyroglobulin complex inside the colloid (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Colloid is found within the lumen of each thyroid follicle.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Thyroglobulin is stored in the thyroid colloid in the lumen of the follicle and is the location where iodination of the thyroglobulin occurs (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A follicular cell, or T thyrocyte, is an epithelial cell of a thyroid follicle; these produce thyroid hormones and become enlarged in some forms of goiter (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The thyroid follicle has two cell types, follicular cells, or T thyrocytes, and parafollicular cells, or C thyrocytes. 

Follicular cells, or T thyrocytes, are endocrine cells that form the wall of each thyroid follicle. Thyroid follicular cells are the only endocrine cells that synthesize its hormonal product and store it extracellularly. In inactive follicles, the follicular cells appear as low cuboidal or squamous. During their active secretory phase, they appear columnar.

The ultrastructure of the follicular cell reflects both secretory and absorptive functions. Thyroglobulin is synthesized on the rough endoplasmic reticulum inside the follicular cell. It is then glycosylated as it passes through the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus. The Golgi apparatus has a supranuclear position and packages the thyroglobulin into vesicles, which move to the surface of the cell and are released into the lumen of the follicle as colloid by a process called exocytosis. The thyroglobulin is then reabsorbed by endocytosis from the colloid into the follicular cells, broken down, and transformed into the two thyroid hormones, T3 and T4. 

Iodide is absorbed into the follicular cell and highly concentrated. It is oxidized and passes into the colloid as iodine, which forms a complex with the thyroglobulin. This is a very important complex, since when its reabsorbed back into the cell, it contributes to the formation of the thyroid hormones. 

Thyroid follicular cells exhibit typical junctional complexes at their apical surfaces. They also possess microvilli. These projections wrap around segments of the colloid, then by endocytosis, the colloid is brought inside the cell as colloidal reabsorption droplets and fuse with lysosomes at the apex of the cell. Within the cell, the thyroglobulin reacts with lysosomal enzymes and other enzymes forming the thyroid hormones T3 and T4, which are released on the basal aspect of the cell into blood or lymphatic capillaries nearby (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). 

In tissue sections, the apical surface of the follicular cells appear as uneven boundaries close to the lumen, representing the endocytotic and exocytotic activity of the follicular cells.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Follicular cells form the lining of each thyroid follicle.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The thyroid follicular cell synthesizes and secretes the thyroid hormones, T3, and T4, which are released on the basal aspect of the cell into neighboring blood or lymphatic capillaries.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Microvilli are the minute cylindrical processes on the free surface of a cell, organized around a core of cross-linked actin filaments anchored to the terminal web, which increase the surface size of the cell; found especially in cells of the proximal convolution of the renal tubules and of the intestinal epithelium (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Thyroid follicular cells possess microvilli on their apical surfaces. They are short in resting follicular cells; however, they elongate and are often branched upon activation (Standring, 2020).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Microvilli are found on the apical surface of thyroid follicular cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The microvilli of thyroid follicular cells wrap around segments of the colloid, and by endocytosis, the colloid is brought inside the cell.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The stroma of thyroid gland is the tissue that forms the framework of the thyroid gland (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The thyroid follicles are surrounded by a delicate connective tissue stroma. A dense network of fenestrated blood capillaries and lymphatic capillaries are found within the stroma, and are accompanied by autonomic nerve fibers.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The stroma of the thyroid gland surrounds the thyroid follicles within the lobules.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The stroma of the thyroid gland acts as a support framework for the follicles and lobules of the thyroid gland.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The perifollicular capillary network is the numerous blood vessels surrounding the thyroid follicles.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Cells in the thyroid follicles produce hormones and secrete them on their basal surfaces into the interstitium. A network of capillaries lies adjacent to the follicles. They are very fenestrated, which is a typical type of capillary you see in endocrine glands. Fenestrations allow easy movement of fluid from the interstitium, containing the secreted hormones, to pass into the blood, and therefore, be carried to the rest of the body.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: An extensive perifollicular capillary network surrounds the thyroid follicles.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The extensive perifollicular capillary network enables the hormones produced in the thyroid gland to enter them and be then transported to target tissues throughout the body.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: An erythrocyte is one of the elements found in peripheral blood; the normal mature form is a nonnucleated, yellowish, biconcave disk, adapted by virtue of its configuration and its haemoglobin content to the transport of oxygen (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Cell Morphology
sections.text:
Erythrocytes are small red biconcave discoid cells. Erythrocytes are not true cells in that they lack a nucleus, organelles, and cannot divide. Erythrocytes have a diameter of 7–8 μm and are smaller than leukocytes but larger than platelets. The edge of an erythrocyte has a thickness of 2.6 μm, while the center has a thickness of 0.8 μm, thus making them biconcave. Erythrocytes have a longer lifespan than the majority of blood cells and can survive for 100–120 days. Erythrocytes are the most numerous cells in the blood and have a concentration of 4.3-5.7 x 1012 cells/L and 3.9-5.0 x 1012 cells/L in males and females, respectively (Pawlina, 2016). 

In the cytoplasm of an erythrocyte contains hemoglobin, which is an oxygen and carbon dioxide-binding protein. It’s a tetrameric protein meaning that it has four subunits and each subunit contains an iron-containing molecule called heme. An iron atom is located in the center of each heme group and binds to oxygen (Silverthorn et al., 2013; Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012). Therefore, one hemoglobin binds four molecules of oxygen. Each erythrocyte contains 250 million molecules of hemoglobin, meaning each erythrocyte can transport around 1 billion oxygen molecules (Reece et al., 2014). 

Erythrocytes have proteins in their cell membrane called glycophorins. Additionally, erythrocytes possess antigens which attach to the glycophorins. There are three main antigens A, B and O that make the ABO blood group system. All three antigens share the same molecular structure but their difference is the presence of an additional sugar molecule. The presence of these antigens indicates an individual’s blood type (Reece et al., 2014; Pawlina, 2016).

—Erythrocytes that possess the O antigen make the O blood type. 

—Erythrocytes that possess the O and A antigens make the A blood type.

—Erythrocytes that possess the O and B antigens make the B blood type. 

—Erythrocytes that possess the O, A, and B antigens make the AB blood type.

sections.name: Production
sections.text:
Erythrocytes are produced in the red bone marrow by pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells and usually takes 5–9 days. A hematopoietic stem cell gives rise to a myeloid stem cell, which undergoes various stages of differentiation until it becomes an erythrocyte. This differentiation is driven by growth factors such as cytokines and hormones. Erythropoietin is a hormone that regulates the synthesis and differentiation of erythrocytes. It is produced by the kidneys when tissues are deprived of oxygen, resulting in an increase in hemoglobin and oxygen transport in the blood circulation. Colony stimulating factors are involved in regulating the production of erythrocytes (Silverthorn et al., 2013).

When erythrocytes approach their maximum lifespan (around 120 days), they become senescent. Subsequently, some erythrocytes rupture while others are phagocytosed by macrophages in the spleen, liver, or bone marrow (Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Erythrocytes function only in the bloodstream. Erythrocytes are elastic and able to fold on themselves, thus allowing them to change their shape and pass through narrow capillaries or adapt during osmotic changes. Their biconcave shape increases their surface area, therefore, enhancing the transportation of oxygen. 

Erythrocytes transport oxygen from the lungs to cells and remove carbon dioxide from cells and transport it to the lungs (Silverthorn et al., 2013).

sections.text:

—Hemolytic Anemia (sickle-cell anemia, thalassemia)

—Polycythemia

—Hereditary spherocytosis

—Hereditary elliptocytosis

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The thyroid plexus is a nerve plexus that accompanies the superior and inferior thyroid arteries into the region of the larynx, pharynx, and thyroid (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The thyroid gland is innervated by the superior, middle, and inferior cervical ganglia of the sympathetic trunk. Postganglionic fibers from the inferior cervical ganglion form a plexus on the inferior thyroid artery and accompany it to the thyroid gland. Some parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve, via the recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves, communicate with this plexus (Standring, 2020).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nerve fibers of the thyroid plexus accompany the thyroid arteries, forming a periarterial plexus on their surface.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: These autonomic nerves are likely vasomotor, not secretomotor, and act on the blood perfusion of the thyroid gland rather than regulating glandular secretion activity (Moore, Dalley and Agur, 2013).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: There is a thin capsule of connective tissue surrounding the thyroid gland, located below the pretracheal fascia. It has septa that extend into the glandular parenchyma creating division between lobules.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The fibrous capsule of the thyroid gland is found superficial to the glandular tissue of the thyroid gland and deep to the pretracheal fascia.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The fibrous capsule of the thyroid gland protects the thyroid gland and its associated neurovasculature.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A melanosome is any of the granules within the pigment cells that facilitates the absorption of light.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: Melanosomes are described as pigmented cytoplasmic granules that facilitate the synthesis, storage, and transportation of melanin, the common light-absorbing pigment in animals. In retinal pigment epithelial cells, melanosomes are retained intracellularly; thus melanosomes and melanin facilitate the absorption of light in this outer epithelial layer of the retina (Wasmeier et al., 2008).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Melanosomes are found in the cytoplasm of the retinal pigment cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Melanosomes play a role in absorbing light entering the retina. The melanin within the melanosomes prevents photo-oxidative stress.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Wasmeier, C., Hume, A. N., Bolasco, G. and Seabra, M. C. (2008) 'Melanosomes at a glance', J Cell Sci, 121(Pt 24), pp. 3995-9.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The pigmented layer of retina is a layer of pigmented epithelium that is the outer of the two parts of the optic part of the retina, extending from the entrance of the optic nerve to the pupillary margin of the iris. It is important in the turnover of rods and cones and functions as a blood-retina barrier to maintain the ionic environment of the retina (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The outermost layer of the retina, the pigmented layer, is a composed of pigment cells arranged as a continuous, single row of cuboidal epithelial cells. There are approximately 4-6 million pigment cells in the retina. These cells tend to have a flat appearance in radial section and a hexagonal or pentagonal appearance in surface view (Standring, 2016). 

Pigment cells contain multiple organelles called melanosomes. Melanosomes are described as pigmented cytoplasmic granules that facilitate the synthesis, storage, and transportation of melanin, the common light-absorbing pigment in animals. In retinal pigment cells, melanosomes are retained intracellularly, thus melanosomes and melanin facilitate the absorption of light in this outer epithelial layer of the retina (Wasmeier et al., 2008).

Pigment cells possess actin-rich apical processes, or microvilli, that measure approximately 5-7 µm in length. These microvilli interdigitate between the outer segments of the photoreceptors beneath them (Wasmeier et al., 2008). The basal surface of the pigment cells contains invaginations, which increases the overall surface area of the pigmented layer for the absorption of nutrients. The lateral membranes of the pigment cells are firmly connected by tight junctions, which collectively form the outer blood-retinal barrier (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001). 

The shape, size, and appearance of the pigment cells varies depending on their location within the retina. For example, cells in the macula measure approximately 12 µm in length and 14 µm in diameter. Moving away from the macula, cells become wider and flatter, with some cells near the ora serrata measuring approximately 60 µm in diameter (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The pigment cells extend from the periphery of the optic disc to the ora serrata, where it is continuous with the outer ciliary epithelium. The pigment cells lie between the choroid’s basal complex (Bruch’s membrane) and the layer of rods and cones. 

Embryologically, the retina is derived from the two layers of the invaginated optic vesicle. The outer layer develops into the layer of pigment cells which lies between and separates the neural retina and the choroid. The inner layer of the optic vesicle forms the other nine layers of the retina collectively known as the neural layer (Standring, 2016). Due to differences in the embryological origins of the pigmented layer and the nine layers beneath it, the border between these two areas is not supported by junctional complexes. Therefore, the neural layers and the pigmented layer of the retina can easily become detached, commonly seen in the instance of trauma and disease; this is known as retinal detachment.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The overall function of the pigment cells is the maintenance and protection of the adjacent photoreceptor cells. They are thought to additionally play an important role in the integrity of the choroidal capillaries (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001).

The pigment cells form and act as the outer blood-retinal barrier. As such, it regulates the transepithelial transport of ions, fluid, and metabolites that reach the photoreceptors via specialized transport proteins and lateral plasma membrane barrier junctions. Further, glucose is passively transported, and amino acids are actively absorbed across this epithelial layer, while waste products are removed (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001).

Another essential role carried out by the pigment cells is in the transport and storage of retinoids. Retinoids are described as analogs of vitamin A, which are fundamental in the maintenance of the visual cycle. The pigment cells are additionally responsible for the ingestion and degradation of the spent outer segments of photoreceptors via phagocytosis (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001).

The pigmented layer plays a critical role in the protection of photoreceptors against light and free radicals. Specifically, the intensity and wavelength of light that reaches the photoreceptors is regulated by macular pigments and melanin which respectively function to filter out reactive blue light and act as a neutral density filter to reduce light passing the pigmented layer. Enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidants are also contained within the pigmented layer which neutralize reactive oxygen species, preventing damage to cellular molecules (Boulton and Dayhaw-Barker, 2001).

Finally, the retinal pigment cells secrete a number of growth factors, which supports the integrity of the choriocapillaris endothelium and the photoreceptors (Standring, 2016).

sections.text:
- Retinal detachment 

- Drusen (macular degeneration)

- Night blindness

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The inner segment of a photoreceptor cell is the portion of a retinal rod or cone that is between the external limiting layer and the outer segment; this part contains the Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum, and numerous mitochondria (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The inner segment is that portion of a photoreceptor is an organelle-rich cellular compartment that is external to the outer limiting membrane and internal to the connecting stalk. Measuring approximately 1.5 µm in length, the inner segment of rod cells is generally much narrower than the inner segment of cone cells, which measure approximately 5–6 µm. The inner segment of both rod and cone cells may be further divided into two distinct sections known as the myoid and the ellipsoid. 

The myoid forms the basal part of the inner segment and houses the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus. The ellipsoid forms the apical portion and contains densely packed mitochondria. Opsin proteins, such as those found in rhodopsin, are produced in the myoid but travel to the outer segment after production to be incorporated into the newly formed membranous discs. Opsin proteins are integral components of the visual cycle. As new discs are added, older discs get pushed toward the pigmented epithelium to be phagocytosed (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The inner segments of the rod cells are largely located in the retinal layer of rods and cones (also known as the outer and inner segments of the retina).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Photoreceptors are amongst the most metabolically active cells in the body. The inner segment of the photoreceptor cell is the primary site for protein synthesis and generating energy for the cell. Thus it is specialized with high density mitochondria to produce energy and Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes drive the protein synthesis.

sections.name: References
sections.text:

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The outer segment of a photoreceptor cell is the part of a retinal rod or cone that is between the inner segment and the pigmented epithelium. This part of the photoreceptor contains numerous visual opsin-bearing membranous discs (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The outer segments of the rod cells are cylindrical, measuring approximately 20–30 µm in length and 1.2-2.0 µm in diameter. They are recognizable by the presence of approximately 1,000 stacked, flattened membranous discs, or lamellae. These discs originate as deep infoldings of the plasma membrane at the base of the outer segment. However, once the discs are fully formed, they bud off and disconnect from the plasma membrane (Molday and Moritz, 2015; Standring, 2016). The membranous discs in the outer segments contain the sensory protein called rhodopsin embedded in the membrane.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The outer segments of the rod cells are located in the layer of outer of the retina. Their tips are deeply inserted into invaginations in the apical membrane and microvillus processes of the retinal pigment epithelium.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The outer segment of a rod cell bears the visual pigment molecule, rhodopsin embedded within it extensive membrane. Rhodopsin is responsible for the absorption of light and the induction of a biochemical cascade that culminates in the production of an electrical signal representing visual information (Molday and Moritz, 2015).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Best disease 

- Retinal disease

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The soma, or cell body, is the portion of a cell that contains the nucleus, independent of projections such as an axon or dendrites (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The soma, or cell body, is the region within the photoreceptor cell that houses the nucleus. The soma of the rod cells is large in diameter, measuring 3–5 µm (Dartt et al., 2010).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The soma of the rod cells is located in the outer nuclear layer of the retina and tend to form several layers vitreal to the soma of the cone cells. It is positioned in between the inner segment and the axonal process of the photoreceptor cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The soma houses the nucleus, which contains the cell’s DNA. It is necessary for the development and maintenance of the cell’s biochemical functions.

sections.name: References
sections.text:

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The nuclei of rod cells are described as more spherical and smaller than those belonging to cone cells. As a result, rod cell nuclei tend to stain darker than their cone counterparts. Anatomically, rod nuclei form several layers internal (or vitreal) to the cone nuclei (Standring, 2016).

The nuclei of cone cells are larger and more oval-shaped than their rod counterparts. They form a single layer that often fringes the outer limiting membrane (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nucleus is located in the soma (or cell body) of the photoreceptor cells and is located in the outer nuclear layer of the retina.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nucleus houses the cell’s genetic information and activation of certain genes initiates the process of transcription and translation that direct protein synthesis in the cell.

sections.name: References

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Mitochondria are the small spherical to rod-shaped cytoplasmic organelles, consisting of inner and outer bilayer membranes with a space between them. The inner membrane is infolded to form a series of projections (cristae), and the space between the cristae is filled by the mitochondrial matrix, which contains DNA, RNA, ribosomes, and granules. Mitochondria generate energy (in the form of ATP synthesis) by the oxidation of nutrients, and they contain the enzymes of the tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle and for fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation. In response to toxic insults, they release enzymes that cause apoptosis. Mitochondria can replicate independently and code for the synthesis of some of their proteins; inheritance of mitochondrial DNA is maternal, and mitochondrial DNA defects cause a variety of diseases (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Mitochondria are small, membrane-bound, ovoid organelles approximately 0.5-2 µm long. Each mitochondrion is lined by an inner and outer membrane. The outer membrane often attaches to other organelles, while the inner membrane is deeply folded to form invaginations, called cristae. The lumen of the mitochondria is surrounded by the inner membrane and contains the mitochondrial matrix (Gouspillou and Hepple, 2017).

Mitochondria contain their own unique DNA, referred to as mitochondrial DNA (or mtDNA), and is different from the nuclear DNA. During fertilization, mitochondria from sperm do not enter the oocyte; therefore, mitochondria are inherited from the mother’s side.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The mitochondria in photoreceptor cells are most numerous in the apical portion of the inner segment. This region is known as the ellipsoid.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Mitochondria are the energy powerhouses of the cell as it forms the majority of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) breakdown of which is the main source of chemical energy. Photoreceptors being amongst the most metabolically active cells in the body it is no surprise that they are found in high density here. Specifically, mitochondria are ideally placed in the inner segment ellipsoid where the cellular work of producing photopigment and photoreceptor membranous discs occurs.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The outer segments of rods and cones have flattened membranous discs which bear visual opsin.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The outer segments of rod cells are composed of approximately 1,000 stacked, flattened membranous discs, or lamellae. These discs originate as deep infoldings of the plasma membrane at the base of the outer segment. The bi-lipid membranous discs become detached from the surrounding plasma membrane following formation and are therefore free floating in the outer segment. 

Embedded within the double membranes of the discs are light-sensitive visual pigment molecules, rhodopsin (Kolb, 1995; Standring, 2016).

There is constant turnover of membranous discs. From proximally, where they are formed at the base of the outer segments older discs are gradually displaced distally, up through the outer segment. At the very tip of the outer segment discs are pinched off, engulfed, and phagocytosed by the apical processes of the pigmented epithelium (Kolb, 1995).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The multiple folded bilaminar membrane forming the discs of rod outer segments extend from the connecting stalk at their bases to the distal tip. The tips are surrounded by multiple microvillus processes of retinal pigment epithelium.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Despite its production in the inner segment of the rod cell, rhodopsin subsequently migrates to the outer segments. The membranous discs of rod cells are largely responsible for housing and anchoring rhodopsin. Rhodopsin controls the absorption and processing of light under dim lighting conditions (Kolb, 1995). Most of the rhodopsin at the tips of rod outer segments are already photoconverted and so the no longer photosensitive pigment is sloughed off and engulfed, and phagocytized by the retinal pigment epithelium.

- Rod-cone dystrophy

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The rod spherule is the pear-shaped ending of a retinal rod cell, which synapses with the bipolar and horizontal cells in the outer plexiform layer (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The synaptic terminals of rod cells are oval to spherical and are called rod spherules. These expansions contain the presynaptic apparatus for connections with bipolar and horizontal cells. They also receive and make electrical synapses with neighboring cones (Csillag, 2007).

Each rod spherule exhibits one or more electron-dense structures, known as a synaptic ribbon. Synaptic ribbons are oriented generally perpendicular to the presynaptic membrane and are surrounded by many neurotransmitter containing vesicles (glutamate). The ribbon promotes the rapid migration of vesicles to the cell membrane and fusion with it to release its neurotransmitters (glutamate) into the synaptic cleft between the spherule and horizontal and bipolar cells (Standring, 2016; Kolb, 1995).

The basal membrane of rod spherules is invaginated by the postsynaptic processes of bipolar cells and horizontal cells in what is called and invaginated synapse. Rod spherules make connections with, on average, four bipolar cell processes. An individual horizontal cell contacts a spherule once, but one spherule may synapse with several horizontal cells. Typically there are a central bipolar cell elements flanked by horizontal cell elements (from separate cells) in an arrangement called a “synaptic triad.” (Boycott and Kolb, 1973).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The rod cell spherules are located in the outer plexiform layer. Adjacent spherules are located at different depths within this layer. Spherules are surrounded by processes of bipolar and horizontal cells as well as the external processes of Müller glia that pass through the outer plexiform layer and outer nuclear layer before forming the outer limiting membrane of the retina.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The rod cell spherules are responsible for making synaptic connections with bipolar and horizontal cells. The photoreceptor cells release glutamate into the synapse.

Note that activation of photoreceptor cells in humans results in hyperpolarization, or inhibition, of that cell. Moreover, when photoreceptors are not activated, for example in a dark room, they remain in a depolarized state, thus constantly releasing the neurotransmitter glutamate. This release of glutamate at the synaptic terminal hyperpolarizes the connecting bipolar and horizontal cells; therefore, these cells are not activated, and the bipolar-ganglion synapse remains unexcited. When photoreceptors become activated by light, they hyperpolarize and the release of glutamate at the rod synaptic terminal ceases. The consequence of this is the depolarization of the connecting bipolar and horizontal cells and the transmission of the visual signal (Standring, 2016; Molday and Moritz, 2015).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The connecting stalk joins the outer and inner segments of the photoreceptor cells.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The connecting stalk is the constricted region of the photoreceptor cells that joins the outer and inner segments. It contains a modified connecting cilium that arises from a basal body in the apical region of the inner segment.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The connecting stalk connects the outer and inner segments of the photoreceptor cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The connecting stalk acts as a conduit between the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptor cells, allowing for the transportation of lipids and proteins from the inner segment to the outer segment.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The Golgi complex is an intracellular compartment of eukaryotes, occupying the perinuclear region and consisting of a number of stacked, flattened sacs with associated tubules and vesicles. Its primary function is to process substances synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum; in addition it synthesizes some carbohydrates. Transport vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the Golgi complex at the cis face, their cargo is processed while passing through the cisternae, and the processed products are transported from the trans face to the trans-Golgi network for sorting and packaging. The mechanism by which cargo moves through the Golgi complex is not clear; one model proposes transport between cisternae by vesicular budding and fusion, while another proposes dynamic remodeling and recycling so that the cisternae themselves change in composition and move in a cis-to-trans direction (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The Golgi complex, or Golgi apparatus, is a membranous intracellular organelle. It is composed of several flattened stacks, or cisternae, and measures approximated 5–10 µm in area (Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The Golgi complex is often found in the myoid zone of the photoreceptor inner segment. This zone is located between the cell nucleus and the zone of high mitochondria density (ellipsoid zone).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The Golgi complex is responsible for the modification, sorting, and packaging of proteins and lipids for intracellular or extracellular transport. Therefore, a large number of vesicles are associated with the Golgi complex.

sections.name: References

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The connecting cilium acts as a communicating channel between the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptor cells.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The connecting cilium is a long, slender, nonmotile, microscopic cellular organelle within the photoreceptor connecting stalk. It measures approximately 0.3 µm in diameter and is composed of microtubules in a 9x2+0 array near the cilium’s base. Here the microtubules are connected to the plasma membrane. This microtubule “doublet” formation transitions to 9x1+0 singlet array more distally and it continues in that configuration through to the outer segment (Chen and Sampath, 2012).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The connecting cilium is fittingly positioned between the inner and outer segments in both rod and cone cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The connecting cilium acts a microscopic channel for the flow of proteins and lipids, from the site of production in the inner segment to the outer segment, with approximately 2,000 opsin molecules transported every minute (Chen and Sampath, 2012).

sections.name: References
sections.text: Chen, J. and Sampath, A. (2012) 'Structure and Function of Rod and Cone Photoreceptors', Retina Fifth Edition, 1, pp. 342-359.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: An axonal process is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The axonal process is the elongated part of the photoreceptor cell that transmits information about the light level in the environment detected by a single photoreceptor and communicated as a voltage change from the cell soma to its synaptic terminal. Rod axons have a diameter of approximately 0.5 µm. 

The length of the axonal process in rod cells varies greatly depending on the species and location within the retina. In primates, axons may measure 200–400 µm in the para-foveal region (Dartt et al., 2010).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The axonal process of the rod cells extends from the cell body in the outer nuclear layer to the spherule synaptic terminal in outer plexiform layer of the retina. They are interspersed between the somata and axons of other rod and cone cells and the external radial processes of Müller glial cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The axonal process carries the electrical signal caused by light stimulation or rod outer segments from the soma (cell body) to the synaptic terminal.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The calyceal processes are small projections that extend from the apex of the inner segments of the photoreceptor cells and form a collar around the base of the outer segments.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Poorly studied, the calyceal processes are described as small microvilli-like projections that extend from the apex of the inner segments of the photoreceptor cells and form a collar around the base of the outer segments. These calyceal processes are composed of polarized actin filaments and are present before the formation of the outer segments (Sahly et al., 2012).

The calyceal processes tend to be uniform in cone cells, usually 14–16 parallel processes of around 3 µm in length. However, the calyceal processes of the rod cells are less regularly arranged. They also tend to be shorter, thinner, and more variable in length with larger spaces between them (Sahly et al., 2012).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Calyceal processes are multiple fingerlike extensions arising from the apical surface of photoreceptor inner segments and protruding distally forming a “collar” around to the proximal end of outer segments.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: There is a cycle of photoreceptor outer segments formation, use and disposal. They are formed proximally at the inner/outer segment junction and are discarded distally at outer segment tips, in a circadian fashion. While the function of calyceal processes is poorly understood, they are believed to play a role in this by shaping outer segments during their formation and growth. It is additionally postulated that calcium within the calyceal processes may influence mechanical tension (Goggolidou, 2018).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A bipolar cell is a nerve cell with two processes. Bipolar neurons located in the inner nuclear layer of the retina are the second neurons in the sensory pathway, making synaptic contacts with photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Appropriately named, bipolar neurons are recognizable by two distinct projections, one axon and one dendrite, attached to a cell body. Known as the second-order neurons in the visual pathway, bipolar neurons are responsible for relaying information from photoreceptors cells to ganglion cells (Remington and Goodwin, 2011). 

In mammals, bipolar neurons are designated as cone bipolar cells or rod bipolar cells, depending on which photoreceptor cell they receive input from. There are approximately 10 distinct forms of cone bipolar cells but only one form of rod bipolar cell (Remington and Goodwin, 2011; Strettoi et al., 2010). 

According to size and connectivity, cone bipolar cells may be largely categorized as midget cone, blue cone, or diffuse cone bipolar cells. A subtype of midget bipolar cells, known as flat midget bipolar cells, synapses on the base of the cone pedicle. Most other midget bipolar cells make contact via direct invagination of the cone pedicle. In the peripheral retina, a midget bipolar cell may contact 2–3 cone cells. However, in the central retina, each midget bipolar cell synapses with just one cone photoreceptor cell, forming a direct channel from photoreceptor to ganglion cells, facilitating high spatial resolution (Standring, 2016). 

Another distinction between bipolar cells may be made from their response to light stimulation. There are ON bipolar cells and OFF bipolar cell differing in their response to the light-induced hyperpolarization of photoreceptor cells and the consequent cessation of glutamate release. Bipolar cells that depolarize following the activation and hyperpolarization of photoreceptor cells are classified as ON cells. On the other hand, bipolar cells that hyperpolarize following the light-induced hyperpolarization of photoreceptor cells are known as OFF cells (Standring, 2016).

Rod bipolar cells all share a single morphology. One rod bipolar cell will contact 40–45 rods in the peripheral retina and 30–35 rods in the central retina. Interestingly, bipolar rod cells do not directly contact ganglion cells, but instead make axodendritic or axoaxonic synapses with amacrine cells which proceed to excite ON retinal ganglion cells and inhibit OFF retinal ganglion cells by dendrodendritic connections. Thus on electron micrographs, one can see an arrangement called a serial synapse whereby a bipolar cell terminal is presynaptic to an amacrine terminal, which itself is presynaptic to a retinal ganglion cell terminal (Standring, 2016; Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Bipolar neurons are radially orientated. Their cell bodies are located in the inner nuclear layer. Within this layer they tend to be in the outer and middle portion, adjacent and vitreal to the horizontal cells. They are more sparse in the inner portion, which is mostly composed of Müller glia. The orientation of bipolar cells is perpendicular to the retinal layers. One process serves as a dendrite extending into the outer plexiform layer and is postsynaptic to photoreceptor cells, horizontal cells, and interplexiform cells. From the opposite side of the cell body, an axonal process extends into the inner plexiform layer where it is presynaptic to amacrine cells processes (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Bipolar cells are largely responsible for the direct and indirect transmission of visual signals from photoreceptor cells to ganglion cells. Specifically, the dendrites of bipolar cells receive input from photoreceptor cells, horizontal cells, and interplexiform cells and synapse directly onto ganglion cells or indirectly via amacrine cells (Remington and Goodwin, 2011).

Following the light-induced hyperpolarization of photoreceptor cells, the release of glutamate at the synaptic clefts is inhibited. ON bipolar cells will depolarize in response to the inhibition of glutamate, while OFF bipolar cells will hyperpolarize. As aforementioned, rod bipolar cells do not directly make contact with ganglion cells, but instead synapse with amacrine cells which excite surrounding ON bipolar cone cells and inhibit OFF bipolar cone cells. This results in an overriding of the cone pathway and facilitates the transmission of scotopic rod signals to ganglion cells in ambient light conditions (Standring, 2016; Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Paraneoplastic retinopathy

- Congenital stationary night blindness

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The calyceal processes are small projections that extend from the apex of the inner segments of the photoreceptor cells and form a collar around the base of the outer segments.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Poorly studied, the calyceal processes are described as small microvilli-like projections that extend from the apex of the inner segments of the photoreceptor cells and form a collar around the base of the outer segments. These calyceal processes are composed of polarized actin filaments and are present before the formation of the outer segments (Sahly et al., 2012).

The calyceal processes tend to be uniform in cone cells, usually 14–16 parallel processes of around 3 µm in length. However, the calyceal processes of the rod cells are less regularly arranged. They also tend to be shorter, thinner, and more variable in length with larger spaces between them (Sahly et al., 2012).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Calyceal processes are multiple fingerlike extensions arising from the apical surface of photoreceptor inner segments and protruding distally forming a “collar” around to the proximal end of outer segments.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: There is a cycle of photoreceptor outer segments formation, use and disposal. They are formed proximally at the inner/outer segment junction and are discarded distally at outer segment tips, in a circadian fashion. While the function of calyceal processes is poorly understood, they are believed to play a role in this by shaping outer segments during their formation and growth. It is additionally postulated that calcium within the calyceal processes may influence mechanical tension (Goggolidou, 2018).

sections.text: - Usher syndrome

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The soma, or cell body, is the portion of a cell that contains the nucleus, independent of projections such as an axon or dendrites (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The soma, or cell body, is the region within the photoreceptor cell that houses the nucleus and most of the protein synthesis and metabolic cellular organelles. The soma of the cone cells is large in diameter, measuring around 5 µm (Besharse and Bok, 2011).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The soma of the cone cells tends to form a single layer in the inner aspect of the outer nuclear layer and often penetrate the outer limiting membrane. The soma is positioned in between the inner segment and the axonal process of the photoreceptor cells. Besides the somata of other cones and rods, the space between photoreceptor cell bodies contains the outer process of Müller glial cells that at their distal end compose the outer limiting membrane.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The soma houses the nucleus, which contains the cell’s DNA. It is necessary for gene expression, transcription and translation that forms the cell developmentally and maintains its biochemical structural and metabolic functions.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Besharse, J. and Bok, D. (2011) The Retina and Its Disorders. Elsevier Science, p. 156-162.

Chen, J. and Sampath, A. (2012) 'Structure and Function of Rod and Cone Photoreceptors', Retina Fifth Edition, 1, pp. 342-359.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The nuclei of rod cells are described as more spherical and smaller than those belonging to cone cells. As a result, rod cell nuclei tend to stain darker than their cone counterparts. Anatomically, rod nuclei form several layers internal (or vitreal) to the cone nuclei (Standring, 2016).

The nuclei of cone cells are larger and more oval-shaped than their rod counterparts. They form a single layer that often fringes the outer limiting membrane (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nucleus is located in the soma (or cell body) of the photoreceptor cells and is located in the outer nuclear layer of the retina.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nucleus houses the cell’s genetic information and activation of certain genes initiates the process of transcription and translation that direct protein synthesis in the cell.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The connecting stalk joins the outer and inner segments of the photoreceptor cells.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The connecting stalk is the constricted region of the photoreceptor cells that joins the outer and inner segments. It contains a modified connecting cilium that arises from a basal body in the apical region of the inner segment.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The connecting stalk connects the outer and inner segments of the photoreceptor cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The connecting stalk acts as a conduit between the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptor cells, allowing for the transportation of lipids and proteins from the inner segment to the outer segment.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Mitochondria are the small spherical to rod-shaped cytoplasmic organelles, consisting of inner and outer bilayer membranes with a space between them. The inner membrane is infolded to form a series of projections (cristae), and the space between the cristae is filled by the mitochondrial matrix, which contains DNA, RNA, ribosomes, and granules. Mitochondria generate energy (in the form of ATP synthesis) by the oxidation of nutrients, and they contain the enzymes of the tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle and for fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation. In response to toxic insults, they release enzymes that cause apoptosis. Mitochondria can replicate independently and code for the synthesis of some of their proteins; inheritance of mitochondrial DNA is maternal, and mitochondrial DNA defects cause a variety of diseases (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Mitochondria are small, membrane-bound, ovoid organelles approximately 0.5-2 µm long. Each mitochondrion is lined by an inner and outer membrane. The outer membrane often attaches to other organelles, while the inner membrane is deeply folded to form invaginations, called cristae. The lumen of the mitochondria is surrounded by the inner membrane and contains the mitochondrial matrix (Gouspillou and Hepple, 2017).

Mitochondria contain their own unique DNA, referred to as mitochondrial DNA (or mtDNA), and is different from the nuclear DNA. During fertilization, mitochondria from sperm do not enter the oocyte; therefore, mitochondria are inherited from the mother’s side.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The mitochondria in photoreceptor cells are most numerous in the apical portion of the inner segment. This region is known as the ellipsoid.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Mitochondria are the energy powerhouses of the cell as it forms the majority of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) breakdown of which is the main source of chemical energy. Photoreceptors being amongst the most metabolically active cells in the body it is no surprise that they are found in high density here. Specifically, mitochondria are ideally placed in the inner segment ellipsoid where the cellular work of producing photopigment and photoreceptor membranous discs occurs.

sections.name: References
sections.text:

Gouspillou, G. and Hepple, R. T. (2017) Mitochondria in Skeletal Muscle Health, Aging and Diseases. Frontiers Research Topics.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The outer segment of a photoreceptor cell is the part of a retinal rod or cone that is between the inner segment and the pigmented epithelium. This part of the photoreceptor contains numerous visual opsin-bearing membranous discs (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Cone outer segments are located in a layer composed almost entirely of rod and cone outer and inner segments. The outer segment of cone cells make contact with the apical processes of the pigmented layer that interdigitate with these outer segments (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: While the spectrally distinct visual pigments of the cones are produced in the inner segment, they are transported to the outer segments. Here they are incorporated within the membrane of the outer segment. Following the absorption of light, a conformational change occurs in the opsin and retinal molecules resulting in the induction of a biochemical cascade which culminates in the production of an electrical signal representing visual information.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Best disease 

- Retinal disease

sections.name: References

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: An axonal process is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The axonal process is the elongated part of the photoreceptor cell that carries membrane potential changes from the soma (or cell body) to other photoreceptor, bipolar, or horizontal cells. Cone axons have a diameter of approximately 1–2 µm and are interspersed between the somas and axonal processes of rod cells.

The length of the axonal process in cone cells varies greatly depending on the species and location within the retina. In primates, cones in the fovea have axonal process as long as 400–600 µm (Besharse and Bok, 2011).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The axonal process of a cone extends from the outer nuclear layer, winds between the cell bodies and axonal processes of other photoreceptors and the external processes of glial cells, to reach the outer plexiform layer of the retina.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The axonal process carries the electrical manifestation of visual stimulation, in the form of a membrane voltage change, from the soma (cell body) to the synaptic terminal.

sections.name: References
sections.text:

Chen, J. and Sampath, A. (2012) 'Structure and Function of Rod and Cone Photoreceptors', Retina Fifth Edition, 1, pp. 342-359.

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The connecting cilium acts as a communicating channel between the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptor cells.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The connecting cilium is a long, slender, nonmotile, microscopic cellular organelle within the photoreceptor connecting stalk. It measures approximately 0.3 µm in diameter and is composed of microtubules in a 9x2+0 array near the cilium’s base. Here the microtubules are connected to the plasma membrane. This microtubule “doublet” formation transitions to 9x1+0 singlet array more distally and it continues in that configuration through to the outer segment (Chen and Sampath, 2012).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The connecting cilium is fittingly positioned between the inner and outer segments in both rod and cone cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The connecting cilium acts a microscopic channel for the flow of proteins and lipids, from the site of production in the inner segment to the outer segment, with approximately 2,000 opsin molecules transported every minute (Chen and Sampath, 2012).

sections.name: References
sections.text: Chen, J. and Sampath, A. (2012) 'Structure and Function of Rod and Cone Photoreceptors', Retina Fifth Edition, 1, pp. 342-359.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cone cell pedicle is the thick triangular or club-shaped ending of a retinal cone cell, which synapses with the bipolar and horizontal cells in the outer plexiform layer (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The cone cell pedicles are located in the outermost portion of the outer plexiform layer. Immediately lateral are neighboring cone pedicles, and, with increasing frequency from central to peripheral retina, the spherules of rod photoreceptors.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The cone cell pedicles are responsible for making synaptic connections with bipolar cells, horizontal cells, and other photoreceptor cells. The photoreceptor cells release glutamate into the synapse.

Note that activation of photoreceptor cells in humans results in hyperpolarization, or inhibition, of that cell. Moreover, when photoreceptors are not activated, for example in a dark room, they remain in a depolarized state, thus constantly releasing the neurotransmitter glutamate. This release of glutamate at the synaptic terminal hyperpolarizes the connecting bipolar and horizontal cells; therefore, these cells are not activated, and the bipolar-ganglion synapse remains unexcited. When photoreceptors become activated by light, they hyperpolarize and the release of glutamate at the rod synaptic terminal ceases. The consequence of this is the depolarization of the connecting bipolar and horizontal cells and the transmission of the visual signal (Standring, 2016; Molday and Moritz, 2015).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The outer segments of rods and cones have flattened membranous discs which bear visual opsin.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The membranous discs of cone cells are present in the outer segment; however, they are less numerous than those in the rod cells and remain attached to the plasma membrane as infoldings at the base of the cell (Standring, 2016). There are additional reports that most, if not all, of the membranous discs in cone outer segments are continuous and remain attached to the plasma membrane, however, many of the connections appear to be very small. Therefore, it is assumed that intradiscal spaces are open to the interphotoreceptor matrix (Heckenlively, Arden and Bach, 2006).

A feature known as cone notches has also been described. These notches distinguish a site of transition between discs that are open to the interphotoreceptor matrix and those that are isolated (Heckenlively, Arden and Bach, 2006). 

While rhodopsin is located on the outer segments of rod cells, a distinct feature of cone cells is the presence of proteins known as cone opsins or photopsins. There are three distinct photopsins, depending on the opsin protein that is present and bound to retinal (Standring, 2016). Each photopsin has a unique spectral sensitivity maximum and distribution.

Similar to rods, the membranous discs of cones are phagocytosed as new ones are manufactured. It should be noted that the incorporation of newly produced proteins in cone cells is more diffuse than that of rod cells.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The membranous discs of rod cells are located in and extend the length of the outer segment of the rod photoreceptor cell.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Despite their production in the inner segment of the cone cell, the spectrally distinct visual pigments are transported to the outer segments. The membranous discs are largely responsible for housing and anchoring the visual pigments. Following the absorption of light, a conformational change occurs in the opsin and retinal molecules resulting in the induction of a biochemical cascade which culminates in the production of an electrical signal representing visual information.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
- Rod-cone degeneration

- Rod-cone dystrophy

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The Golgi complex is an intracellular compartment of eukaryotes, occupying the perinuclear region and consisting of a number of stacked, flattened sacs with associated tubules and vesicles. Its primary function is to process substances synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum; in addition it synthesizes some carbohydrates. Transport vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the Golgi complex at the cis face, their cargo is processed while passing through the cisternae, and the processed products are transported from the trans face to the trans-Golgi network for sorting and packaging. The mechanism by which cargo moves through the Golgi complex is not clear; one model proposes transport between cisternae by vesicular budding and fusion, while another proposes dynamic remodeling and recycling so that the cisternae themselves change in composition and move in a cis-to-trans direction (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The Golgi complex, or Golgi apparatus, is a membranous intracellular organelle. It is composed of several flattened stacks, or cisternae, and measures approximated 5–10 µm in area (Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The Golgi complex is often found in the myoid zone of the photoreceptor inner segment. This zone is located between the cell nucleus and the zone of high mitochondria density (ellipsoid zone).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The Golgi complex is responsible for the modification, sorting, and packaging of proteins and lipids for intracellular or extracellular transport. Therefore, a large number of vesicles are associated with the Golgi complex.

sections.name: References
sections.text:

Pawlina, W. 2016. Histology: A text and atlas with correlated cell and molecular biology. 7th ed. Philadelphia: Wolters Kluwer.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The inner segment of a photoreceptor cell is the portion of a retinal rod or cone that is between the external limiting layer and the outer segment; this part contains the Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum, and numerous mitochondria (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Measuring approximately 5–6 µm in length, the inner segments of cone cells are generally much broader than that of rod cells. A general feature of inner segments of both rod and cone cells is that they may be divided into two regions, the myoid and the ellipsoid. 

The myoid forms the proximal part of the inner segment, closest to the cell body, and houses the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus. The ellipsoid forms the distal portion and contains densely packed mitochondria. Opsin proteins, such as those found in rhodopsin, are produced in the myoid but travel to the outer segment after production to be incorporated into newly forming membranous discs. Opsin proteins are integral components of the visual cycle. As new discs are added proximally, older discs move distally, toward the pigmented epithelium to be phagocytosed (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The inner segments of cone cells form a retinal layer sublayer between the cone cell body (outer nuclear layer) and the outer segment layer.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The inner segment of cone cells is highly specialized to supply the energy demand of these cells, and to support their requirements for protein synthesis. The inner segment of the photoreceptor cell is the primary site for these functions in photoreceptors.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Standring, S. (2016) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. Gray's Anatomy Series 41 edn.: Elsevier Limited.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The epineurium is the outermost layer of connective tissue of a peripheral nerve, surrounding the entire nerve and containing its supplying blood vessels and lymphatics (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The superficial (or external) epineurium is found encasing all fascicles of the nerve. It is about 60–100 nm thick. However thickness is related to the number of fasciculi present; the more fasciculi present the thicker the epineurium (Barral and Croibier, 2007). This structure contains fibroblasts, collagen fibers (types I and III), lymphocytes, and mast cells. The superficial epineurium also contains lymphatic vessels, vasa nervorum, and the nervi nervorum, which innervate the sheaths of nerve trunks (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The epineurium is formed of loose connective tissue. It is divided into the superficial and deep epineurium. The superficial epineurium can be observed surrounding the nerve trunk, which contains multiple fascicles. It can be traced backwards to spinal meninges where spinal dura mater merges with the external epineurium just when the spinal nerve exits the intervertebral foramen. The deep epineurium refers to the layer of epineurium which penetrates within the nerve and separates the fascicles from one another (Snell, 2011).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The superficial epineurium plays a role in protecting the internal nerve fiber it surrounds, cushioning it from damage e.g., during compression.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Pressure palsies in bedridden patients
