sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The endoneurium is the connective tissue in a peripheral nerve fascicle; it forms an interstitial layer around the neurilemma that surrounds individual myelinated nerve fibers and Remak bundles of unmyelinated fibers (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The endoneurium is the connective tissue layer surrounding a nerve fiber (neuron) including the neurolemma and the myelin sheath. This connective tissue is made up of a fibrous matrix largely composed of collagen type III fibers (reticulin), which are arranged into intricate bundles, parallel to the long axis of the nerve. They tend to become somewhat concentrated around individual Schwann cell-axon units and vessels of the endoneurium. The primary cellular constituents of the endoneurium are fibroblasts, however resident macrophages and mast cells are also present (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The endoneurium is surrounded by endoneurial fluid at a slightly higher pressure than that found external to the endoneurial channel. Within the endoneurial channel, tiny capillaries are present which are comprised of a single layer of non-fenestrated endothelial cells. These serve as part of the blood-nerve barrier (Peltonen, Alanne and Peltonen, 2013).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The endoneurium plays a role in isolating nerve signals. Each peripheral nerve contains numerous axons that transmit to several muscles in the body. The endoneurium is in control of keeping these signals separate ensuring they are transmitted to the correct location. The endoneurium also protects the delicate axons from potential harm. Another function of the endoneurium, which is shared by the perineurium and epineurium, is the protection of neurons from damage (Carp, 2015).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Advanced axonal neuropathy

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The axon is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs. The larger axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Axons are a part of the nerve cell or neuron. They can be described as an appendage of the nerve cell body giving rise to numerous collateral branches containing presynaptic complexes. Axons are comprised of a gelatinous, relatively firm cord of neuronal cytoplasm. This cord is known as the axoplasm. This axoplasm is surrounded by the axonal part of the neuronal cell membrane, which is referred to as the axolemma. Axons vary in diameter from about 0.1 µm to about 20 µm. Axons also vary in length, they can be anywhere between less than 1 cm to more than a meter long (Carp, 2015).

There are two types of axons, myelinated and unmyelinated. Myelinated axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath while unmyelinated axons are not. Nodes of Ranvier refer to the gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon and the axon is exposed to the extracellular fluid.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
Myelinated axons are concentrically enveloped by myelin which is produced by myelinating Schwann cells. The territory of an individual Schwann cell along the length of the axon is defined as an internode, while the internodal length is the distance between two successive nodes of Ranvier. The span between these nodes varies dependent on axon diameter. It is at these nodes voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated. Conduction in myelinated axons is saltatory and extremely quick.

Unmyelinated axons are enclosed by overlapping Schwann cells followed by a surrounding basal lamina. Within each Schwann cell, individual axons are usually isolated from their neighbor by delicate processes of cytoplasm. The absence of myelin sheaths and nodes of Ranvier in unmyelinated axons results in electrotonic conduction, not saltatory, and the passage of impulses is therefore relatively slow.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Axons are the main conducting unit of the neuron. They transfer electrical signals along a range of distances. The nodes of Ranvier function as a generator of action potentials. This is achieved through the region of the membrane exposed at the node of Ranvier possessing special channel proteins, which allow ions to enter and exit the cell (Waxman, Kocsis and Stys, 1995).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Tetrodotoxin poisoning

Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Waxman, S. G., Kocsis, J. D. and Stys, P. K. (1995) The Axon: Structure, Function, and Pathophysiology. Oxford University Press.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The myelin sheath is the cylindrical covering on the axons of some neurons; it consists of concentric layers of myelin, formed in the peripheral nervous system by the plasma membrane of Schwann cells, and in the central nervous system by oligodendrocytes. It is interrupted at intervals along its length by gaps known as nodes of Ranvier. Myelin is an electrical insulator that serves to speed the conduction of nerve impulses (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The myelin sheath tightly holsters the axon, it is a semi-crystalline lipid-protein-water layer. This layer is discontinuous and interrupted at regular intervals. Schwann cells produce myelin sheaths in the peripheral nervous system. A myelin sheath is formed when the Schwann cell wraps around the nerve axon in a spiral fashion, creating a number of layers, or lamellae. The process is known as myelination. Each myelin-producing cell surrounds only one segment of any given axon. Periodic interruptions where short portions of the axon are left uncovered by myelin are known as the nodes of Ranvier (Patestas and Gartner, 2016).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Nodes of Ranvier are gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon, thus exposing it to the extracellular fluid. The nodes of Ranvier contain a high concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels. These voltage-gated sodium channels enable the nodes to function as generators of action potentials. This is achieved through the exchange of ions into and out of the ion channels.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The Myelin sheath acts as an insulator for the axons improving their electrical conductance. The myelin sheath also has a protective role in that it acts as a physical barrier separating the axon from the electrically charged atoms and molecules of the extracellular fluid. Myelination has also been shown to reduce the energy required for transmission of action potentials (through the mechanism of saltatory conduction) (Patestas and Gartner, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The axon is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs. The larger axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Axons are a part of the nerve cell or neuron. They can be described as an appendage of the nerve cell body giving rise to numerous collateral branches containing presynaptic complexes. Axons are comprised of a gelatinous, relatively firm cord of neuronal cytoplasm. This cord is known as the axoplasm. This axoplasm is surrounded by the axonal part of the neuronal cell membrane, which is referred to as the axolemma. Axons vary in diameter from about 0.1 µm to about 20 µm. Axons also vary in length, they can be anywhere between less than 1 cm to more than a meter long (Carp, 2015).

There are two types of axons, myelinated and unmyelinated. Myelinated axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath while unmyelinated axons are not. Nodes of Ranvier refer to the gaps found in the continuity of the myelin sheath surrounding an axon. At these gaps there is no myelin covering the axon and the axon is exposed to the extracellular fluid.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
Myelinated axons are concentrically enveloped by myelin which is produced by myelinating Schwann cells. The territory of an individual Schwann cell along the length of the axon is defined as an internode, while the internodal length is the distance between two successive nodes of Ranvier. The span between these nodes varies dependent on axon diameter. It is at these nodes voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated. Conduction in myelinated axons is saltatory and extremely quick.

Unmyelinated axons are enclosed by overlapping Schwann cells followed by a surrounding basal lamina. Within each Schwann cell, individual axons are usually isolated from their neighbor by delicate processes of cytoplasm. The absence of myelin sheaths and nodes of Ranvier in unmyelinated axons results in electrotonic conduction, not saltatory, and the passage of impulses is therefore relatively slow.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Axons are the main conducting unit of the neuron. They transfer electrical signals along a range of distances. The nodes of Ranvier function as a generator of action potentials. This is achieved through the region of the membrane exposed at the node of Ranvier possessing special channel proteins, which allow ions to enter and exit the cell (Waxman, Kocsis and Stys, 1995).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: There are two types of fascicles within the nerve, primary and secondary fascicles. A group of nerve fibers bundled together is known as a primary fascicle. Primary fascicles are separated by the perineurial septa, a layer of intrafascicular connective tissue. Several primary fascicles cluster or bundle together to form a single secondary fascicle, which is ensheathed by the perineurium (Barral and Croibier, 2007).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The fasciculus plays a role in protecting the nerve fibers. It provides the necessary environment for the nerve to function correctly. The fasciculus also plays a role in organization of the nerve fibers within the nerve. For example, before branching, fascicles destined toward a common branch are arranged into fascicle groups.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Some Schwann cells do not form myelin sheaths around the nerve fiber. Instead they lie along the long axis of the nerve fiber.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
Schwann cells are specialized glial cells located in the peripheral nervous system. These Schwann cells surround peripheral axons and are distributed along them in longitudinal chains, in mature peripheral nerves. However, their association is dependent on whether the axon is myelinated or unmyelinated. Myelin-producing Schwann cells are different from that of mature non-myelinating Schwann cells (Standring, 2016). 

Schwann cells of unmyelinated neurons align along the long axis of the axon, where the axon fits into the grooves of the cell surface. The lip of the groove may be open, thus, exposing the axonal surface. A single, or multiple axons, may be arranged in this manner in the Schwann cell surface.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Schwann cell lineage arises from neural crest cells that differentiate to become Schwann cell precursors, and then differentiate further to become immature Schwann cells. These immature Schwann cells undergo final differentiation to become either myelinating or non-myelinating Schwann cells.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The perineurial septum is an extension of the perineurium that passes through the (secondary) nerve fascicles.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The intrafascicular vessels are located within the perineurial septa.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The perineurial septa divides the secondary fascicles into the smaller, primary fascicles (Barral and Croibier, 2007).

sections.name: References
sections.text: Barral, J. P. and Croibier, A. (2007) Manual Therapy for the Peripheral Nerves. Churchill Livingstone/Elsevier.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The perineurium is an intermediate layer of connective tissue in a peripheral nerve, surrounding each bundle (fasciculus) of nerve fibers (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text:
The perineurium is a continuous layer that surrounds several primary fascicles within the nerve trunk. Note that several primary fascicles together constitute a single secondary fascicle. Perineurial septae extend into the (secondary) fascicle, subdividing it into several smaller bundles of fibers, or primary fascicles (Barral and Croibier, 2007).

The perineurium is smooth and transparent, unlike the epineurium which is tough and mechanically resistant. The perineurium is composed of layers of large, flat perineurial cells that are arranged concentrically. The number of layers of the perineurium varies, depending on the location of the nerve within the body. For example, the sciatic nerve may contain 15 layers; however, at the most distal part of the nerve, there may only be one or two layers (Peltonen et al., 2013). Each layer has a prominent basal lamina, up to 500 nm thick, and provides an additional barrier to the nerve fascicle (Standring, 2016).

The perineurium contains a thick extracellular matrix of collagen and fibronectin, which is capable of modulating external stretch forces.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Within the perineurium, primary fascicles are bundled together to form secondary fascicles. At the nerve’s proximal end, the perineurium is continuous with the leptomeningeal coverings (arachnoid and pia) of the spinal cord (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The perineurium is a metabolically active diffusion barrier. Along with the endoneurium, the perineurium forms a blood—nerve barrier, which plays a role in maintaining osmotic balance and fluid pressure within the endoneurium. It also isolates the nerve fibers within the fascicles from pathogens and extraperineual fluids (Standring, 2016). The perineurium also has a role in protection of the nerve fibers contained within. The collagen fiber matrix of the perineurium prevents the fascicle from becoming compressed, or ‘kinked’, during movements, such as flexion of a joint. The perineurium is suspected to play a role in nerve fiber regeneration in the peripheral nervous system. There is remarkable somatotopic organization of fiber types within fascicles. Both myelinated and non-myelinated nerve fibers are segregated into fascicles or sub-segregated within fascicles based on their function.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Adipose tissue is a connective tissue made up of fat cells in a meshwork of areolar tissue (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: Adipose tissue is formed of adipocytes and found inside the dense connective tissue surrounding the fascicles in a nerve.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Interfascicular adipose tissue is directly enclosed by the epineurium.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Adipose tissue acts as an insulator and facilitates mobility between nerves. This interfascicular fat also serves as a cushion by preventing damage to the nerve fibers during compression. There is also strong evidence to suggest that intrafascicular fat plays a role in regeneration of nerves (Walocko et al., 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The epineurial nerves are part of the nervi nervorum and supply the nerve.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The epineurial nerves are located in the external epineurium and form part of the nervi nervorum. The nervi nervorum can be described as the nerves innervating a nerve. They are made up of sympathetic and sensory nerve fibers found within the connective tissue of the nerve trunk (Bove and Light, 1997).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nervi nervorum originates from nerve fibers and the perivascular plexus (nerves innervating the blood vessels of the nerve). They serve as the intrinsic innervation of nerve sheaths and are found within all connective tissue coverings of the nerve trunk, including epineurium, perineurium and endoneurium.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nervi nervorum are typically capable of mechanoreceptor function and some are capable of nociception, which is the detection of noxious chemical, mechanical and thermal stimuli (Bove and Light, 1997).

sections.name: References
sections.text: Bove, G. M. and Light, A. R. (1997) 'The nervi nervorum: Missing link for neuropathic pain?', Pain Forum, 6(3), pp. 181-190.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The epineurium is the outermost layer of connective tissue of a peripheral nerve, surrounding the entire nerve and containing its supplying blood vessels and lymphatics (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The deep (or internal) epineurium is located between the fascicles of the nerve trunk and is an inward extension of the external epineurium. It is composed of loose connective tissue, which includes fibroblasts, collagen (types I and III), and variable amounts of adipose tissue, which separate nerve fascicles from each other, within the nerve trunk (Standring, 2016). The deep epineurium also contains lymphatics and vasa nervorum, a network of fine blood vessels passing across the perineurium communicating with the endoneurium.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Condensed loose connective tissue arising from the mesoderm forms the epineurium. The epineurium is then divided into the superficial and deep epineurium. The deep epineurium separates individual fascicles from one another while the superficial epineurium surrounds the entire nerve.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The deep epineurium, like the superficial epineurium, protects the internal nerve fibers. Connective tissue in its structure acts as a cushion, preventing compression or damage of the nerve. The deep epineurium also facilitates gliding between the fascicles (Barral and Croibier, 2007).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The interfascicular veins are part of the vasa nervorum and help drain the nerve.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The intrafascicular veins are located within the fascicle and form part of the vasa nervorum, small vessels that supply blood to peripheral nerves. This blood supplies nourishment to the nerve. This network of vessels supplies blood to the interior parts of the nerves and their coverings. The vasa vasorum are located within the connective tissue of the nerve scattered between the fascicles (Boissaud-Cooke, Pidgeon and Tunstall, 2015).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The vasa nervorum are the smallest vessels in the epineurial, perineurial, and endoneurial layers.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The vasa nervorum supply the peripheral nerves with the molecular nutrients needed to carry out their cellular functions and for survival (Carp, 2015).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The epineurial veins are part of the vasa nervorum and help drain the nerve.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The epineurial veins are located in the external epineurium and form part of the vasa nervorum, small vessels that supply blood to peripheral nerves. This network of vessels supplies blood to the interior parts of the nerves and their coverings. The vasa vasorum are located within the connective tissue of the nerve scattered between the fascicles (Boissaud-Cooke, Pidgeon and Tunstall, 2015).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The vasa nervorum are the smallest vessels in the epineurial, perineurial, and endoneurial layers.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The vasa nervorum supply the peripheral nerves with the molecular nutrients needed to carry out their cellular functions and for survival (Carp, 2015).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The mesoneurium surrounds the nerve fiber tissue and helps suspend it within surround tissues.

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The mesoneurium is the outermost layer of peripheral nerves. It is formed by loose areolar connective tissue, consisting of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers, which are arranged around nerve in an unorganized manner (Carp, 2015).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The mesoneurium wraps around the external epineurium. The mesoneurium is also the entry point for many of the blood vessels that supply the vasa nervorum, the intricate network of small blood vessels within the nerve trunk.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The mesoneurium suspends nerves within the soft tissue and provides some protection from compressive and tensile forces impacting on the nerve trunk (Carp, 2015). The mesoneurium also enables nerves to glide past one another and other body tissues, limiting frictional forces. The mesoneurium can also be seen to facilitate sliding motions between the mesoneurium and the external epineurium facilitating extensibility of the nerve.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The plasma membrane is the structure enveloping a cell, enclosing the cytoplasm and forming a selective permeability barrier; it consists of a lipid bilayer with integral and peripheral proteins and contains channels and pumps to transport substances across the membrane, as well as receptors to receive stimuli from the external environment and transduce them into intracellular signals (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The sperm’s plasma membrane is a dynamic structure and is unique when compared with that of somatic cells. It is divided into various domains based on its location, composition, and function. 

In the sperm head, there are two notable regions of the plasma membrane, the acrosomal region and the postacrosomal region. The plasma membrane that surrounds the tail aspect of the sperm is divided into the middle piece, the principal piece, and the distal piece domains (Toshimori, 2000).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The plasma membrane is the outermost part of the sperm and it encases the entirety of the sperm cell.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The plasma membrane plays a number of roles, which are vital for fertilization to occur. Modification of the plasma membrane is paramount for the initiation of processes, such as capacitation, acrosome reaction, and binding of the sperm head with the plasma membrane of the ovum, to occur. Most of these modifications occur as the sperm passes through the epididymis and in the uterine tube, oviduct (or fallopian tube) of the female reproductive tract (Toshimori, 2000).

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Toshimori, K. (2000) Sperm Plasma Membrane Modifications Associated with Fertilization in Mammals. Journal of Reproduction and Development, 46, 65-78.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The end ring is a dark ringlike structure at the posterior end of the middle piece of a spermatozoon (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The end ring or annulus is a fibrous ring that marks the junction between the middle piece and principal piece of the sperm tail. It is made up of tightly packed subunits of filamentous material that measure between 3-4 nm in diameter (Guraya, 2012).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The end ring tightly adheres to the plasma membrane of the sperm and the submitochondrial reticulum is attached to the end ring at the point where the middle piece and the principal piece meet.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The annulus is fundamental for the structural stability, as well as the functional effectiveness of the tail of the sperm. It ensures that cytoplasmic contents are confined and do not progress beyond its distal aspects. There’s also a possibility that the annulus inhibits the caudal displacement of the mitochondria. The annulus is also involved in the development of the fibrous sheath of the principal piece (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cytoplasm is the protoplasm of a cell exclusive of that of the nucleus; it consists of a continuous aqueous solution (cytosol) and the organelles and inclusions suspended in it and is the site of most of the chemical activities of the cell (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The cytoplasm of a cell includes an aqueous solution, the cytosol, and the organelles of the cell suspended in it. It is tightly enclosed by the plasma membrane. The sperm contains a limited amount of cytoplasm. During normal spermatogenesis (or maturation), spermatids lose most of their cytoplasm. Remnants may remain as a cytoplasmic droplet at the neck region of the sperm and is shed during ejaculation. However, retention of the droplets may indicate failure of normal maturation and cause infertility (Rengan et al, 2012).

The mature sperm retains a thin layer of cytoplasm underneath the plasma membrane. In the head, the space occupied by cytoplasm between the acrosome and the nucleus is known as the subacrosomal (or perinuclear) space. The cytoplasm between the outer membrane of the acrosome and the plasma membrane is the periacrosomal space.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The cytoplasm is the site where most chemical activities of the cell occur.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The mitochondrial sheath is a sheath of circumferentially oriented mitochondria, arranged end to end, that surrounds the middle piece of a spermatozoon and is thought to control the movements of the tail (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The middle piece of the sperm tail is considered the powerhouse of the sperm. It contains the proximal part of the axoneme, surrounded by the dense outer fibers, surrounded again by a mitochondrial sheath.

The middle piece of the tail has a larger diameter than the rest of the tail due to the presence of mitochondria in this area. The mitochondrial sheath consists of 70-100 condensed and protracted mitochondria that are lined up end-to-end, encircling the outer dense fibers and the axoneme as a helix (Schatten and Constantinescu, 2008).

The mitochondrial sheath is attached to the submitochondrial reticulum, a meshwork of filaments that lies underneath. The submitochondrial reticulum is attached to the end ring (or annulus), the point where the middle piece and the principal piece meet. It is thought that the function of the submitochondrial reticulum is to facilitate and support this arrangement in the midpiece (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014).

Sperm mitochondria-associated cysteine-rich protein (SMCP) is a structural protein that is restricted to the capsule associated with the mitochondrial outer membrane. It maintains the helical structure of the mitochondrial sheath (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The mitochondrial sheath is situated in the proximal aspect of the tail, within the middle piece. It lies just outside the outer dense fibers.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell, which provides the energy required for the movement of the tail to facilitate motility of the sperm. The mitochondrial sheath acts as scaffolding for the numerous mitochondria, which are situated around and along the length outer dense fibers (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The axoneme is the central core of a cilium or flagellum, consisting of a central pair of microtubules surrounded by nine other microtubule pairs (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The axoneme forms the core structure of the sperm tail. It is a cylindrical cytoskeletal structure that extends from the neck to the point where the tail terminates. 

The axoneme is composed of two centrally located microtubule singlets, which are encased by nine microtubule doublets. This is commonly referred to as the “9 + 2” complex. 

The major component proteins of the axoneme are cytoskeletal tubulin and the motor protein dynein. The microtubules are composed of dimers of α-tubulin and β-tubulin. Each of the microtubule doublets is made up of a complete α-microtubule, onto which a β-microtubule attaches. Two dynein arms extend from the α-microtubule to the β-microtubule of the neighboring doublet (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The axoneme stretches across the entire length of the tail, from the neck region (just beneath the centriole) to the point where the tail terminates. The axoneme is the only structure present in the final 5–7 μm of the sperm tail (Standring, 2016).

The central pair of microtubules extend beyond the middle piece into the neck of the sperm, as far as the articular plate (capitulum). The outer doublets end just distal to the neck, where there is the remnants of the distal centriole (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The axoneme acts as scaffold for the sperm tail, providing it with support and an ability to bend and unbend in various directions.

The motor dyneins associated with the microtubules of the axoneme have ATPase activity. Dyneins hydrolyze ATP and undergo a conformational change. They reach towards the minus end of the β-microtubule, resulting in the α- and β-microtubules in a doublet to slide past one another. The coordinated sliding in the doublets results in the propagation of a bending wave down the tail of the sperm, resulting in motility (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

The central pair of microtubules in the axoneme of the spermatozoon is involved in specific aspects of motility. The pair coordinates the sliding movements of the doublet microtubules, as well as taxis and reversal of the tail’s beating motion. These roles are essential for fertilization as evidence has shown that the absence of central pair form the spermatozoon tail results in the paralysis of the axoneme, and thus infertility (Linck et al, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The outer dense fibers are associated with the axoneme and provide strength to the sperm tail.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The outer dense fibers are noncontractile cytoskeletal structures found in the middle piece and most of the principal piece of the sperm tail. The outer dense fibers consist of nine fibers that lie alongside the axoneme. Each of the nine fibers lie opposite a microtubule doublet of the axoneme. 

From a cross sectional view, the outer dense fibers are tear-shape and are not uniform throughout the length of the tail (Kumar & Sharma, 2017). The thickest fibers are situated within the proximal aspect of the middle piece and fibers 1, 5, 6, and 9 tend to be the thickest here. The fibers terminate in the principal piece as the fibrous sheath begins to taper inwards. It is usually the larger aforementioned fibers that are the last to terminate. (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The outer dense fibers are situated within the tail of the sperm. They lie alongside the axoneme and stretch from the distal end of the neck to the distal aspect of the principal piece. Essentially, the fibers extend up to 60% of the length of the principal piece (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

In the middle piece of the tail, the outer dense fibers are surrounded by the mitochondrial sheath, while in the middle piece, the outer dense are surrounded by the fibrous sheath.

The striated columns that form part of the neck are continuous with the outer dense fibers.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The tensile strength of the outer dense fibers aids in shielding the sperm from the damage incurred by the shearing forces met as the sperm travels through the epididymis during ejaculation. Additionally, the outer dense fibers play a role in stabilizing the axoneme, thereby facilitating the motility of the sperm (Zhao et al, 2018). The outer dense fibers, although noncontractile, may provide elastic recoil necessary for sperm motility.

sections.text:
The sperm’s plasma membrane is a dynamic structure and is unique when compared with that of somatic cells. It is divided into various domains based on its location, composition, and function. 

In the sperm head, there are two notable regions of the plasma membrane, the acrosomal region and the postacrosomal region. The plasma membrane that surrounds the tail aspect of the sperm is divided into the middle piece, the principal piece, and the distal piece domains (Toshimori, 2000).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The plasma membrane is the outermost part of the sperm and it encases the entirety of the sperm cell.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The plasma membrane plays a number of roles, which are vital for fertilization to occur. Modification of the plasma membrane is paramount for the initiation of processes, such as capacitation, acrosome reaction, and binding of the sperm head with the plasma membrane of the ovum, to occur. Most of these modifications occur as the sperm passes through the epididymis and in the uterine tube, oviduct (or fallopian tube) of the female reproductive tract (Toshimori, 2000).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The axoneme is the central core of a cilium or flagellum, consisting of a central pair of microtubules surrounded by nine other microtubule pairs (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The axoneme forms the core structure of the sperm tail. It is a cylindrical cytoskeletal structure that extends from the neck to the point where the tail terminates. 

The axoneme is composed of two centrally located microtubule singlets, which are encased by nine microtubule doublets. This is commonly referred to as the “9 + 2” complex. 

The major component proteins of the axoneme are cytoskeletal tubulin and the motor protein dynein. The microtubules are composed of dimers of α-tubulin and β-tubulin. Each of the microtubule doublets is made up of a complete α-microtubule, onto which a β-microtubule attaches. Two dynein arms extend from the α-microtubule to the β-microtubule of the neighboring doublet (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The axoneme stretches across the entire length of the tail, from the neck region (just beneath the centriole) to the point where the tail terminates. The axoneme is the only structure present in the final 5–7 μm of the sperm tail (Standring, 2016).

The central pair of microtubules extend beyond the middle piece into the neck of the sperm, as far as the articular plate (capitulum). The outer doublets end just distal to the neck, where there is the remnants of the distal centriole (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The axoneme acts as scaffold for the sperm tail, providing it with support and an ability to bend and unbend in various directions.

The motor dyneins associated with the microtubules of the axoneme have ATPase activity. Dyneins hydrolyze ATP and undergo a conformational change. They reach towards the minus end of the β-microtubule, resulting in the α- and β-microtubules in a doublet to slide past one another. The coordinated sliding in the doublets results in the propagation of a bending wave down the tail of the sperm, resulting in motility (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

The central pair of microtubules in the axoneme of the spermatozoon is involved in specific aspects of motility. The pair coordinates the sliding movements of the doublet microtubules, as well as taxis and reversal of the tail’s beating motion. These roles are essential for fertilization as evidence has shown that the absence of central pair form the spermatozoon tail results in the paralysis of the axoneme, and thus infertility (Linck et al, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The outer dense fibers are associated with the axoneme and provide strength to the sperm tail.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The outer dense fibers are noncontractile cytoskeletal structures found in the middle piece and most of the principal piece of the sperm tail. The outer dense fibers consist of nine fibers that lie alongside the axoneme. Each of the nine fibers lie opposite a microtubule doublet of the axoneme. 

From a cross sectional view, the outer dense fibers are tear-shape and are not uniform throughout the length of the tail (Kumar & Sharma, 2017). The thickest fibers are situated within the proximal aspect of the middle piece and fibers 1, 5, 6, and 9 tend to be the thickest here. The fibers terminate in the principal piece as the fibrous sheath begins to taper inwards. It is usually the larger aforementioned fibers that are the last to terminate (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The outer dense fibers are situated within the tail of the sperm. They lie alongside the axoneme and stretch from the distal end of the neck to the distal aspect of the principal piece. Essentially, the fibers extend up to 60% of the length of the principal piece (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

In the middle piece of the tail, the outer dense fibers are surrounded by the mitochondrial sheath, while in the middle piece, the outer dense are surrounded by the fibrous sheath.

The striated columns that form part of the neck are continuous with the outer dense fibers.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The tensile strength of the outer dense fibers aids in shielding the sperm from the damage incurred by the shearing forces met as the sperm travels through the epididymis during ejaculation. Additionally, the outer dense fibers play a role in stabilizing the axoneme, thereby facilitating the motility of the sperm (Zhao et al, 2018). The outer dense fibers, although noncontractile, may provide elastic recoil necessary for sperm motility.

sections.text: - Asthenozoospermia

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Zhao, W., Li, Z., Ping, P., Wang, G., Yuan, X. & Sun, F. (2018) Outer dense fibers stabilize the axoneme to maintain sperm motility. J Cell Mol Med, 22(3), 1755-1768.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The fibrous sheath surrounds the principal piece of the tail of a spermatozoon (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The fibrous sheath is a cylindrical cytoskeletal structure that determines the scope of the principal piece of the sperm tail and is adherent to the plasma membrane.

The fibrous sheath takes the shape of a tapering cylinder, which constitutes two longitudinal filamentous columns affixed by circumferential ribs. The longitudinal columns course along the edges of microtubule doublets three and eight of the axoneme and are affixed to the outer dense fibers three and eight in the proximal aspect of the principal piece (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014). 

The circumferential ribs of the fibrous sheath are made up of tightly packed circumferentially arranged filamentous material. Each rib measures approximately 50nm in width and lies 10-20nm away from the adjacent ribs. The ribs widened distally as they fuse with the longitudinal columns and with themselves. 

At the distal aspect of the fibrous sheath, the thickness of the ribs is significantly reduced. The ribs, as well as the outer dense columns terminate at the distal margin of the principal piece (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The fibrous sheath is located in the principal piece of the tail of the sperm. It is situated outside of the axoneme and the outer dense fibers. It lies deep to the plasma membrane and is adherent to it.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The fibrous sheath regulates the directionality of the sperm’s tail beat, thereby restricting the sliding of the microtubule doublets in the axoneme during tail motion, as well as regulating the bending of the tail (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.text:

- Flagella dyskinesia 

- Asthenozoospermia

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The nucleus is a flattened ovoid disc that constitutes the major part of the head of the sperm. It contains hypercondensed chromatin, which makes its volume about 5% less than that of a somatic cell (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014).

Just like every other cell, the nucleus of the sperm has a bilaminar nuclear envelope (inner and outer membranes) that encases the nucleus. Unlike the nuclear envelope in other cells, it is mostly devoid of nuclear pores, which were eliminated during spermatogenesis. However, at the base of the nucleus, an area is called the redundant nuclear envelope has an abundance of nuclear pores.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nucleus of the sperm contains the male genetic material, which is essential for the creation of a diploid individual at fertilization.

sections.name: References

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The acrosome is the cap-like, membrane-bound structure derived from Golgi elements found at the anterior portion of the head of a spermatozoon; it contains lysosomal enzymes and a proteolytic enzyme, which are believed to facilitate entry of spermatozoa into oocytes (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The head of the sperm is composed of a nucleus and the acrosome, both of which are surrounded by cytoskeleton and minimal cytoplasm.

The acrosome is a cap-like structure that drapes over about 50-70% of the proximal aspect of the sperm head. It is enclosed by an inner and outer acrosomal membrane. It is derived from the Golgi vesicles during spermatogenesis. It is essentially a hydrolytic and digestive enzyme-rich vesicle that releases its contents on approaching an oocyte in order for fertilization to occur. The acrosome is essentially a specialized lysosome since it contains acid phosphatase, hyaluronidase, neuraminidase and a trypsin-like protease (called acrosin).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The acrosome lies just beneath the periacrosomal space and the plasma membrane of the sperm and above the subacrosomal space. The acrosome terminates on reaching the postacrosomal sheath.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The acrosome is essentially a specialized lysosome since it contains acid phosphatase, hyaluronidase, neuraminidase and a trypsin-like protease (called acrosin). These enzymes are required for the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida (Grudzinskas and Yovich, 1995). 

Fertilization cannot be completed without a process known as capacitation, of which the acrosome is a necessary participant. Capacitation is essentially the functional maturation of a sperm cell and is completed after the sperm has made its journey to the uterine tube, oviduct (or fallopian tube). Various structural and biochemical changes occur during capacitation in which sperm change their behaviour, including the acrosome reaction. Following capacitation, sperm develop the ability to penetrate the cumulus of the egg and bind to the zona pellucida. This stimulates the release of digestive enzymes from the acrosome to aid in the dissolution of the zona pellucida in the vicinity of the sperm head, allowing it to access the perivitelline space (Standring, 2016; Plant and Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nuclear envelope is the structure enclosing the cell nucleus and separating it from the cytoplasm, consisting of two concentric lipid bilayers (the inner and outer membranes) separated by a 30 nm wide perinuclear space. The outer membrane is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and nuclear pore complexes bridging both membranes provide communication between the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Just like every other cell, the nucleus of the sperm has a bilaminar nuclear envelope (inner and outer membranes) that encases the nucleus. Unlike the nuclear envelope in other cells, it is mostly devoid of nuclear pores, which were eliminated during spermatogenesis. However, at the base of the nucleus, an area called the redundant nuclear envelope has an abundance of nuclear pores.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The basal plate is attached to the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nuclear envelope is responsible for the exchange of materials between the nucleus and the cytoplasm of a cell. It also provides a scaffold for the organization of chromatin within the nucleus and the cytoskeleton outside.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The postacrosomal sheath is a broad band encircling the postacrosomal region of the nucleus of a spermatozoon (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The postacrosomal sheath is a component of the perinuclear theca. The perinuclear theca forms a firm protective shell around the nucleus of the sperm and is made up of a complex of proteins, which are linked and stabilized by disulphide bonds. 

The perinuclear theca can be divided into three segments, corresponding to the regions they are located, and have specific functions during fertilization. The subacrosomal layer is situated underneath the acrosome and provides support to it. The equatorial segment is composed of the outer and inner acrosomal membranes. It conveys receptor molecules required for the binding of the sperm head to the egg. The postacrosomal sheath is the first organelle of the sperm to come in contact with the oocyte cytoplasm after sperm-oocyte plasma fusion. It disperses in the oocyte’s cytoplasm and is thought to activate the oocyte to initiate the embryonic cell cycle, possesses a complex of signaling proteins, which propel the pathway of oocyte activation and the development of the zygote (De Jonge & Barratt, 2006).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The postacrosomal sheath is located just beneath the acrosome and is sandwiched between the nuclear envelope and the plasma membrane.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
A number of the proteins contained within the perinuclear theca have cell-signaling functions, which are activated once they are discharged. They are discharged when the perinuclear theca disintegrates into the cytoplasm of the oocyte during the process of fertilization (Jonge & Barratt, 2006).

The postacrosomal sheath possesses a complex of signaling proteins (Sperm Borne Oocyte Activating Factors), which propel the pathway of oocyte activation and development of the zygote. Following the fusion of the sperm head and the membrane of the oocyte, some of these Sperm Borne Oocyte Activating Factors spread across the oocyte membrane, activating the signaling mechanisms that result in the activation of the oocyte, as well as the commencement of the development of the zygote. An additional number of proteins associated with the postacrosomal sheath remain in the nucleus of the sperm and transforms it into the male pronulceus (De Jonge & Barratt, 2006).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The plasma membrane is the structure enveloping a cell, enclosing the cytoplasm and forming a selective permeability barrier; it consists of a lipid bilayer with integral and peripheral proteins and contains channels and pumps to transport substances across the membrane, as well as receptors to receive stimuli from the external environment and transduce them into intracellular signals (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The sperm’s plasma membrane is a dynamic structure and is unique when compared with that of somatic cells. It is divided into various domains based on its location, composition, and function. 

In the sperm head, there are two notable regions of the plasma membrane, the acrosomal region and the postacrosomal region. The plasma membrane that surrounds the tail aspect of the sperm is divided into the middle piece, the principal piece, and the distal piece domains (Toshimori, 2000).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The plasma membrane is the outermost part of the sperm and it encases the entirety of the sperm cell.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The plasma membrane plays a number of roles, which are vital for fertilization to occur. Modification of the plasma membrane is paramount for the initiation of processes, such as capacitation, acrosome reaction, and binding of the sperm head with the plasma membrane of the ovum, to occur. Most of these modifications occur as the sperm passes through the epididymis and in the uterine tube, oviduct (or fallopian tube) of the female reproductive tract (Toshimori, 2000).

sections.name: References

Toshimori, K. (2000) Sperm Plasma Membrane Modifications Associated with Fertilization in Mammals. Journal of Reproduction and Development, 46, 65-78.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cytoplasm is the protoplasm of a cell exclusive of that of the nucleus; it consists of a continuous aqueous solution (cytosol) and the organelles and inclusions suspended in it and is the site of most of the chemical activities of the cell (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The cytoplasm of a cell includes an aqueous solution, the cytosol, and the organelles of the cell suspended in it. It is tightly enclosed by the plasma membrane. The sperm contains a limited amount of cytoplasm. During normal spermatogenesis (or maturation), spermatids lose most of their cytoplasm. Remnants may remain as a cytoplasmic droplet at the neck region of the sperm and is shed during ejaculation. However, retention of the droplets may indicate failure of normal maturation and cause infertility (Rengan et al, 2012).

The mature sperm retains a thin layer of cytoplasm underneath the plasma membrane. In the head, the space occupied by cytoplasm between the acrosome and the nucleus is known as the subacrosomal (or perinuclear) space. The cytoplasm between the outer membrane of the acrosome and the plasma membrane is the periacrosomal space.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The cytoplasm is the site where most chemical activities of the cell occur.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The postacrosomal sheath is a broad band encircling the postacrosomal region of the nucleus of a spermatozoon (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The postacrosomal sheath is a component of the perinuclear theca. The perinuclear theca forms a firm protective shell around the nucleus of the sperm and is made up of a complex of proteins, which are linked and stabilized by disulphide bonds. 

The perinuclear theca can be divided into three segments, corresponding to the regions they are located, and have specific functions during fertilization. The subacrosomal layer is situated underneath the acrosome and provides support to it. The equatorial segment is composed of the outer and inner acrosomal membranes. It conveys receptor molecules required for the binding of the sperm head to the egg. The postacrosomal sheath is the first organelle of the sperm to come in contact with the oocyte cytoplasm after sperm-oocyte plasma fusion. It disperses in the oocyte’s cytoplasm and is thought to activate the oocyte to initiate the embryonic cell cycle, possesses a complex of signaling proteins, which propel the pathway of oocyte activation and the development of the zygote (De Jonge & Barratt, 2006).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The postacrosomal sheath is located just beneath the acrosome and is sandwiched between the nuclear envelope and the plasma membrane.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
A number of the proteins contained within the perinuclear theca have cell-signaling functions, which are activated once they are discharged. They are discharged when the perinuclear theca disintegrates into the cytoplasm of the oocyte during the process of fertilization (Jonge & Barratt, 2006).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nuclear envelope is the structure enclosing the cell nucleus and separating it from the cytoplasm, consisting of two concentric lipid bilayers (the inner and outer membranes) separated by a 30 nm wide perinuclear space. The outer membrane is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and nuclear pore complexes bridging both membranes provide communication between the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Just like every other cell, the nucleus of the sperm has a bilaminar nuclear envelope (inner and outer membranes) that encases the nucleus. Unlike the nuclear envelope in other cells, it is mostly devoid of nuclear pores, which were eliminated during spermatogenesis. However, at the base of the nucleus, an area called the redundant nuclear envelope has an abundance of nuclear pores.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The basal plate is attached to the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nuclear envelope is responsible for the exchange of materials between the nucleus and the cytoplasm of a cell. It also provides a scaffold for the organization of chromatin within the nucleus and the cytoskeleton outside.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The acrosome is the cap-like, membrane-bound structure derived from Golgi elements found at the anterior portion of the head of a spermatozoon; it contains lysosomal enzymes and a proteolytic enzyme, which are believed to facilitate entry of spermatozoa into oocytes (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The head of the sperm is composed of a nucleus and the acrosome, both of which are surrounded by cytoskeleton and minimal cytoplasm.

The acrosome is a cap-like structure that drapes over about 50-70% of the proximal aspect of the sperm head. It is enclosed by an inner and outer acrosomal membrane. It is derived from the Golgi vesicles during spermatogenesis. It is essentially a hydrolytic and digestive enzyme-rich vesicle that releases its contents on approaching an oocyte in order for fertilization to occur. The acrosome is essentially a specialized lysosome since it contains acid phosphatase, hyaluronidase, neuraminidase and a trypsin-like protease (called acrosin).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The acrosome lies just beneath the periacrosomal space and the plasma membrane of the sperm and above the subacrosomal space. The acrosome terminates on reaching the postacrosomal sheath.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The acrosome is essentially a specialized lysosome since it contains acid phosphatase, hyaluronidase, neuraminidase and a trypsin-like protease (called acrosin). These enzymes are required for the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida (Grudzinskas and Yovich, 1995). 

Fertilization cannot be completed without a process known as capacitation, of which the acrosome is a necessary participant. Capacitation is essentially the functional maturation of a sperm cell and is completed after the sperm has made its journey to the uterine tube, oviduct (or fallopian tube). Various structural and biochemical changes occur during capacitation in which sperm change their behaviour, including the acrosome reaction. Following capacitation, sperm develop the ability to penetrate the cumulus of the egg and bind to the zona pellucida. This stimulates the release of digestive enzymes from the acrosome to aid in the dissolution of the zona pellucida in the vicinity of the sperm head, allowing it to access the perivitelline space (Standring, 2016; Plant and Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.text:
- Globozoospermia

- Teratozoospermia

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The nucleus is a flattened ovoid disc that constitutes the major part of the head of the sperm. It contains hypercondensed chromatin, which makes its volume about 5% less than that of a somatic cell (Plant and Zeleznik, 2014).

Just like every other cell, the nucleus of the sperm has a bilaminar nuclear envelope (inner and outer membranes) that encases the nucleus. Unlike the nuclear envelope in other cells, it is mostly devoid of nuclear pores, which were eliminated during spermatogenesis. However, at the base of the nucleus, an area is called the redundant nuclear envelope has an abundance of nuclear pores.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nucleus of the sperm contains the male genetic material, which is essential for the creation of a diploid individual at fertilization.

sections.name: References

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A vacuole is any membrane-bound space or cavity within a cell (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The nuclear vacuoles are thought to develop as a consequence of incomplete chromatin condensation during the process of spermatogenesis. They have been observed in 90% of structurally and functionally normal sperm, and differ in number, size, and location. Some can be so large that they contort the shape of the sperm head (Guraya, 2012). 

The nuclear vacuoles can exist in both singular and multiple forms and contain materials such as granular cytoplasmic substances and remnants of nuclear and plasma membranes.

The number and size of nuclear vacuoles are indicative of the maturity or immaturity of the nucleus of the sperm. Large vacuoles are mostly observed in mature sperm (Toshimori, 2009).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Nuclear vacuoles are situated within the nucleus of the sperm.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The function of nuclear vacuoles is not well known. It is still unclear whether or not they have an effect on fertilization. However, since nuclear vacuoles are associated with incomplete chromatin condensation, they may be associated with abnormal sperm morphology (Komiya et al, 2014).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The centriole is either of the two cylindrical organelles located in the centrosome and containing nine triplets of microtubules arrayed around their edges; during cell division the centrioles are duplicated, with the resulting pairs migrating to opposite poles of the cell, where they serve to organize the spindles. They are capable of independent replication and of migrating to form basal bodies (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The centriole is a cylindrical organelle that is located near the nucleus of most eukaryotes. Initially, in spermatids, there is a proximal and a distal centriole; however, the distal centriole becomes disorganized in late spermatids. In the mature sperm, the proximal centriole is located in the neck, deep to the striated columns. 

The proximal centriole of the sperm is made up of nine triplets of microtubules, organized just like a pinwheel. It forms a spherical shape that is surrounded by a dense pericentriolar material. Collectively, the centriole and the pericentriolar material make up the centrosome (Sathananthan and Deen, 2014).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The centriole is located within the neck of the sperm, deep within the striated columns and inferior to the basal plate. The axoneme commences at the distal end of the centriole.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The centrioles play the role of a microtubule organizing center, where it regulates microtubule nucleation (formation of new microtubules) and spatial organization (Plant & Zeleznik, 2014).

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Plant, T. M. & Zeleznik, A. J. (2014) Knobil and Neill's Physiology of Reproduction. Elsevier Science.

Sathananthan, P. A. H. & Deen, F. (2014) Microscopic Images of Human Sperm, Oocytes and Embryos for Assisted Reproductive Technology Including Embryonic Stem Cells.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: During cell division, centrioles are duplicated and form the mitotic spindle and so have a vital role in equal segregation of chromosomes between daughter cells. Abnormalities in the regulation of centriole duplication can lead to abnormalities of the microtubule organizing center and therefore abnormal sorting of chromosomes during cell divisions. These malfunctions are related to malignant cell transformations (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The articular plate, basal plate, and the striated columns are referred to as the connecting piece between the sperm head and tail.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The articular plate is a dense fibrous structure found in the neck of the sperm. It conforms to the concave shape of the basal plate at the base of the nucleus, thus acting like a ball and socket joint at the interface between the head and the neck of the sperm.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The articular plate is in contact with the basal plate, proximally, and the striated columns are continuous with the articular plate, distally.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Collectively, the articular plate, basal plate, and the striated columns are referred to as the ‘connecting piece’ between the sperm head and tail. Therefore, the articular plate acts as a structural anchorage and an articulation between the head and tail.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The articular plate, basal plate, and the striated columns are referred to as the connecting piece between the sperm head and tail.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The basal plate is an electron dense structure located at the interface between the head and the neck of the sperm. It is attached to the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope. The basal plate is concave in shape and is adjacent to the convex surface of the articular plate. Together, these two structures act like a ball and socket joint.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Collectively, the articular plate, basal plate, and the striated columns are referred to as the ‘connecting piece’ between the sperm head and tail. The basal plate allows for the articulation between the head and the neck of the sperm.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The articular plate, basal plate, and the striated columns are referred to as the connecting piece between the sperm head and tail.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The striated columns are found in the neck and are approximately 1-2 μm in length. They are composed of nine columns that extend from the articular plate and are continuous with the nine outer dense fibers in the sperm tail (Schatten & Constantinescu, 2008). The striated columns inherit their name from their striated appearance. This is due to the dense segments alternating with light bands (similar to that in the sarcomere).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The striated columns are continuous with the articular plate, proximally, and are continuous with the outer dense fibers, distally. The centriole is found within the striated column.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Collectively, the articular plate, basal plate, and the striated columns are referred to as the ‘connecting piece’ between the sperm head and tail. Therefore, the striated column acts as a structural anchorage between the head and tail.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Schatten, H. & Constantinescu, G. M. (2008) Comparative Reproductive Biology. Wiley.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The redundant nuclear envelope is located at the base of the nucleus and contains several nuclear pores.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Just like every other cell, the nucleus of the sperm has a bilaminar nuclear envelope (inner and outer membranes) that encases the nucleus. Unlike the nuclear envelope in other cells, it is mostly devoid of nuclear pores, which were eliminated during spermatogenesis. However, at the base of the nucleus, an area called the redundant nuclear envelope has an abundance of nuclear pores.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The redundant nuclear envelope lies in an area at the base of the nucleus, caudal to the posterior ring.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The function of the redundant nuclear envelope is not well understood. Considering it is situated in the posterior aspect of the nucleus, in an area adjacent to the cytoplasm, it is the only part of the sperm that information exchange between the nucleus and the constituents of the cytoplasm occurs. This theory is also backed up by the presence of nuclear pores in this region of the nuclear envelope, thus, it may have some functional significance (Guraya, 2012).

sections.name: References

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Gustatory glands are serous secreting glands in the posterior part of the tongue near the vallate papillae (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The gustatory glands are exocrine glands embedded within the lamina propria of the tongue, located within the sulci between the mucosal elevations enclosing the vallate papillae. Their ducts open up into the base of the vallate papilla where they secrete enzymes to assist in macronutrient breakdown. These glands are innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The primary function of the gustatory glands is for initial lubrication and enzymatic digestion. They secrete lingual lipase, an enzyme that initiates lipid hydrolysis. The volume of the secretions helps to lubricate the oral cavity.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The muscles of the tongue include the extrinsic and intrinsic muscles that move the tongue (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
Function
sections.text:
The extrinsic muscle of the tongue work to alter the position of the tongue. The genioglossus muscle enables the tongue to stick out of the mouth. Synchronized bilateral movement of both muscles functions to lower the central part of the tongue, while individual genioglossal movements cause the tongue to move to the opposing side. The hyoglossus muscle depresses the tongue, while the styloglossus muscle allows the tongue to be brought back and upwards. The palatoglossus muscle closes off the oral cavity from the oropharynx by elevating the tongue root to make contact with the palatoglossal arch.

The intrinsic muscles of the tongue are responsible for changing its shape, movements required for deglutition and phonation.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A taste bud is one of the minute, bud-shaped sensory organs of the tongue, situated around the bases of the vallate, fungiform, and foliate papillae. It contains several types of specialized epithelial cells, including taste receptor, supporting, and basal cells, and is innervated by gustatory nerve fibers (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
Taste buds are located all over the tongue, but predominantly within the gustatory lingual papillae. The taste buds are not distributed equally and have different populations among the gustatory lingual papillae. 

The taste buds are most abundant towards the posterior parts of the tongue and the vallate papillae, on average, contain 250 buds each (Standring, 2016). The taste buds of the vallate papillae are located in the lateral walls of the papillae.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The sensation of taste is mediated by the taste buds. The chemosensory receptors of the taste cells in the taste buds are activated upon detection of nutrients and toxins in the oral cavity. The information is transmitted to the nerve fibers via synapses located at the base of the taste bud.

It contains several types of specialized epithelial cells, including taste receptor, supporting, and basal cells, and is innervated by gustatory nerve fibers (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Taste buds are located all over the tongue, but predominantly within the gustatory lingual papillae. The taste buds are not distributed equally and have different populations among the gustatory lingual papillae. 

The taste buds of the fungiform papillae are the least abundant. They may form in groups of small quantities, with the taste buds being clustered close together. They are located at the apex of the papillae, readily in contact with any food particles that they come into contact with.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The sensation of taste is mediated by the taste buds. The taste buds of the fungiform papillae are based on the apex of the taste buds, prepared for chemosensory activation upon detection of nutrients and toxins in the oral cavity. The information is transmitted to the nerve fibers via synapses located at the base of the taste bud.

There are over a thousand taste buds shared over the lateral sides of the tongue, especially within the sulci between the ridges of the foliate papillae (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The taste buds of the foliate papillae are arranged in single file in the lateral epithelium, perpendicular to the surface of the vertical ridges. These lines of taste buds also face a parallel line of taste buds on the wall of the next ridge. Therefore, the taste buds on the same sulcus wall are lateral to each, and they are facing another line of taste buds on the opposite sulcal wall.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: General sensory innervation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (originating from the mandibular nerve CNV3). Special sensory fibers of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, excluding the vallate papillae, run within the chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve) and its fibers accompanies the lingual nerve. General and special sensory innervation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is conveyed by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CNIX). This includes special sensory innervation of the vallate papillae.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The sensory innervation to the taste buds is elaborate and well distributed. There are various patterns of innervation among the taste buds, with individual sensory nerve fibers splitting and diverging among the taste buds. Other terminal fibers from may be attributed to just one taste bud, but they distribute themselves to the different taste cells comprising that taste bud. In contrast to this, a single taste bud may receive a broad innervation stemming from multiple nerve branch inputs. Overall, these alternating methods of innervation provide a complex neural meshwork coursing throughout the taste buds.

In general, each taste bud receives one of two fiber types. The first type of nerve fiber splits within the periphery of the taste bud, forming a neural web on the outskirts on the bulb-shaped collection of sensory cells. These nerves present as free nerve endings. The other type of nerve fiber forms a central, inner web of innervation. These are arranged in a series of synapses (Standring, 2016).

There is a broad and complex innervation for the tongue’s ordinary and special senses. General sensory innervation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (originating from the mandibular nerve CN V3). Special sensory fibers of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, excluding the vallate papillae, run within the chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve) and its fibers accompanies the lingual nerve. General and special sensory innervation of the posterior one third of the tongue are conveyed by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). This includes special sensory innervation of the vallate papillae.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The sensation of taste is important for discerning between desirable foods, initiating swallowing, and regulating gastrointestinal secretions. These highly sensitive functions are the primary reasoning behind the broad, dense neural distribution.
