sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The lamina propria is the connective tissue coat of a mucous membrane just deep to the epithelium and basement membrane (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The lamina propria is a loose connective areolar tissue layer forming a deeper part of the mucosal layer of the oral mucosa. It serves as a protective barrier, as well as providing immune cells when needed.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The lamina propria houses a rich supply of immune cells in response to the desquamation of superficial epithelial apoptotic or necrotic cells. It also serves a mechanical protective function by its service as a barrier, preventing internal tissue access of external pathogens and microorganisms.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The lamina propria is situated deep to the basement membrane of the olfactory epithelium, separating it from the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Anosmia

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The lingual artery provides the majority of blood supply to the tongue via its dorsal and deep lingual branches.

sections.name: Description
sections.text:
The lingual artery provides the majority of blood supply to the tongue via its dorsal and deep lingual branches. 

The lingual artery is derived from the external carotid artery. It moves towards the bottom of the oral cavity, sharply meandering upwards and proceeding to the tip of the tongue, where it joins with its fellow lingual artery of the opposite side. Here they form a dense anastomosis to richly supply the surround musculature with blood. 

The dorsal lingual branch of the lingual artery supplies the posterior third of the tongue. They provide blood to the mucous membrane and surrounding structures of the oropharynx. These include the palatine tonsils, soft palate, epiglottis, and palatoglossal arches. This supply is consolidated by the formation of anastomosis among the dorsal lingual arteries. There is partial contribution to this by branches from the superior laryngeal anastomoses.

The deep lingual artery is the terminal branch of the lingual artery. At the anterior border of the hyoglossus muscle, it ascends between the inferior longitudinal muscle of the tongue laterally and the genioglossus muscle medially. It passes forwards in a tortuous manner near the lingual surface adjacent to the frenulum. Here it is accompanied by the lingual nerve.

Venous drainage occurs via the lingual vein and its tributaries. The lingual vein is formed by the joining of the dorsal and deep lingual veins. The dorsum and sides of the tongue are drained by dorsal lingual veins, while the tip of the tongue and deeper mass are drained by the deep lingual vein. The lingual vein travels between the hyoglossus and genioglossus muscles to link up to the internal jugular vein.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The fungiform papillae are the knoblike projections on the tongue, scattered singly among the filiform papillae (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The majority of the fungiform papillae are located at the anterior margin of the tongue, including the tip of the tongue. There are some located among the filiform papillae along the dorsum of the tongue. 

The fungiform papillae have broad spherical heads; hence their name is derived from the Latin for mushroom. Their taste buds are located at the apex of the papillae, readily in contact with any food particles that they come into contact with. The papillae tend to be larger and slightly flatter than the filiform papillae. They are red due to their densely vascularized core and thin epithelium.

The fungiform papillae are protected by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium and participate in gustation.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The fungiform papillae are one of the three types of lingual papillae involved in gustation, which is the detection of the different tastes of salty, bitter, sour, and sweet, and savory (Ikeda, 2002). It is important that all areas of the tongue are responsive to the different modalities of taste. However, some taste buds respond to a greater amount of chemical activation, while some respond to less. The simultaneous activation of different taste buds is what leads to the recognition of specific tastes.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ikeda, K. (2002) New seasonings. Chem Senses, 27(9), 847-9.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The vallate papillae are the largest papillae of the tongue, 8 to 12 in number, arranged in the form of a V anterior to the sulcus terminalis of the tongue (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The vallate papillae are both the largest in size and lowest in number. There is usually only 8–12 in total on the tongue surface. They are centrally located, directly in front of the terminal sulcus of the tongue, the boundary between the oral and pharyngeal regions of the tongue. These papillae are broader at their apex, and they are encircled by marginally raised mucosal mounds (hence, they are also known as the circumvallate papillae). In between the papilla and the mucosal mound is a groove. The taste buds are located in the walls of the papilla, while several salivary glands open at the floor of the groove. The taste buds of the vallate papillae are innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The vallate papillae are involved in savory taste detection (Ikeda, 2002).

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Ikeda, K. (2002) New seasonings. Chem Senses, 27(9), 847-9.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The filiform papillae are the threadlike elevations that cover most of the tongue surface (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The filiform papillae are widely distributed along the entire dorsal surface of the tongue. They are threadlike (filum) and usually have peaked or pointed tips, which are more rounded in the anterior regions of the tongue. They are composed of connective tissue cores which are columnar in shape with a central upper depression. These have hair-like protrusions emanating from it, with varying quantity and thickness based on location of papillae (Kobayashi et al., 1994).

The filiform papillae are unique in terms of the lingual papillae as they predominantly have a keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and are the only papillae without taste buds, so they do not participate in gustation. Their role is focused on mastication due to their large population and friction-generating ability.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The filiform papillae increase the total surface area of the tongue and, thus, the total contact area between the food particles and the tongue.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Kobayashi, K., Kumakura, M., Shinkai, H. & Ishii, K. (1994) Three-dimensional fine structure of the lingual papillae and their connective tissue cores in the human tongue. Kaibogaku Zasshi, 69(5), 624-35.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The foliate papillae are the parallel mucosal folds on the margins of the tongue at the junction of its body and root (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The foliate papillae are located on the posterolateral sides of the tongue bilaterally, just at the margin of the sulcus terminalis. They appear as an array of vertical, red ridges. These ridges are close together, and there are thin sulci between them. There is an abundance of taste buds with the ridges, lining the lateral walls. 

Foliate papillae are covered by a non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and participate in gustation by activation of the taste buds and the resulting signal transduction.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The foliate papillae are anterior to the palatoglossal arches at the isthmus of the fauces, and just anterolateral to the terminal sulcus of the tongue. The vertical ridges of the foliate papillae are in contact with the lower back teeth and the accompanying gingiva.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The foliate papillae are one of the three types of lingual papillae involved in gustation, which is the detection of the different tastes of salty, bitter, sour, and sweet, and savory (Ikeda, 2002). It is important that all areas of the tongue are responsive to the different modalities of taste. However, some taste buds respond to a greater amount of chemical activation, while some respond to less. The simultaneous activation of different taste buds is what leads to the recognition of specific tastes.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A pinocytotic vesicle is any of the small fluid-filled vesicles found in the cytoplasm during pinocytosis, formed by invaginations of the cell membrane (caveolae), which pinch off and become free (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: A pinocytotic vesicle (80–150 nm in diameter) forms when the plasmalemma engulfs fluid or small proteins and any molecules in solution in the extracellular fluid. This process is called pinocytosis and is a common process in almost all human cells.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Pinocytotic vesicles are located in the apical regions of the cell cytoplasm.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: A pinocytotic vesicle engulfs fluid or small proteins and any molecules in solution in the extracellular fluid.

sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a special form of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in association with the T tubules in the sarcoplasm of striated muscle and comprising a system of cisternae and tubules forming a plexus around each myofibril. It contains large numbers of calcium pumps and ryanodine receptors and is a storage compartment for calcium ions, which it releases in response to an action potential in the adjacent T tubule to cause muscular contraction (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is an organelle that consists of a network of loose flattened tubules with various compartments, many of which contain Ca2+. The two ends of the SR are wider, thus form terminal sacs called cisternae. Two cisternae of adjacent sarcoplasmic reticula and one transverse tubule form a functional unit called a triad, which operates to elicit the release of Ca2+ from SR stores (Maclennan and Zvaritch, 2011).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in skeletal muscle. It forms a network of tubules that extend through a muscle fiber. The flattened tubules surround, but do not make direct contact with the myofibrils in a muscle fiber.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum functions as an intracellular calcium store. Depolarization of the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane results in the release of calcium ions (Ca2+). This release of calcium ions triggers the cascade required for contraction.

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Fatigue

—Central core disease

sections.name: References
sections.text:

Maclennan, D. H. and Zvaritch, E. (2011) 'Mechanistic models for muscle diseases and disorders originating in the sarcoplasmic reticulum', Biochim Biophys Acta, 1813(5), pp. 948-64.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: An intermediate filament is a class of cytoplasmic filaments, 8–11 nm in diameter, that predominantly act as structural components of the cytoskeleton and also allow various movements in cellular processes. Different types contain different, tissue-specific proteins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: Intermediate filaments are like ropes forming an intersecting cytoskeletal network. They are around 10 nm in diameter and are composed of desmin or vimentin. They attach to the dense bodies, linking them to the sarcolemma (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Intermediate filaments have a structural role maintaining the stability of cell-to-cell junctions and adherence of the cell to the extracellular matrix. They also function as part of the cytoskeleton, thus supporting the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
–Several diseases can be attributed to defects in the assembly of intermediate filaments. A characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease is disarray of intermediate filaments in some neurons (Ross & Pawlina, 2016).

–“Mallory bodies” in hepatocytes in alcoholic liver cirrhosis is the accumulation of inclusions containing predominantly keratin intermediate filaments (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

–Some specific types of intermediate filaments occurring in tumors allow the origins of the cell causing the tumor to be identified (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The sarcolemma is the delicate plasma membrane that invests every striated muscle fiber (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The sarcolemma is the fine, delicate, extensible membrane surrounding each muscle fiber. It is composed of a cell, or plasma, membrane which presents an extracellular matrix of collagen fibrils and polysaccharides that make contact with the basal lamina. The sarcolemma also contains tunnel-like invaginations into the sarcoplasm, which are known as transverse tubules (T tubules) in striated muscle and caveolae in smooth muscle (Standring, 2020).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Transmembrane proteins found within the sarcolemma facilitate a physical connection between the actin cytoskeleton of the muscle fiber and the extracellular basal lamina (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Like other types of cell membranes, the sarcolemma forms a defined barrier between extracellular and intracellular environments.

sections.name: References
sections.text:
Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

Martini, F. H., Nath, J. L. and Bartholomew, E. F. (2017) Fundamentals of Anatomy & Physiology. Pearson Education.

Standring, S. (2020) Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice. 42nd edn.: Elsevier Health Sciences.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The sarcoplasm is the interfibrillary matter of the striated muscles; the substance in which the fibrillae of the muscle fiber are embedded (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm equivalent within muscle cells. It contains many of the same organelles, cytoskeleton, and matrix which is important in many cell functions. The sarcoplasm is slightly adapted to respond to the high energy demands of muscle cells, such as having a higher concentration of glycosomes and myoglobin.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The sarcoplasm is an aqueous substance found within the sarcolemma, which contains many cellular organelles such as the sarcoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, ribosomes, and Golgi apparatus.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Similar to the cytoplasm in other cells, the sarcoplasm acts as a medium for many important metabolic processes.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Smooth muscle cells contain a single nucleus occupying the broadest region of the cell. In an uncontracted cell viewed in longitudinal section, the nucleus is an elongated structure with ends tapered. If the cell is sectioned transversely, the nucleus will appear as a circular/rounded profile.

Nuclei have a wrinkled or corkscrew appearance when viewed in a longitudinal section after contraction of the cell during fixation. This is a useful characteristic when trying to distinguish a smooth muscle cell from a fibroblast or fibrocyte in routine histological sections.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Smooth muscle cells contain a single nucleus occupying the broadest region of the cell.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nucleus is the control center of the cell and houses the genome (genetic information) in eukaryotic cells. It enables DNA replication and synthesizes ribosomal (rRNA), messenger (mRNA), and transfer (tRNA) ribonucleic acid.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A caveola is a small (approximately 50 nm), flask-shaped invagination of the plasma membrane occurring in nearly all animal cells, coated with the membrane protein caveolin and rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids. Caveolae are a special form of lipid raft and are associated with endocytosis, budding from the plasma membrane to form pinosomes; they also concentrate signaling molecules and have been implicated in other processes, including the export of cholesterol to serum lipoproteins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: Most cells in the body utilize a process called pinocytosis to ingest fluid and small protein molecules via small vesicles about 80–150 nm in diameter. It is a continual process, so small vesicles are continually forming at the cell surface. Most of the vesicles eventually fuse with lysosomes although they are very numerous in endothelial cells as they move materials from their surface of origin to the other side. They are also numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the sarcolemma (plasma membrane) are referred to as caveolae. Cytoplasmic vesicles are in close proximity to sparse amounts of smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Caveolae are numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the smooth muscle sarcolemma (plasma membrane).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Smooth muscle cells lack T tubules. Caveolae and vesicles function to deliver Ca+ to the cytoplasm as a consequence of depolarization of the sarcolemma and activation of voltage-sensitive Ca+ channels or direct activation of gated Ca+ release channels in the sER by a second messenger molecule. Ca+ can also be released into the cytoplasm via ligated Ca+ channels activated by hormones also by second messenger pathways. 

Increasing the intracellular concentration of Ca+ is responsible for contraction of the smooth muscle cell. Contraction of smooth muscle cells is initiated by mechanical impulses, neural stimulation via neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine and norepinephrine, or chemical stimuli of the cells.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The thick myofilament is one of the thick contractile myofilaments in a muscle cell, composed mainly of myosin (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Myosin is the main component of the thick myofilaments. It is a large complex molecule consisting of two identical heavy chains and two pairs of light chains. Each myosin heavy chain consists of two thin, rodlike molecules (2–3 nm thick and 150 nm long) twisted together (Mescher, 2013). 

Small globular projections form the heads of each myosin heavy chain. The heads contain binding sites for both ATP and actin and demonstrate motor and ATPase activity. Four light chains are associated with the head.

A thick myofilament consists of several hundred myosin molecules (1.6 μm long and 14 nm wide) arranged so their rodlike portions overlap, and their globular heads oriented toward either end (Mescher, 2013; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). 

The head of the myosin molecule, and a small portion of the rodlike portion, forms cross-bridges between thin and thick myofilaments. These bridges convert chemical energy into mechanical energy.

Thick myofilaments differ from those in skeletal muscle in that the polarity of the myosin heads is identical along one side of the filament and the opposite on the other side. This allows overlapping thin myofilaments to be pulled along the whole length of the thick myofilament.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Thick myofilaments are scattered throughout the sarcoplasm of smooth muscle cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Myosin converts chemical energy (ATP) to mechanical energy, and so generates force and movement.

Muscle contraction results from the binding of myosin to actin myofilaments, allowing myosin to function as a motor that drives myofilament sliding and so movement.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The thin filament is one of the thin contractile myofilaments in a muscle cell, composed mainly of actin (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Thin myofilaments are composed of actin, tropomyosin, and caldesmon. 

Actin is the main component of the thin myofilament. It is a long filamentous (F-actin) polymer consisting of two strands of globular (G-actin) monomers twisted around each other to form a double helical formation about 1 μm long and 8 nm wide. Each G-actin monomer has a binding site for myosin (Mescher, 2013).

Tropomyosin is a long (about 40 nm), thin molecule consisting of two polypeptide chains and bound head to tail to form filaments that coil over the two actin strands. Each tropomyosin molecule extends along a length of seven G-actin molecules (Mescher, 2013).

Unlike skeletal muscle, smooth muscle cells do not contain troponin (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). Instead, caldesmon interacts with tropomyosin forming a caldesmon-tropomyosin complex, which regulates the interaction of actin with myosin. 

In relaxed smooth muscle, the caldesmon-tropomyosin complex blocks the myosin binding sites on the actin filaments. This is controlled by regulatory molecules (such as calmodulin) that are dependent on Ca2+. Calmodulin binds to Ca2+ creating a Ca2+-calmodulin complex. This complex binds to caldesmon and releases it from actin, thus exposing the myosin binding sites (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Vetterkind and Morgan, 2012).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The bulk of the smooth muscle sarcoplasm contains thin myofilaments of the contractile apparatus. They are attached to cytoplasmic densities or dense bodies (similar to Z lines of skeletal muscle fibers) located at the cell membrane and distributed throughout the sarcoplasm linked to intermediate filaments.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Muscle contraction results from the binding of myosin to actin myofilaments, allowing myosin to function as a motor that drives myofilament sliding and creating movement.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The Golgi complex is an intracellular compartment of eukaryotes, occupying the perinuclear region and consisting of a number of stacked, flattened sacs with associated tubules and vesicles. Its primary function is to process substances synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum; in addition it synthesizes some carbohydrates. Transport vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the Golgi complex at the cis face, their cargo is processed while passing through the cisternae, and the processed products are transported from the trans face to the trans-Golgi network for sorting and packaging. The mechanism by which cargo moves through the Golgi complex is not clear; one model proposes transport between cisternae by vesicular budding and fusion, while another proposes dynamic remodeling and recycling so that the cisternae themselves change in composition and move in a cis-to-trans direction (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The Golgi complex or Golgi apparatus is a crescent shaped, parallel stack of membrane-limited tubules or cisternae. It is closely associated with small vesicles involved in vesicular transport. The Golgi complex is very well developed in secretory cells. The Golgi complex exhibits structural polarity. It has a “cis face” (or entry face, which is the convex part of the complex) and a “trans face” (or exit face) (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The Golgi complex is closely associated with the nucleus and the “cis face” is adjacent to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The Golgi complex accepts proteins and various other molecules synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum. Each cistern of the Golgi complex contains different types of enzymes and so perform different enzymatic reactions. 

As some proteins move within the Golgi cisternae, carbohydrates and lipids are added to these proteins to form glycoproteins and glycolipids, respectively. In addition, proteins are added to lipids to form lipoproteins. Some proteins are isolated to be included in new plasmalemma.

As these molecules pass further through the Golgi complex, they are sorted and repackaged into a secretory vesicle. These secretory molecules are either destined to become lysosomes, migrate to the plasmalemma, or exported outside of the cell. 

The Golgi apparatus is involved in making carbohydrates (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Atrophy of the Golgi complex and subsequent functional errors in specific neurons and loss of these neurons in the brain has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A caveola is a small (approximately 50 nm), flask-shaped invagination of the plasma membrane occurring in nearly all animal cells, coated with the membrane protein caveolin and rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids. Caveolae are a special form of lipid raft and are associated with endocytosis, budding from the plasma membrane to form pinosomes; they also concentrate signaling molecules and have been implicated in other processes, including the export of cholesterol to serum lipoproteins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: Most cells in the body utilize a process called pinocytosis to ingest fluid and small protein molecules via small vesicles about 80–150 nm in diameter. It is a continual process, so small vesicles are continually forming at the cell surface. Most of the vesicles eventually fuse with lysosomes although they are very numerous in endothelial cells as they move materials from their surface of origin to the other side. They are also numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the sarcolemma (plasma membrane) are referred to as caveolae. Cytoplasmic vesicles are in close proximity to sparse amounts of smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Caveolae are numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the smooth muscle sarcolemma (plasma membrane).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Smooth muscle cells lack T tubules. Caveolae and vesicles function to deliver Ca+ to the cytoplasm as a consequence of depolarization of the sarcolemma and activation of voltage-sensitive Ca+ channels or direct activation of gated Ca+ release channels in the sER by a second messenger molecule. Ca+ can also be released into the cytoplasm via ligated Ca+ channels activated by hormones also by second messenger pathways. 

Increasing the intracellular concentration of Ca+ is responsible for contraction of the smooth muscle cell. Contraction of smooth muscle cells is initiated by mechanical impulses, neural stimulation via neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine and norepinephrine, or chemical stimuli of the cells.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The basal lamina is the layer of the basement membrane lying next to the basal surface of the adjoining cell layer; composed of an electron-dense lamina densa and an electron-lucent lamina lucida; sometimes used to denote the lamina densa alone (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The external lamina (or basal lamina) is made up of several different proteins and carbohydrates, such as collagen, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins. It forms a matrix which surrounds the muscle fiber and plays a central role in its structure and function.

The term “external lamina” replaces “basal lamina” in nonepithelial cells such as muscle cells, adipocytes, and supporting cells in the peripheral nervous system.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The external lamina surrounds the muscle fiber and is directly linked to the sarcolemma.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The external lamina has several important roles in the structure and function of the muscle fiber such as mechanical support to underlying structures. It also acts as a scaffold for many important cells which act on the muscle fiber. The external lamina matrix has been found to be a component of important molecular signaling, i.e., it contains an enzyme, acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine during neuromuscular transmissions. Its role seems to be important in a wide range of functions from development to myogenesis and synaptogenesis.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A dense body is any of the small regions of increased density in the sarcoplasm of skeletal muscles to which myofilaments seem to attach (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: Dense bodies are functionally similar to Z disks of skeletal and cardiac muscle. They contain attachment proteins, such as alpha-actinin, that bind to thin myofilaments and intermediate filaments.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Cytoplasmic densities or dense bodies are located at the sarcolemma (cell membrane) of smooth muscle cells and are distributed throughout the sarcoplasm (cytoplasm).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Dense bodies are important in transmitting the contractile forces within the cell and at the cell surface, therefore changing the shape of the cell.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Gap junctions are a type of intercellular junction comprising a narrowed portion (about 3 nm) of the intercellular space that contains channels or pores (about 2 nm) composed of hexagonal arrays of membrane-spanning proteins around a central lumen (connexon) through which pass ions and small molecules such as most sugars, amino acids, nucleotides, vitamins, hormones, and cyclic AMP. In electrically excitable tissues, these gap junctions serve to transmit electrical impulses via ionic currents and are known as electrotonic synapses; they are present in such tissues as myocardial tissue and the central nervous system (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: Gap junctions appear as a close (2 nm) apposition of adjacent cell membranes. The individual structural unit of a gap junction is the connexon formed from six gap junction proteins called connexins joining together and creating a pore about 1.5–2 nm in diameter (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). Individual connexons of adjacent cells align to form a hydrophilic channel between the adjacent cells.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Gap junctions appear as a close (2 nm) apposition of adjacent cell membranes.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Gap junctions permit the exchange of small molecules e.g., ions, signaling molecules (such as hormones), and small metabolites, between adjacent cells causing the cells to act in a coordinated manner.

Contraction of smooth muscle is slow and prolonged. 

Smooth muscle is innervated by the autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation), and in most cases, an individual nerve ending supplies groups of cells, rather than individual cells. Gap junctions connecting adjacent smooth muscle cells allows excitation from a nerve fiber to spread across the cells, resulting in synchronous contractions (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: About 21 members of the connexin protein family have been identified. Mutations in gene coding connexin-26 (Cx26) is associated with congenital deafness; mutations of Cx46 and Cx50 genes have been associated with people with inherited cataracts (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Mitochondria are the small spherical to rod-shaped cytoplasmic organelles, consisting of inner and outer bilayer membranes with a space between them. The inner membrane is infolded to form a series of projections (cristae), and the space between the cristae is filled by the mitochondrial matrix, which contains DNA, RNA, ribosomes, and granules. Mitochondria generate energy (in the form of ATP synthesis) by the oxidation of nutrients, and they contain the enzymes of the tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle and for fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation. In response to toxic insults, they release enzymes that cause apoptosis. Mitochondria can replicate independently and code for the synthesis of some of their proteins; inheritance of mitochondrial DNA is maternal, and mitochondrial DNA defects cause a variety of diseases (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The mitochondrion is a double membrane-bound organelle about 0.5–1 μm wide and up to 10 μm in length. The space between the inner and outer membrane is the intermembrane space. 

Mitochondria occur in a variety of shapes and sizes. The only cells that lack mitochondria are erythrocytes (red blood cells) and terminal keratinocytes. 

The outer mitochondrial membrane is about 6–7 nm thick and contains mitochondrial porins which are voltage-dependent anion channels. Small molecules, ions, and metabolites can enter the intermembrane space but cannot enter the inner mitochondrial membrane. In addition, the outer membrane possesses various receptors, for molecules that translocate in the intermembrane space, and various enzymes. 

The inner mitochondrial membrane is thinner and rich in cardiolipin which is a phospholipid that makes the inner membrane impermeable to ions and less permeable to all other elements. The inner membrane invaginates to form long parallel stacks of membranous components called cristae that run perpendicular to the long axis of the mitochondrion and increase the surface area of the inner membrane. Cristae contain respiratory chain enzymes. Among these respiratory enzymes is ATP synthetase which is responsible for oxidative phosphorylation, a process of cellular respiration and the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is an energy-rich molecule.

Cristae that form parallel plates in mitochondria produce proteins, whereas in mitochondria that produce steroids, the cristae adopt a tubular form. 

The numbers of mitochondria, as well as the number and complexity of the cristae, will correlate with the activity of the cell. Therefore, very active cells, such as a skeletal muscle fiber and a cardiomyocyte (cardiac muscle cell), will contain large numbers of mitochondria with extensive cristae.

The inner mitochondrial membrane surrounds the mitochondrial fluid (matrix) which contains mitochondrial DNA and RNA. The mitochondrial DNA encodes thirteen enzymes which are involved in the process of oxidative phosphorylation. It also contains two rRNAs, and twenty-two tRNAs that are involved in the translation of the mitochondrial mRNA. In addition, mitochondria exhibit a complete system of proteins for protein and ribosomal synthesis. Mitochondrial proteins are formed both by mitochondrial and nuclear DNA. 

Matrix granules that store Ca2+ are also housed within the matrix of the mitochondrion. 

Mitochondria contribute to the acidophilia of the cytoplasm in cells where they aggregate in large numbers.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The mitochondria are scattered throughout the cell, but are less abundant in smooth muscle, when compared to skeletal or cardiac muscle.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The mitochondria are the power houses of the cell and produce chemical energy by producing high energy ATP molecules. The mitochondria are also able to induce apoptosis (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
–Mutations in mitochondrial DNA result in several inherited disorders. 

–Mitochondrial related diseases (mitochondrial myopathies) become most evident in tissues such as skeletal muscle that require large amounts of energy (ATP) generated by mitochondria.

–Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia affects the inability to move the eyes due to weakening of extraocular muscles and the eyebrows. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy affects vision due to the degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and their axons as a result of mutations in the mitochondrial genome.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A ribosome is a large molecular structure, approximately 12 nm wide and 25 nm long, having two dissociable subunits, that is the site of protein synthesis. Ribosomes found in the cytosol of eukaryotes have a sedimentation coefficient of 80S; the subunits have coefficients of 60S and 40S and together contain four different ribosomal RNA (rRNA) chains and about 80 different proteins. Ribosomes found in prokaryotes and mitochondria are smaller (70S, with 50S and 30S subunits containing a total of three rRNAs and 55 proteins) and also differ from eukaryotic ribosomes in their sensitivity to certain antibiotics (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: Ribosomes are protein complexes and consist of rRNA synthesized in the nucleolus. They appear in electron micrographs as small, electron-dense particles 20–30 nm in two different forms (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
Firstly, ribosomes position loosely within the cytoplasm or as a chain of ribosomes called polyribosomes. 

Secondly, ribosomes (and polyribosomes) can be attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Individual ribosomes or polyribosomes in the cytoplasm of the cell freely associated, means they're involved with making proteins that the cell uses for itself.

Proteins synthesized by those ribosomes in collaboration with the endoplasmic reticulum is destined to be exported from the cell or incorporated into the plasmalemma. In some cases, the proteins are stored within the cell e.g., in lysosomes and in the granules of white blood cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The sarcoplasm is the interfibrillary matter of the striated muscles; the substance in which the fibrillae of the muscle fiber are embedded (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm equivalent within muscle cells. It contains many of the same organelles, cytoskeleton, and matrix which is important in many cell functions. The sarcoplasm is slightly adapted to respond to the high energy demands of muscle cells, such as having a higher concentration of glycosomes and myoglobin.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The sarcoplasm is an aqueous substance found within the sarcolemma, which contains many cellular organelles such as the sarcoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, ribosomes, and Golgi apparatus.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Similar to the cytoplasm in other cells, the sarcoplasm acts as a medium for many important metabolic processes.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A pinocytotic vesicle is any of the small fluid-filled vesicles found in the cytoplasm during pinocytosis, formed by invaginations of the cell membrane (caveolae), which pinch off and become free (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: A pinocytotic vesicle (80–150 nm in diameter) forms when the plasmalemma engulfs fluid or small proteins and any molecules in solution in the extracellular fluid. This process is called pinocytosis and is a common process in almost all human cells.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Pinocytotic vesicles are located in the apical regions of the cell cytoplasm.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: A pinocytotic vesicle engulfs fluid or small proteins and any molecules in solution in the extracellular fluid.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The basal lamina is the layer of the basement membrane lying next to the basal surface of the adjoining cell layer; composed of an electron-dense lamina densa and an electron-lucent lamina lucida; sometimes used to denote the lamina densa alone (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The external lamina (or basal lamina) is made up of several different proteins and carbohydrates, such as collagen, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins. It forms a matrix which surrounds the muscle fiber and plays a central role in its structure and function.

The term “external lamina” replaces “basal lamina” in nonepithelial cells such as muscle cells, adipocytes, and supporting cells in the peripheral nervous system.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The external lamina surrounds the muscle fiber and is directly linked to the sarcolemma.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The external lamina has several important roles in the structure and function of the muscle fiber such as mechanical support to underlying structures. It also acts as a scaffold for many important cells which act on the muscle fiber. The external lamina matrix has been found to be a component of important molecular signaling, i.e., it contains an enzyme, acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine during neuromuscular transmissions. Its role seems to be important in a wide range of functions from development to myogenesis and synaptogenesis.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The sarcolemma is the delicate plasma membrane that invests every striated muscle fiber (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The sarcolemma is the fine, delicate, extensible membrane surrounding each muscle fiber. It is composed of a cell, or plasma, membrane which presents an extracellular matrix of collagen fibrils and polysaccharides that make contact with the basal lamina. The sarcolemma also contains tunnel-like invaginations into the sarcoplasm, which are known as transverse tubules (T tubules) in striated muscle and caveolae in smooth muscle (Standring, 2020).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Transmembrane proteins found within the sarcolemma facilitate a physical connection between the actin cytoskeleton of the muscle fiber and the extracellular basal lamina (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Like other types of cell membranes, the sarcolemma forms a defined barrier between extracellular and intracellular environments.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The thin filament is one of the thin contractile myofilaments in a muscle cell, composed mainly of actin (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Thin myofilaments are composed of actin, tropomyosin, and caldesmon. 

Actin is the main component of the thin myofilament. It is a long filamentous (F-actin) polymer consisting of two strands of globular (G-actin) monomers twisted around each other to form a double helical formation about 1 μm long and 8 nm wide. Each G-actin monomer has a binding site for myosin (Mescher, 2013).

Tropomyosin is a long (about 40 nm), thin molecule consisting of two polypeptide chains and bound head to tail to form filaments that coil over the two actin strands. Each tropomyosin molecule extends along a length of seven G-actin molecules (Mescher, 2013).

Unlike skeletal muscle, smooth muscle cells do not contain troponin (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). Instead, caldesmon interacts with tropomyosin forming a caldesmon-tropomyosin complex, which regulates the interaction of actin with myosin. 

In relaxed smooth muscle, the caldesmon-tropomyosin complex blocks the myosin binding sites on the actin filaments. This is controlled by regulatory molecules (such as calmodulin) that are dependent on Ca2+. Calmodulin binds to Ca2+ creating a Ca2+-calmodulin complex. This complex binds to caldesmon and releases it from actin, thus exposing the myosin binding sites (Ross and Pawlina, 2016; Vetterkind and Morgan, 2012).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The bulk of the smooth muscle sarcoplasm contains thin myofilaments of the contractile apparatus. They are attached to cytoplasmic densities or dense bodies (similar to Z lines of skeletal muscle fibers) located at the cell membrane and distributed throughout the sarcoplasm linked to intermediate filaments.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Muscle contraction results from the binding of myosin to actin myofilaments, allowing myosin to function as a motor that drives myofilament sliding and creating movement.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The thick myofilament is one of the thick contractile myofilaments in a muscle cell, composed mainly of myosin (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Myosin is the main component of the thick myofilaments. It is a large complex molecule consisting of two identical heavy chains and two pairs of light chains. Each myosin heavy chain consists of two thin, rodlike molecules (2–3 nm thick and 150 nm long) twisted together (Mescher, 2013). 

Small globular projections form the heads of each myosin heavy chain. The heads contain binding sites for both ATP and actin and demonstrate motor and ATPase activity. Four light chains are associated with the head.

A thick myofilament consists of several hundred myosin molecules (1.6 μm long and 14 nm wide) arranged so their rodlike portions overlap, and their globular heads oriented toward either end (Mescher, 2013; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). 

The head of the myosin molecule, and a small portion of the rodlike portion, forms cross-bridges between thin and thick myofilaments. These bridges convert chemical energy into mechanical energy.

Thick myofilaments differ from those in skeletal muscle in that the polarity of the myosin heads is identical along one side of the filament and the opposite on the other side. This allows overlapping thin myofilaments to be pulled along the whole length of the thick myofilament.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Thick myofilaments are scattered throughout the sarcoplasm of smooth muscle cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Myosin converts chemical energy (ATP) to mechanical energy, and so generates force and movement.

Muscle contraction results from the binding of myosin to actin myofilaments, allowing myosin to function as a motor that drives myofilament sliding and so movement.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Gap junctions are a type of intercellular junction comprising a narrowed portion (about 3 nm) of the intercellular space that contains channels or pores (about 2 nm) composed of hexagonal arrays of membrane-spanning proteins around a central lumen (connexon) through which pass ions and small molecules such as most sugars, amino acids, nucleotides, vitamins, hormones, and cyclic AMP. In electrically excitable tissues, these gap junctions serve to transmit electrical impulses via ionic currents and are known as electrotonic synapses; they are present in such tissues as myocardial tissue and the central nervous system (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: Gap junctions appear as a close (2 nm) apposition of adjacent cell membranes. The individual structural unit of a gap junction is the connexon formed from six gap junction proteins called connexins joining together and creating a pore about 1.5–2 nm in diameter (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013). Individual connexons of adjacent cells align to form a hydrophilic channel between the adjacent cells.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Gap junctions appear as a close (2 nm) apposition of adjacent cell membranes.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Gap junctions permit the exchange of small molecules e.g., ions, signaling molecules (such as hormones), and small metabolites, between adjacent cells causing the cells to act in a coordinated manner.

Contraction of smooth muscle is slow and prolonged. 

Smooth muscle is innervated by the autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation), and in most cases, an individual nerve ending supplies groups of cells, rather than individual cells. Gap junctions connecting adjacent smooth muscle cells allows excitation from a nerve fiber to spread across the cells, resulting in synchronous contractions (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: About 21 members of the connexin protein family have been identified. Mutations in gene coding connexin-26 (Cx26) is associated with congenital deafness; mutations of Cx46 and Cx50 genes have been associated with people with inherited cataracts (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Smooth muscle cells contain a single nucleus occupying the broadest region of the cell. In an uncontracted cell viewed in longitudinal section, the nucleus is an elongated structure with ends tapered. If the cell is sectioned transversely, the nucleus will appear as a circular/rounded profile.

Nuclei have a wrinkled or corkscrew appearance when viewed in a longitudinal section after contraction of the cell during fixation. This is a useful characteristic when trying to distinguish a smooth muscle cell from a fibroblast or fibrocyte in routine histological sections.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Smooth muscle cells contain a single nucleus occupying the broadest region of the cell.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nucleus is the control center of the cell and houses the genome (genetic information) in eukaryotic cells. It enables DNA replication and synthesizes ribosomal (rRNA), messenger (mRNA), and transfer (tRNA) ribonucleic acid.

sections.name: References

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a special form of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in association with the T tubules in the sarcoplasm of striated muscle and comprising a system of cisternae and tubules forming a plexus around each myofibril. It contains large numbers of calcium pumps and ryanodine receptors and is a storage compartment for calcium ions, which it releases in response to an action potential in the adjacent T tubule to cause muscular contraction (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is an organelle that consists of a network of loose flattened tubules with various compartments, many of which contain Ca2+. The two ends of the SR are wider, thus form terminal sacs called cisternae. Two cisternae of adjacent sarcoplasmic reticula and one transverse tubule form a functional unit called a triad, which operates to elicit the release of Ca2+ from SR stores (Maclennan and Zvaritch, 2011).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in skeletal muscle. It forms a network of tubules that extend through a muscle fiber. The flattened tubules surround, but do not make direct contact with the myofibrils in a muscle fiber.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum functions as an intracellular calcium store. Depolarization of the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane results in the release of calcium ions (Ca2+). This release of calcium ions triggers the cascade required for contraction.

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
—Fatigue

—Central core disease

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A caveola is a small (approximately 50 nm), flask-shaped invagination of the plasma membrane occurring in nearly all animal cells, coated with the membrane protein caveolin and rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids. Caveolae are a special form of lipid raft and are associated with endocytosis, budding from the plasma membrane to form pinosomes; they also concentrate signaling molecules and have been implicated in other processes, including the export of cholesterol to serum lipoproteins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: Most cells in the body utilize a process called pinocytosis to ingest fluid and small protein molecules via small vesicles about 80–150 nm in diameter. It is a continual process, so small vesicles are continually forming at the cell surface. Most of the vesicles eventually fuse with lysosomes although they are very numerous in endothelial cells as they move materials from their surface of origin to the other side. They are also numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the sarcolemma (plasma membrane) are referred to as caveolae. Cytoplasmic vesicles are in close proximity to sparse amounts of smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Caveolae are numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the smooth muscle sarcolemma (plasma membrane).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Smooth muscle cells lack T tubules. Caveolae and vesicles function to deliver Ca+ to the cytoplasm as a consequence of depolarization of the sarcolemma and activation of voltage-sensitive Ca+ channels or direct activation of gated Ca+ release channels in the sER by a second messenger molecule. Ca+ can also be released into the cytoplasm via ligated Ca+ channels activated by hormones also by second messenger pathways. 

Increasing the intracellular concentration of Ca+ is responsible for contraction of the smooth muscle cell. Contraction of smooth muscle cells is initiated by mechanical impulses, neural stimulation via neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine and norepinephrine, or chemical stimuli of the cells.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The Golgi complex is an intracellular compartment of eukaryotes, occupying the perinuclear region and consisting of a number of stacked, flattened sacs with associated tubules and vesicles. Its primary function is to process substances synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum; in addition it synthesizes some carbohydrates. Transport vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the Golgi complex at the cis face, their cargo is processed while passing through the cisternae, and the processed products are transported from the trans face to the trans-Golgi network for sorting and packaging. The mechanism by which cargo moves through the Golgi complex is not clear; one model proposes transport between cisternae by vesicular budding and fusion, while another proposes dynamic remodeling and recycling so that the cisternae themselves change in composition and move in a cis-to-trans direction (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The Golgi complex or Golgi apparatus is a crescent shaped, parallel stack of membrane-limited tubules or cisternae. It is closely associated with small vesicles involved in vesicular transport. The Golgi complex is very well developed in secretory cells. The Golgi complex exhibits structural polarity. It has a “cis face” (or entry face, which is the convex part of the complex) and a “trans face” (or exit face) (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The Golgi complex is closely associated with the nucleus and the “cis face” is adjacent to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The Golgi complex accepts proteins and various other molecules synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum. Each cistern of the Golgi complex contains different types of enzymes and so perform different enzymatic reactions. 

As some proteins move within the Golgi cisternae, carbohydrates and lipids are added to these proteins to form glycoproteins and glycolipids, respectively. In addition, proteins are added to lipids to form lipoproteins. Some proteins are isolated to be included in new plasmalemma.

As these molecules pass further through the Golgi complex, they are sorted and repackaged into a secretory vesicle. These secretory molecules are either destined to become lysosomes, migrate to the plasmalemma, or exported outside of the cell. 

The Golgi apparatus is involved in making carbohydrates (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016; Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Atrophy of the Golgi complex and subsequent functional errors in specific neurons and loss of these neurons in the brain has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: An intermediate filament is a class of cytoplasmic filaments, 8–11 nm in diameter, that predominantly act as structural components of the cytoskeleton and also allow various movements in cellular processes. Different types contain different, tissue-specific proteins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: Intermediate filaments are like ropes forming an intersecting cytoskeletal network. They are around 10 nm in diameter and are composed of desmin or vimentin. They attach to the dense bodies, linking them to the sarcolemma (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Intermediate filaments have a structural role maintaining the stability of cell-to-cell junctions and adherence of the cell to the extracellular matrix. They also function as part of the cytoskeleton, thus supporting the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
–Several diseases can be attributed to defects in the assembly of intermediate filaments. A characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease is disarray of intermediate filaments in some neurons (Ross & Pawlina, 2016).

–“Mallory bodies” in hepatocytes in alcoholic liver cirrhosis is the accumulation of inclusions containing predominantly keratin intermediate filaments (Ross and Pawlina, 2016).

–Some specific types of intermediate filaments occurring in tumors allow the origins of the cell causing the tumor to be identified (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The sarcoplasm is the interfibrillary matter of the striated muscles; the substance in which the fibrillae of the muscle fiber are embedded (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm equivalent within muscle cells. It contains many of the same organelles, cytoskeleton, and matrix which is important in many cell functions. The sarcoplasm is slightly adapted to respond to the high energy demands of muscle cells, such as having a higher concentration of glycosomes and myoglobin.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The sarcoplasm is an aqueous substance found within the sarcolemma, which contains many cellular organelles such as the sarcoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, ribosomes, and Golgi apparatus.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Similar to the cytoplasm in other cells, the sarcoplasm acts as a medium for many important metabolic processes.

sections.name: References

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Autonomic nerve fibers are peripheral nerve fibers that innervate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glandular epithelium, or synapse in autonomic ganglia. They either stimulate and activate the muscle or tissue (preganglionic and postganglionic visceral efferent fibers) or receive sensory impulses from them (visceral afferent fibers) (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Smooth muscle contraction is not subject to voluntary control and is regulated, in most cases, by sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves of the autonomic nervous system. 

Nerve fibers have enlargements, or swellings, called varicosities that are in close contact with a smooth muscle cell. Within the varicosities are synaptic vesicles containing neuromuscular transmitters, such as acetylcholine or norepinephrine (noradrenaline). 

Unlike the neuromuscular junctions in skeletal muscle where the nerve terminal is in direct contact with the muscle cells, the nerve terminals are located some distance from the smooth muscle cells. Synaptic vesicles released rely on diffusion to reach the adjacent target smooth muscle cells, which may be at a distance of 10–20 μm (Ross and Pawlina, 2016). Vesicles bind to the sarcolemma of the smooth muscle cells to stimulate a contraction. However, neurotransmitters do not reach all the smooth muscle cells. Instead, gap junctions between adjacent cells allows the signal to pass from one cell to the next and enables communication between cells to regulate the coordinated contraction of the entire sheet of smooth muscle (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Nerve fibers travel within the connective tissue between the smooth muscle bundles.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Autonomic nerve fibers release neurotransmitters that bind to the sarcolemma of smooth muscle cells, triggering muscle contraction.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A motor neuron is an efferent neuron conveying motor impulses (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: Motor neurons are usually made up of large and myelinated alpha-efferent axons. They arise from motor neuron cell bodies in the anterior horns of the gray matter within the spinal cord. Their terminal branches are short unmyelinated twigs which travel through the endomysium to form part of the neuromuscular junction.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
The motor neuron axon branches into many terminal branches, which enter the endomysium. The myelin sheath of the axon ends at the neuromuscular junction, however, the terminal branches are covered by a thin layer, the neurilemma, which arises from the outer membrane of the Schwann cell. This external lamina of the Schwann cell, fuses with the sarcolemma, covering the points of contact between axonal branches and the muscle cell (Martini, Nath and Bartholomew, 2017). 

The terminal axonal branches are dilated into a presynaptic structure which sits in shallow depressions on the surface of the muscle fiber. These areas are the receptor regions. The sarcolemma at these points will have deep junctional folds for increased surface area, ready to receive neurotransmitters responsible for muscle contraction.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The function of the neuromuscular junction is to induce an action potential across the muscle fiber, initiating muscle contraction. 

The nerve action potential travels across the axon of the motor neuron to its terminal branches and to the dilated presynaptic structures which sit within shallow depressions on the muscle fiber. These dilated ends contain both mitochondria and vesicles, the latter of which contain the neurotransmitter, acetylcholine. The nerve action potential triggers the release of acetylcholine which diffuses across the space between the presynaptic dilation and the sarcolemma. This space is called the synaptic cleft. The sarcolemma at these junctions contains a series of folds to increase the surface area as they contain acetylcholine receptors. Once the acetylcholine binds with their respective receptors, it induces an action potential across the muscle. The action potential will move along the surface of the muscle cell, along the t tubules that penetrate the sarcoplasm initiating release of CA2+ which in turn induces the contraction cycle (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A myelin sheath is the cylindrical covering on the axons of some neurons; it consists of concentric layers of myelin, formed in the peripheral nervous system by the plasma membrane of Schwann cells, and in the central nervous system by oligodendrocytes. It is interrupted at intervals along its length by gaps known as nodes of Ranvier. Myelin is an electrical insulator that serves to speed the conduction of nerve impulses (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: The myelin sheath tightly holsters the axon. It is a semi-crystalline lipid-protein-water layer. This layer is discontinuous and interrupted at regular intervals. Schwann cells produce myelin sheaths in the peripheral nervous system. A myelin sheath is formed when the Schwann cell wraps around the nerve axon in a spiral fashion, creating many layers, or lamellae. This is known as myelination. Each myelin-generating cell furnishes myelin for only one segment of any given axon. The periodic interruptions where short portions of the axon are left uncovered by myelin are known as the nodes of Ranvier (Patestas and Gartner, 2016).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nodes of Ranvier, which are found periodically along the myelin sheath of myelinated axons, contain a concentration of voltage-gated sodium channels. These voltage-gated sodium channels enable the nodes to function as generators of action potentials. This is achieved through the exchange of ions into and out of the ion channels.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The Myelin sheath acts as an insulator for the axons improving their electrical conductance. The myelin sheath also has a protective role in that it acts as a physical barrier separating the axon from the electrically charged atoms and molecules of the extracellular fluid. Myelination has also been shown to reduce the energy required for transmission of action potentials (Wang et al., 2008).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A Schwann cell is any of the large nucleated cells whose cell membrane spirally enwraps the axons of myelinated peripheral neurons and is the source of myelin; a single Schwann cell supplies the myelin sheath between two nodes of Ranvier (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: Schwann cells are glial-type supporting cells of the peripheral nervous system. They are fusiform in appearance and present a lipid-dense cell membrane. Terminal Schwann cells are a specialized type of non-myelinating Schwann cells present at the neuromuscular junction. The terminal branches of the axon are covered by a thin layer, the neurilemma, which arises from the outer membrane of the terminal Schwann cells (Armati, 2007).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Schwann cells are distributed along a peripheral axon in a chain. They can provide an insulating layer, known as a myelin sheath around axons larger than 2 μm; this myelin sheath is composed of the Schwann cell’s cell membrane, which wraps around the axon multiple times. Terminal Schwann cells do not form a myelin sheath around the neuromuscular junction; therefore they are also known as non-myelinating Schwann cells (Zänker and Entschladen, 2007).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Schwann cells have multiple functions within the peripheral nervous system. Terminal Schwann cells envelop the motor end plate and are involved in the regulation and maintenance of the nerve terminal. The neurilemma formed by the terminal Schwann cells is involved in the regeneration of injured axons (Zänker and Entschladen, 2007).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: - Guillain-Barré syndrome

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The endoneurium is the connective tissue in a peripheral nerve fascicle; it forms an interstitial layer around the neurilemma that surrounds individual myelinated nerve fibers and Remak bundles of unmyelinated fibers (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure/Morphology
sections.text: The endoneurium is the connective tissue layer surrounding a nerve fiber (neuron) including the neurolemma and the myelin sheath. This connective tissue is made up of a fibrous matrix largely composed of collagen type III fibers (reticulin), which are arranged into intricate bundles, parallel to the long axis of the nerve. They tend to become somewhat concentrated around individual Schwann cell-axon units and vessels of the endoneurium. The primary cellular constituents of the endoneurium are fibroblasts, however resident macrophages and mast cells are also present (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The fibrous and cellular components of the endoneurium are bathed in endoneurial fluid at a slightly higher pressure than that found external to the endoneurial channel. Within the endoneurial channel, tiny capillaries are present which are comprised of a single layer of non-fenestrated endothelial cells. These serve as part of the blood-nerve barrier (Peltonen et al., 2013)

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The endoneurium plays a role in isolating nerve signals. Each peripheral nerve contains numerous axons that transmit to several muscles in the body. The endoneurium is in control of keeping these signals separate ensuring they are transmitted to the correct location. The endoneurium also protects the delicate axons from potential harm. Another function of the endoneurium, which is shared by the perineurium and epineurium, is the protection of neurons from damage (Carp, 2015).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Advanced axonal neuropathy

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The endomysium is the sheath of delicate reticular fibrils that surrounds each muscle fiber (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: The endomysium is the smallest component of the connective tissue which runs throughout the muscle. Unlike the epimysium and perimysium, the endomysium is made up of loose reticular fibers and some fibroblasts scattered throughout (Mescher, 2013).

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The endomysium surrounds individual muscle fibers and their external lamina forming their external environment. The endomysium is continuous with the larger connective tissue septa which constitute the perimysium. Small blood vessels and the smallest axonal terminal branches are present throughout the endomysium (Standring, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The endomysium plays an important role by transferring tension between the myofibrils it surrounds, contractile force produced in these fibers are transmitted to adjacent fibers. 

Due to the presence of the capillary network, it acts as the site of metabolic exchange between the blood and muscle.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The basal lamina is the layer of the basement membrane lying next to the basal surface of the adjoining cell layer; composed of an electron-dense lamina densa and an electron-lucent lamina lucida; sometimes used to denote the lamina densa alone (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: The basal lamina is made up of several different proteins and carbohydrates, such as collagen, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins. It forms a matrix which surrounds the muscle fiber and plays a central role in its structure and function.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The basal lamina surrounds the muscle fiber and is directly linked to the sarcolemma.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The basal lamina has several important roles in the structure and function of the muscle fiber such as mechanical support to underlying structures. It also acts as a scaffold for many important cells which act on the muscle fiber. The basal lamina matrix is a component of important molecular signaling, i.e., it contains an enzyme, acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine during neuromuscular transmissions. Its role seems to be important in many functions from development to myogenesis and synaptogenesis.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: —Muscular dystrophy

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A capillary is any of the minute vessels that connect the arterioles and venules, forming a network in nearly all parts of the body. Their walls act as semipermeable membranes for the interchange of various substances, including fluids, between the blood and tissue fluid. The two principal types are continuous and fenestrated capillaries (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text: Similar to capillaries elsewhere in the body, capillaries surrounding muscle fibers have a single cell thick endothelial layer. They constitute part of the microcirculation.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
After the main arterial supply enters the muscle at the neurovascular hilum, it branches into smaller arteries and arterioles. These vessels give off the capillaries which travel through the endomysium. 

The capillaries will run parallel to the direction of the muscle fibers with a varying degree of branching around fibers. Muscle fibers responsible for sustained activities such as posture than compared to muscle fibers only frequently used, will have a much denser anastomosis of capillaries surrounding them.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Capillaries are responsible for delivering oxygenated blood to the muscle fiber.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A myofibril is one of the slender threads that can be made visible in a muscle fiber by maceration in certain acids. They run parallel with the long axis of the fiber, and are composed of numerous myofilaments (Dorland, 2011). The endomembrane system refers to the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the transverse tubules (Wirtz et al., 2012).

sections.name: Structure
sections.text:
Myofibrils are arranged in bundles enclosed by a plasma membrane called the sarcolemma. Each myofibril is surrounded by a sarcoplasmic reticulum and by transverse tubules, which are collectively known as the endomembrane system (Wirtz et al., 2012). 

The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized type of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in skeletal muscle. It forms a network of tubules that extend through the muscle fiber. The flattened tubules surround, but do not make direct contact with the myofibrils in a muscle fiber. 

Transverse tubules are extensions of the sarcolemma, made up of interconnecting rings, each of which surround individual myofibrils.

sections.name: Key Features/Anatomical Relations
sections.text:
Myofibrils are arranged in bundles enclosed by a plasma membrane called the sarcolemma. This structure is collectively called a muscle fiber. A connective tissue layer, the endoneurium, surrounds the sarcolemma. 

Each myofibril is made up of numerous sarcomeres that are positioned end to end. The light regions of the sarcomere do not refract light and are considered isotropic. These regions are called I-bands. I-bands are composed of thin filaments of the protein actin and its associated proteins, such as tropomyosin and troponin. I-bands are dissected by a Z-line. The area between successive Z-lines are called sarcomeres. The sections of thick filament that are not superimposed by the thin filaments when the myofibril is relaxed is called the H-band (Laing and Nowak, 2005).

The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is an organelle that consists of a network of loose flattened tubules with various compartments, many of which contain Ca2+. The two ends of the SR are wider, to from terminal sacs, called cisternae. Two cisternae of adjacent sarcoplasmic reticula and one transverse tubule form a functional unit called a triad, which operates to elicit the release of Ca2+ from SR stores.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The protein bands of the myofibril facilitate contraction and relaxation of the muscle by gliding the thin actin and thick myosin filaments over each other. 

The primary function of transverse tubules is to facilitate the conduction of signals from outside the fiber to the myofibrils. Transverse tubules are the site for excitation-contraction coupling. When an electric signal excites the sarcolemma, the signal travels down along the T-tubules to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases Ca2+ for contraction. 

The sarcoplasmic reticulum functions as an intracellular calcium store. Depolarization of the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane results in the release of calcium ions (Ca2+). This release of calcium ions triggers the cascade required for contraction.

sections.text:

—Actin myopathy

—Hyaline body myopathy

—Muscular dystrophy
