sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The axon hillock is the conical expansion of an axon at its point of attachment to the body of the nerve cell (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The initial segment of the axon arises from the axon hillock which is a pyramidal-shaped region of the cell body lacking ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, and the Golgi complex. Smaller cytoplasmic organelles such as microtubules, intermediate filaments, mitochondria, and vesicles pass from the axon hillock to the axon. 

The axon hillock is a useful landmark to distinguish an axon from a dendrite in microscopic preparations.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The axon hillock is the region of the nerve cell body where the initial segment of the axonal process originates.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: An action potential is stimulated by impulses carried to the axon hillock.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The Golgi complex is an intracellular compartment of eukaryotes, occupying the perinuclear region and consisting of a number of stacked, flattened sacs with associated tubules and vesicles. Its primary function is to process substances synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum; in addition it synthesizes some carbohydrates. Transport vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the Golgi complex at the cis face, their cargo is processed while passing through the cisternae, and the processed products are transported from the trans face to the trans-Golgi network for sorting and packaging. The mechanism by which cargo moves through the Golgi complex is not clear; one model proposes transport between cisternae by vesicular budding and fusion, while another proposes dynamic remodelling and recycling so that the cisternae themselves change in composition and move in a cis-to-trans direction (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The Golgi complex, or Golgi apparatus, is a crescent shaped, parallel stack of membrane-limited tubules or cisternae that are closely associated with small vesicles involved in vesicular transport. The Golgi complex is very well developed in secretory cells or in neurons making neurotransmitters and trophic factors (Mescher, 2013).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The Golgi complex is closely associated with the nucleus and is adjacent to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Dendrites and axons are devoid of the Golgi complex (Mescher, 2013).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The Golgi complex accepts proteins and various other molecules synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum. As some proteins move within the Golgi cisternae, carbohydrates and lipids are added to these proteins to form glycoproteins and glycolipids, respectively. In addition, proteins are added to lipids to form lipoproteins. Some proteins are isolated to be included in new plasmalemma (Mescher, 2013).

As these molecules pass further through the Golgi complex, they are sorted and repackaged into secretory vesicles. These vesicles are either destined to become lysosomes, migrate to the plasmalemma, or in the case of neurons, contain neurotransmitters and trophic factors (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Atrophy of the Golgi complex and subsequent functional errors in specific neurons and loss of these neurons in the brain has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (Ovalle and Nahirney, 2021).(Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nucleolus is a rounded, dense body, present in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells during interphase, that is the site of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesis and ribosomal subunit assembly. It consists of (a) a fibrillar center, containing the rRNA genes, surrounded by (b) the pars fibrosa, a dense fibrillar component where transcription occurs, and (c) the pars granulosa, a granular component where the ribosomal subunits are assembled. Multiple nucleoli occur in some cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The most predominant, non-membranous structure in the nucleus is the spherical nucleolus. It surrounds rRNA genes that are transcriptionally active. The nucleolus is the site of synthesis of ribosomal ribonucleic acid (rRNA), ribosomal production and assembly. The diameter of the nucleolus is 1–2 mm, but this varies within different populations of cells. In cells that are most active in synthesizing proteins, the nucleolus is well developed and prominent. It is not uncommon for some cells to contain more than one nucleolus (Mescher, 2013).

Like heterochromatin, the nucleolus stains with basic dyes and hematoxylin.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nucleolus is located at the center of the nucleus.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nucleolus synthesizes and assembles ribosomal ribonucleic acid (rRNA).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Nucleoli house proteins for ribosome synthesis and oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes that control cell proliferation. Structural and functional faults in nucleoli have been the basis of a number of disease processes including some types of cancers (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nucleus is a spheroid body within a eukaryotic cell, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear envelope, and containing chromatin, a nucleolus, and nucleoplasm. In the nucleus, the cell's genetic information is stored on the chromosomes and RNA transcription and processing occur (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text: The nerve cell body contains a large, spherical, euchromatic nucleus with at least one prominent nucleolus. The nuclear membrane is a double membranous envelope that surrounds the nucleus. However, the nuclear membrane is not continuous as it fuses at locations all around the nucleus to form nuclear pores. Between the two nuclear membranes is a perinuclear cisternal space.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nucleus is located centrally within the cell body. In cases of cell injury, the nucleus becomes displaced to the periphery (Splittgerber, 2018).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nucleus is the control center of the cell and houses the genome (genetic information) in eukaryotic cells. It enables DNA replication and synthesizes ribosomal (rRNA), messenger (mRNA), and transfer (tRNA) ribonucleic acid.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The myelin sheath gap, or node of Ranvier, are the constrictions occurring on myelinated nerve fibers at regular intervals of about 1 mm; at these sites the myelin sheath is absent and the axon is enclosed only by Schwann cell processes (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
The myelin sheath is produced by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system.

Oligodendrocytes are small cells and extend long processes towards neighboring axons. Each process wraps around a portion of the same axon or several axons. The myelin sheath that wraps around the axon becomes segmented at regular intervals by the nodes of Ranvier, or myelin sheath gaps.

The area between adjacent nodes of Ranvier is known as the internode. The length of the internode is correlated with the diameter of the axon (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Nodes of Ranvier are located in the intervals between adjacent myelin sheaths. “Foot processes” extending from the astrocyte cell body can be found in large numbers at the nodes of Ranvier (Splittgerber, 2018).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nodes of Ranvier facilitate the rapid conduction of nerve impulses. Sodium channels embedded in the axolemma are greatest in density at the nodes of Ranvier and lowest in density at the internodes (Standring, 2016). The high concentration of sodium channels at the nodes facilitates “saltatory conduction” which is the process by which the action potential is propagated from node to node very rapidly along myelinated nerve fibers.

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Deficiencies in any of the oligodendrocytes myelin-specific proteins seem related to demyelinating diseases of the central nervous system. Multiple sclerosis is characterized by demyelination in white matter of the CNS. The degenerated myelin sheaths are removed by microglial cells and then astrocytes proliferate to form a gliotic scar (Splittgerber, 2018).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The terminal bouton is a button-like terminal enlargement of an axon that ends in relation to another neuron at a synapse (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Usually axons branch profusely at their termination. This is known as terminal arborization. Each branch of this arborization ends in a dilation called a terminal bouton or axon terminal.

Terminal boutons are unmyelinated, specialized, presynaptic endings that are in close proximity with the postsynaptic plasmalemma or axolemma of target cells. This close relationship is referred to as synapses, which are junctions between neurons and other neurons or effector cells. Axon terminals can form:
—axodendritic synapses, which are connections between axons and dendrites:
—axosomatic synapses, which are connections of axons with cell bodies;
—axo-axonic synapses, which are connections between other axons;
—neuromuscular junctions, which are connections between nerve cells and muscles (Standring, 2016).

Terminal boutons of the presynaptic neuron contain numerous small clear synaptic vesicles and large dense-core vesicles. These synaptic vesicles are membranous sacs filled with neurotransmitters. Most neurotransmitters are synthesized in the nerve cell body and transported to the axon terminals, although some neurotransmitters can be synthesized at axon terminals if the necessary precursors are provided by anterograde axonal transport. As nerve impulses end at the terminal boutons, neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis and the added presynaptic membrane are recycled by endocytosis to form new synaptic vesicles (Mescher, 2013). 

Terminal boutons contain numerous mitochondria since energy is required for the release of neurotransmitters.

Presynaptic axon terminals contain smooth endoplasmic reticulum, which synthesizes new cell membrane since, during exocytosis of the neurotransmitters, the cell membrane does not remain intact (Mescher, 2013).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Terminal boutons form functional junctions between other neurons or effector cells. As nerve impulses end at the terminal boutons, neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic cleft and can either excite or inhibit other neurons or effector cells.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The axon is the process of a neuron by which impulses travel away from the cell body; at the terminal arborization of the axon, the impulses are transmitted to other nerve cells or to effector organs. The larger axons are surrounded by a myelin sheath (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Most neurons have only one thin axon that arises from the axon hillock. An axon is tubular with a uniform diameter along its entire length, although the diameter varies depending on the type of neuron. Very short axons can be 0.1 mm in length, whereas long axons can be about 1 m long. An axon is bound by plasmalemma known as axolemma. The cytoplasm of an axon is known as the axoplasm. The axoplasm contains mitochondria, cytoskeletal elements, and some cisternae of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. The axoplasm is devoid of Nissl granules and Golgi complexes (Mescher, 2013; Splittgerber, 2018). 

In myelinated axons, the portion between the axon hillock and the first region of myelination (about 50–100 μm) is known as the initial segment. It is the most excitable part of the axon and is where action potentials are generated (Splittgerber, 2018).

In the central nervous system, oligodendrocytes form the myelin sheath that wraps around the axon, whereas in the peripheral nervous system, myelin sheath is formed by Schwann cells. Myelinated axons conduct electrical impulses much faster than non-myelinated axons of the same size. Axons with a large diameter conduct nerve impulses very fast. In contrast, axons with a small diameter, conduct nerve impulses very slowly. The myelin sheath that wraps around the axon becomes segmented at regular intervals by the nodes of Ranvier (or myelin sheath gaps). 

The terminals of axons are unmyelinated. The majority of terminals of an axon expand into presynaptic boutons to either form connections with dendrites, axons, or cell bodies of other neurons. These presynaptic boutons can also form connections peripherally within muscle fibers, glands, or other effector cells.

Usually, axons do not branch close to the cell body but can have some collateral branches along their length and branch profusely right before their termination.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The axon is the conducting portion of the cell and conveys information away from the nerve cell body towards an effector cell or another neuron. An action potential is generated at the initial segment of the axon. The axolemma is specialized in impulse conduction as it contains various ion channels that are required for generating an action potential (Mescher, 2013; Ross and Pawlina, 2006). 

Cytoskeletal elements found within the axoplasm provide structural strength to the axon. In addition, they transport substances away from the nerve cell body (anterograde flow). Retrograde flow transports molecules (taken up by endocytosis at the axon terminals) back towards the nerve cell body (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Marieb, Wilhelm and Mallatt, 2012).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
Axonal retrograde transport has the potential to transport viruses and toxins, etc., back to the nerve cell bodies.

Local anesthetics inhibit sodium transport and therefore the generation of an action potential or nerve impulse.

The axon is dependent on the nerve cell body for maintenance. If the axon is severed, its peripheral length will degenerate.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A dendrite is one of the threadlike extensions of the cytoplasm of a neuron, which typically branch into tree-like processes. In unipolar and bipolar neurons, there is a single dendrite, which proximally resembles an axon but branches distally; in multipolar neurons there are many short, branching dendrites. Dendrites form most of the receptive surface of a neuron (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Features
sections.text:
Dendrites are short, tree-like, highly branched processes, generally radiating from the cell body, increasing the receptive area of the cell. Dendrites are unmyelinated, usually tapered, and their diameter is greater than the diameter of the neuronal axon. Dendrites become thinner as they branch. The cytoplasm of the dendrites near the cell body contains Nissl granules, ribosomes, rough endoplasmic reticulum, smooth endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, microtubules, neurofilaments, and actin filaments. However, they do not contain Golgi complex (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Dendrites are overproduced during embryonic development but become reduced in number and size later on (Splittgerber, 2018).

Small mushroom shaped “dendritic spines,” 1–3 μm long and less than 1 μm wide, are connected to the dendrite process.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Dendrites generally radiate from the neuron cell body.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Dendrites function as receptors to enable a single neuron to receive and integrate information arriving on numerous axon terminals from other nerve cells or the external environment. Dendritic spines house the synapses communicating with the neuron from other nerve cell processes.

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: General anesthetics block synaptic transmission.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The Golgi complex is an intracellular compartment of eukaryotes, occupying the perinuclear region and consisting of a number of stacked, flattened sacs with associated tubules and vesicles. Its primary function is to process substances synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum; in addition it synthesizes some carbohydrates. Transport vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the Golgi complex at the cis face, their cargo is processed while passing through the cisternae, and the processed products are transported from the trans face to the trans-Golgi network for sorting and packaging. The mechanism by which cargo moves through the Golgi complex is not clear; one model proposes transport between cisternae by vesicular budding and fusion, while another proposes dynamic remodeling and recycling so that the cisternae themselves change in composition and move in a cis-to-trans direction (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The Golgi complex or Golgi apparatus is a crescent shaped, parallel stack of membrane-limited tubules or cisternae. It is closely associated with small vesicles involved in vesicular transport. The Golgi complex is very well developed in secretory cells. The Golgi complex exhibits structural polarity and has a “cis face” or an entry face (which is the convex part of the complex) and a “trans face” or an exit face (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The Golgi complex is closely associated with the nucleus and the “cis face” is adjacent to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The Golgi complex accepts proteins and various other molecules synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum. Each cistern of the Golgi complex contains different types of enzymes and so perform different enzymatic reactions. 

As some proteins move within the Golgi cisternae, carbohydrates and lipids are added to these proteins to form glycoproteins and glycolipids, respectively. In addition, proteins are added to lipids to form lipoproteins. Some proteins are isolated to be included in new plasmalemma.

As these molecules pass further through the Golgi complex, they are sorted and repackaged into a secretory vesicle. These secretory molecules are either destined to become lysosomes, migrate to the plasmalemma, or exported outside of the cell. 

The Golgi apparatus is involved in making carbohydrates (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Atrophy of the Golgi complex and subsequent functional errors in specific neurons and loss of these neurons in the brain has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A lysosome is a membrane-bound cytoplasmic organelle, generally 250–750 nm in diameter, containing hydrolytic enzymes in an acidic environment and involved in intracellular digestion. Lysosomal enzyme defects result in the progressive accumulation of undigested products within the cell, which leads to lysosomal storage disease (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
Lysosomes are single, membrane-bound, usually spherical, organelles (0.05-0.5 μm) that contain very strong, hydrolytic, destructive enzymes. The hydrolytic enzymes are redirected from the rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi complex secretory pathways to primary lysosomes.

Traditionally, lysosomes were described as being bound by a membrane produced in the Golgi complex. That membrane was to protect the exterior part of the lysosomes, and the rest of the cell, from the destructive enzymes even though they are inactive at the pH of the cytosol. 

The primary lysosome fuses with the membrane of an endosome or phagosome and becomes a secondary lysosome or late endosome in which the hydrolytic enzymes are activated and digest the contents of that endosome or phagosome (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Lysosomes are involved in digesting materials ingested by the cells, other cell components or large molecules, and even damaged or redundant organelles (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Many diseases result from deficiencies of lysosomal enzymes. The different diseases affect many cell types so they present as a variety of symptoms. The diseases are characterized by the absence (or inactivity) of specific lysosomal enzymes and so their inability to degrade certain substances. These substances then accumulate in the cell cytoplasm and disrupt normal functional activities of the cell. The inherited “lysosomal storage disease” or “Tay-Sachs disease” is a non-curable, deadly disease that mostly causes damage to nerve cells (neurons). Missing or defective lysosomal enzymes are unable to digest some complex membrane lipids and so this builds up within cells (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a region of the endoplasmic reticulum composed of tubular elements lacking ribosomes and associated with many metabolic processes, including carbohydrate metabolism, the synthesis of lipids, cholesterol, and carbohydrates, and drug metabolism (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a network of interconnected membranous tubules and vesicles. It may be an extension of the rough endoplasmic reticulum or, be located separately. It’s also called agranular endoplasmic reticulum, because it has no ribosomes associated with it. In skeletal muscle cells and cardiomyocytes (cardiac muscle cells), the smooth endoplasmic reticulum is known as sarcoplasmic reticulum (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum makes fatty acids, phospholipids, and steroids. It also contains a collection of enzymes that degrade toxic substances, drugs, and alcohol. It metabolizes glycogen and is involved with cell membrane production and recycling.

The sarcoplasmic reticulum (in skeletal muscle fibers and cardiomyocytes) stores and releases Ca2+ (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is a region of the endoplasmic reticulum that bears large numbers of ribosomes on the outer surface of its membrane and is specialized for protein synthesis and folding (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The endoplasmic reticulum is a vast membranous network throughout the cell and is the largest organelle in the cell. It consists of sacs, cisterns (or passageways) interconnecting tubules and comes in two forms that each can extend the full extent of the cell cytoplasm. 

One form is called rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER). It’s a network of flattened membranous sacs termed cisternae. It’s also known as granular endoplasmic reticulum (gER), because it has ribosomes and/or polyribosomes associated with the cytosolic side of the membrane. These ribosomes attached to the external face of the membranes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum are attached only when a protein is being made. They become detached after the protein is completed (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is continuous with the membrane of the nuclear envelope.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The rough endoplasmic reticulum possesses enzymes and protein complexes. Its protein complexes function as molecular chaperones which guide the nascent (newly formed) protein folding, inhibit aggregation, and monitor the quality of the proteins within the rough endoplasmic reticulum. 

Proteins that are synthesized within the rough endoplasmic reticulum are either destined to become:

- intracellularly stored, such as in lysosomes and specific granules of leukocytes; 

- intracellularly stored prior to exocytosis, such as in exocrine cells;

- incorporated as integral membrane proteins into the plasmalemma. 

The rough endoplasmic reticulum also exhibits a mechanism that prevents faulty proteins that did not fold or assemble properly from being forwarded to other organelles or for secretion. This mechanism is known as the endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation. With this mechanism, unsalvageable proteins translocate back into the cytosol, become conjugated with a regulatory protein known as ubiquitin and are eventually degraded by proteasomes (Mescher, 2013). 

The region of the cytoplasm actively synthesizing proteins stains intensely with basic dyes due to the presence of RNA. Large clumps of rough endoplasmic reticulum in large motor neurons are called Nissl bodies or Nissl substance (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: If the endoplasmic reticulum is stressed, it may activate the “unfolded protein response” (UPR) due to abnormal proteins accumulating within the cistern of the endoplasmic reticulum. The UPR attempts to restore normal function by the endoplasmic reticulum but dysfunction of the UPR can lead to a number of neurodegenerative diseases (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A transport vesicle is a vesicle, coated with clathrin or coat protein (COP), that carries substances between intracellular compartments (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Proteins synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum are packaged into a transport vesicle. That transport vesicle then enters the “cis face” of the Golgi complex and the components or the products pass from one cisterna to the next via a chain of transport vesicles through the entire Golgi complex. They are then repackaged into a secretory vesicle at the “trans face” (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Transport vesicles are located entering the “cis face” of the Golgi complex and between cisternae of the Golgi complex.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Proteins synthesized by the endoplasmic reticulum are packaged into a transport vesicle. That transport vesicle then enters the “cis face” of the Golgi complex and the components or the products pass from one cisterna to the next via a chain of transport vesicles through the entire Golgi complex. They are then repackaged into a secretory vesicle at the “trans face” (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Some transport vesicles leave the “trans face” and distribute proteins to a number of intercellular destinations (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: In endocytosis, an endosome is a vesicle that has lost its coat of clathrin. Four classes of endosomes (early, recycling, and late endosomes and multivesicular bodies) are distinguishable; whether they are distinct organelles or functional subsets of a single compartment is uncertain (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
Endosomes form a system of vesicles (early endosomes) within the cytosol near the cell surface and are a result of fusion of vesicles originating by endocytosis from the plasmalemma. Clathrin-coated vesicles fuse with endosomes. These early endosomes recycle some of the plasmalemma components back to the cell surface, particularly clathrin to form new coated pits, then proceed to go deeper into the cell with other endosomes to become late endosomes. 

Some endosomes are functionally connected to the transport vesicles in the rough endoplasmic reticulum (and most likely the Golgi complex) to deliver hydrolytic enzymes to late endosomes that carry a mannose-6-phosphate (M-6-P) receptor. These are endosomes destined to be lysosomes (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Early endosomes transport and sort proteins received by endocytosis and direct them to appropriate cellular compartments. Late endosomes are lysosomes (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A clathrin-coated vesicle is a transport vesicle having a clathrin coat, involved in the transport of products from the Golgi complex to lysosomes, the transport of molecules taken up by endocytosis, and the retrieval of synaptic vesicle membrane following neurotransmitter release (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The formation of a phagosome is usually a receptor-mediated process allowing only specific molecules to enter the cell. The receptors specific for a particular molecule accumulate at locations along the plasmalemma where the protein clathrin also accumulates. This accumulation on the cytoplasmic surface of the plasmalemma appears like a coated pit when viewed with an electron microscope. The type of vesicle then formed is referred to as a clathrin-coated vesicle (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Coated vesicles are located in the apical regions of the cell cytoplasm (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: A clathrin-coated vesicle contains products ingested by the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A secretory vesicle is membrane-bound vesicles derived from the trans-Golgi network that contain secretory products for delivery to the plasma membrane and subsequent release from the cell (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
Proteins that pass through the Golgi complex are sorted, modified, and then repackaged into a secretory vesicle. The secretory vesicle then passes to the plasmalemma. The secretory vesicle itself fuses with the plasmalemma and releases the secretory product. That process is called exocytosis.

Secretory vesicles are only visible with the light microscope when large amounts of proteins are stored in large secretory vesicles (e.g., pancreatic acinar cells) and then only released by exocytosis after appropriate stimulation.

Secretory vesicles that contain digestive enzymes are named zymogen granules (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Secretory vesicles are located near the “trans” surface of the Golgi Complex and the plasmalemma (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The secretory vesicle contains materials produced by the endoplasmic reticulum but then sorted and packaged by the Golgi complex. The secretory vesicle releases the secretory product via a process called exocytosis (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Mitochondria are the small spherical to rod-shaped cytoplasmic organelles, consisting of inner and outer bilayer membranes with a space between them. The inner membrane is infolded to form a series of projections (cristae), and the space between the cristae is filled by the mitochondrial matrix, which contains DNA, RNA, ribosomes, and granules. Mitochondria generate energy (in the form of ATP synthesis) by the oxidation of nutrients, and they contain the enzymes of the tricarboxylic acid (Krebs) cycle and for fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation. In response to toxic insults, they release enzymes that cause apoptosis. Mitochondria can replicate independently and code for the synthesis of some of their proteins; inheritance of mitochondrial DNA is maternal, and mitochondrial DNA defects cause a variety of diseases (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The mitochondrion is a double membrane-bound organelle about 0.5-1 μm wide and up to 10 μm long. The space between the inner and outer membrane is the intermembrane space. 

Mitochondria occur in a variety of shapes and sizes. The only cells that lack mitochondria are erythrocytes (red blood cells) and terminal keratinocytes. 

The outer mitochondrial membrane is about 6–7 nm thick and contains mitochondrial porins which are voltage-dependent anion channels. Small molecules, ions, and metabolites can enter the intermembrane space but cannot enter the inner mitochondrial membrane. In addition, the outer membrane possesses various receptors for molecules that translocate in the intermembrane space and various enzymes. 

The inner mitochondrial membrane is thinner and rich in cardiolipin which is a phospholipid that makes the inner membrane impermeable to ions and not so permeable to all other elements. The inner membrane invaginates to form long parallel stacks of membranous components called cristae that run perpendicular to the long axis of the mitochondrion and increase the surface area of the inner membrane. Cristae contain respiratory chain enzymes. Among these respiratory enzymes is ATP synthetase which is responsible for oxidative phosphorylation, a process of cellular respiration and the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is an energy-rich molecule.

Cristae form parallel plates in mitochondria that produce proteins, whereas in mitochondria that produce steroids, the cristae adopt a tubular form. 

The amount of mitochondria and the number and complexity of the cristae will correlate with the activity of the cell. Therefore, very active cell, such as a skeletal muscle cells and cardiomyocytes (cardiac muscle cell), will contain large numbers of mitochondria with extensive cristae.

The inner mitochondrial membrane surrounds the mitochondrial fluid (matrix) which contains mitochondrial DNA and RNA. 

The mitochondrial DNA encodes thirteen enzymes which are involved in the process of oxidative phosphorylation. It also contains two rRNAs, and twenty-two tRNAs that are involved in the translation of the mitochondrial mRNA. In addition, mitochondria exhibit a complete system of proteins for protein synthesis and ribosomal synthesis. Mitochondrial proteins are formed both by mitochondrial and nuclear DNA. 

Matrix granules that store Ca2+ are also housed within the matrix of the mitochondrion. 

Mitochondria contribute to the acidophilia of the cytoplasm in cells where they aggregate in large numbers (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Mitochondria are mobile and aggregate within the cell cytoplasm where energy is required.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Mitochondria generate energy using a number of different metabolic pathways to breakdown energy-rich organic substances taken in by the cell, e.g., pyruvates and fatty acids. When they break these components down, they store about half the energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). ATPase will readily release this energy as required by the cell’s activities. The remainder is dissipated as heat to maintain body temperature.

Mitochondria can make their own ribosomes and have the necessary components for protein synthesis. 

Mitochondria can initiate apoptosis, i.e., programmed cell death (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
Mutations in mitochondrial DNA result in a number of inherited disorders. Mitochondrial related diseases (mitochondrial myopathies) become most evident in tissues such as skeletal muscle that require large amounts of energy (ATP) generated by mitochondria (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia affects the inability to move the eyes due to weakening of extraocular muscles and the eyebrows. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy affects vision due to the degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and their axons as a result of mutations in the mitochondrial genome (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is a region of the endoplasmic reticulum that bears large numbers of ribosomes on the outer surface of its membrane and is specialized for protein synthesis and folding (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The endoplasmic reticulum is a vast membranous network throughout the cell and is the largest organelle in the cell. It consists of sacs, cisterns (or passageways) interconnecting tubules and comes in two forms that each can extend the full extent of the cell cytoplasm. 

One form is called rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER). It’s a network of flattened membranous sacs termed cisternae. It’s also known as granular endoplasmic reticulum (gER), because it has ribosomes and/or polyribosomes associated with the cytosolic side of the membrane. These ribosomes attached to the external face of the membranes of the rough endoplasmic reticulum are attached only when a protein is being made. They become detached after the protein is completed (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is continuous with the membrane of the nuclear envelope.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
The rough endoplasmic reticulum possesses enzymes and protein complexes. Its protein complexes function as molecular chaperones which guide the nascent (newly formed) protein folding, inhibit aggregation, and monitor the quality of the proteins within the rough endoplasmic reticulum. 

Proteins that are synthesized within the rough endoplasmic reticulum are either destined to become:

- intracellularly stored, such as in lysosomes and specific granules of leukocytes; 

- intracellularly stored prior to exocytosis, such as in exocrine cells;

- incorporated as integral membrane proteins into the plasmalemma. 

The rough endoplasmic reticulum also exhibits a mechanism that prevents faulty proteins that did not fold or assemble properly from being forwarded to other organelles or for secretion. This mechanism is known as the endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation. With this mechanism, unsalvageable proteins translocate back into the cytosol, become conjugated with a regulatory protein known as ubiquitin and are eventually degraded by proteasomes (Mescher, 2013). 

The region of the cytoplasm actively synthesizing proteins stains intensely with basic dyes due to the presence of RNA. Large clumps of rough endoplasmic reticulum in large motor neurons are called Nissl bodies or Nissl substance (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: If the endoplasmic reticulum is stressed, it may activate the “unfolded protein response” (UPR) due to abnormal proteins accumulating within the cistern of the endoplasmic reticulum. The UPR attempts to restore normal function by the endoplasmic reticulum but dysfunction of the UPR can lead to a number of neurodegenerative diseases (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A peroxisome is a microbody present in all animal cells except erythrocytes and many plant cells, containing over 50 enzymes that participate in a variety of oxidative processes, including reactions involving hydrogen peroxide, purine metabolism, cellular lipid metabolism, and gluconeogenesis (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Peroxisomes are small, spherical membrane bound sacs (0.5-1.2 μm in diameter) derived from smooth endoplasmic reticulum containing enzymes involved in oxidative digestion (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Peroxisomes are involved in the oxidation of specific organic substrates including long chain fatty acids. They can convert hydrogen peroxide that is formed during the various metabolic activities to water due to them containing the enzyme catalase. This catalase activity (particularly in cells in the liver and kidney) also facilitates them degrading toxic molecules including drugs (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) is due to a membrane protein being absent in peroxisomes. This protein transports an enzyme into the peroxisome that regulates the breakdown of very long-chain fatty acids ingested in a normal diet. The fatty acids accumulate in the cell and in the case of nerve cells (neurons) eventually cause disintegration of their myelin covering. This build-up of fatty acid also affects the function of cells in the adrenal gland (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A proteasome is a large, cylindrical protease complex occurring in both the nucleoplasm and cytoplasm, consisting of a 20S core that in eukaryotes and Archaea is capped by a regulatory complex at one or both ends; it degrades intracellular proteins that have been marked by the attachment of ubiquitin (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Sometimes proteins may form that are abnormal or are short-lived proteins that become inactivated (e.g., regulatory proteins). Cells are able to break down these proteins without using lysosomal pathways in large protein complexes called proteasomes (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Proteasomes are located throughout the cell cytoplasm.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The protein complexes (proteasomes) degrade unwanted proteins into amino acids and small polypeptides (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: One of the consequences of Parkinson’s disease is that the digestion of proteins by proteasomes fails and so the abnormal proteins can affect the death of nerve cells (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Pigment granules are small masses of coloring matter occurring in pigment cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Melanin
sections.text: Melanin is a brown pigment and protects the very basal cell layers of the epidermis from any damage from excessive ultraviolet light. These basal cells are dividing constantly to give rise to layers of the epidermis. Melanin protects those dividing cells from any DNA damage that may be caused by excessive ultraviolet light. There is also neuromelanin which is a similar product in the retina (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Lipofuscin
sections.text: When lysosomes breakdown cellular components, the breakdown products remain inside the cell as residual bodies or age pigment. It has a yellow-orange stain or color and it is termed lipofuscin. Lipofuscin is common in skeletal muscle fibers, cardiomyocytes (cardiac muscle cells), neurons, and macrophages. They increase in amounts with age (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Hemosiderin
sections.text: A similar pigment to lipofuscin is called hemosiderin. Hemosiderin is the residual component of the iron-storage complex from the breakdown of hemoglobin. Red blood cells (erythrocytes) only live for about 120 days. When they pass through the spleen, older and less flexible erythrocytes get caught in the network of reticular fibers in the spleen, and macrophages come along and break them down. The macrophages reuse part of the components of hemoglobin but the residual amount in their cytoplasm contains an orange-brown component called hemosiderin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Lipid droplets are the lipid-storage organelles of eukaryotic cells.

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Lipid droplets dominate the cytoplasm of adipocytes (fat cells). They appear clear in the cytoplasm under the microscope because, being of a lipid component, it is lost during the traditional processing of tissue and therefore, their original presence just appears as a ghostly white space within the cell.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Lipid droplets store precursors for the production of steroid hormones and provide an energy source for cellular metabolism (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Accumulation of triglycerides (stored as lipid droplets) in abnormal quantities is a characteristic feature of a number of diseases including atherosclerosis and alcoholic liver disease (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Glycogen is a large polysaccharide similar to amylopectin but more highly branched, consisting of chains of glucose residues in a-(1,4) linkage with branches created by a-(1,6) linkages. It constitutes the major carbohydrate reserve of animals, stored primarily in liver and muscle, and is synthesized and degraded for energy as demanded (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Glycogen is the non-membranous storage form of glucose and is common as clusters of granules 25-40 nm in diameter in liver cells, skeletal muscle fibers, and adipocytes. They are a little larger than ribosomes but in the liver cells they can form aggregates about 90-95 nm in diameter.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Normally glycogen would be located in close proximity to the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER), since the enzymes within the sER breakdown glycogen into glucose (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Glycogen stored in granules is one of the energy sources for the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Glycogen storage diseases are inherited disorders that affect the production or breakdown of glycogen. A deficiency in the enzyme glucose-6-phosphate causes abnormal accumulation of glycogen in liver and muscle cells (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A ribosome is a large molecular structure, approximately 12 nm wide and 25 nm long, having two dissociable subunits, that is the site of protein synthesis. Ribosomes found in the cytosol of eukaryotes have a sedimentation coefficient of 80S; the subunits have coefficients of 60S and 40S and together contain four different ribosomal RNA (rRNA) chains and about 80 different proteins. Ribosomes found in prokaryotes and mitochondria are smaller (70S, with 50S and 30S subunits containing a total of three rRNAs and 55 proteins) and also differ from eukaryotic ribosomes in their sensitivity to certain antibiotics (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
Ribosomes are protein complexes and consist of rRNA synthesized in the nucleolus. They appear in electron micrographs as small, electron-dense particles 20-30 nm in two different forms. 

Firstly, they could be loosely lying within the cytoplasm. Sometimes, they're combined with a messenger RNA to produce a chain of ribosomes called polyribosomes. 

Secondly, ribosomes (and polyribosomes) can be attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum.

Because of the phosphate groups of rRNA act as anions, ribosomes are intensely basophilic and so will stain with basic dyes and hematoxylin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Firstly, ribosomes position loosely within the cytoplasm or as a chain of ribosomes called polyribosomes. Secondly, ribosomes (and polyribosomes) can be attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Individual ribosomes or polyribosomes in the cytoplasm of the cell are freely associated, meaning they are involved with making proteins that the cell uses for itself.

Proteins synthesized by those ribosomes in collaboration with the endoplasmic reticulum is destined to be exported from the cell or incorporated into the plasmalemma. In some cases, the proteins are stored within the cell e.g., in lysosomes and in the granules of white blood cells (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A microtubule is a tubular cytoplasmic structure, 25 nm in diameter and of variable length, composed of α- and β-tubulin dimers, whose orientation imparts polarity; microtubules are involved in maintenance of cell shape and in the movements of organelles and inclusions and form the spindle fibers of mitosis. In cilia and flagella, they are constantly arranged with two single microtubules in the center and nine pairs of doublets arrayed around the central two. A neural microtubule is a microtubule occurring in a neuron (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Microtubules are dynamic tubes of polymerized tubulin molecules that can rapidly form and then disassemble. Microtubules are 20-25 nm in diameter with the tube wall about 5 nm thick and radiate out to the cell periphery from a microtubule organizing center (MTOC), or centrosome, which is usually located close to the cell nucleus. Therefore, they maybe several micrometers in length (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Microtubules radiate out to the cell periphery from a microtubule organizing center (MTOC).

sections.name: Function
Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Any defect in the protein components (or the assembly) of microtubules can affect cilia motility, and therefore non-clearance of secretions on respiratory tract epithelium, impaired ciliary transport of the ovum in the uterine tube and so infertility in women, and sperm motility and so male sterility (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: A microfilament is composed of G-actin coiled around each other to form an F-actin filament and having a plus-minus polarity. Microfilaments are components of the cytoskeleton and participate in the formation of adherens junctions and tight junctions (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Actin molecules within the cell cytoplasm can spontaneously form microfilaments 6-8 nm in diameter. Numerous actin binding proteins give the actin filaments specific characteristics. In most cells, actin filaments are often grouped as a thin sheet just beneath the plasmalemma (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Microfilaments help to maintain cell shape and in some specialized cells (e.g., muscle cells) facilitate muscle contraction and intracellular movement presumably by interactions with myosin. 

Since the microfilaments are located as a thin sheet under the plasmalemma, they are associated with endocytosis, exocytosis, and cell migration processes. They may also appear throughout the cytoplasm and assist movement of cytoplasmic contents such as organelles, vesicles, and granules (cytoplasmic streaming).

They also provide the supportive and rigid structural core of a microvillus and form the terminal web just below the cell surface. Microfilaments form lamellipodia and assist cell migration (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Cells that are mobile are dependent on actin filaments. Any toxic substance that prevents assembly and polymerization of the actin filament such as cytochalasin B and D (from fungi) and phalloidin (from mushrooms) inhibit migration of leukocytes, lymphocytes, and phagocytes (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: An intermediate filament is a class of cytoplasmic filaments, 8–11 nm in diameter, that predominantly act as structural components of the cytoskeleton and also allow various movements in cellular processes. Different types contain different, tissue-specific proteins (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Intermediate filaments are filaments structured like ropes and have a size range of 8-12 nm. They may consist of several proteins (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Intermediate filaments have a structural role maintaining the stability of cell to cell junctions and adherence of the cell to the extracellular matrix. They also function as part of the cytoskeleton, thus supporting the cell (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
Several diseases can be attributed to defects in the assembly of intermediate filaments. A characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease is disarray of intermediate filaments in some neurons (Ross & Pawlina, 2016).

“Mallory bodies” in hepatocytes in alcoholic liver cirrhosis is the accumulation of inclusions containing predominantly keratin intermediate filaments (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

Some specific types of intermediate filaments occurring in tumors allow the origins of the cell causing the tumor to be identified (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The centriole is either of the two cylindrical organelles located in the centrosome and containing nine triplets of microtubules arrayed around their edges; during cell division the centrioles are duplicated, with the resulting pairs migrating to opposite poles of the cell, where they serve to organize the spindles. They are capable of independent replication and of migrating to form basal bodies (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The centriole is a cylindrical structure (0.15 μm in diameter and about 0.3-0.5 μm long) consisting of nine microtubules arranged in triplets. A pair of centrioles are oriented at right angles to each other and they are located near the nucleus and Golgi complex. They are associated with a zone of dense centrosomal matrix or pericentriolar material and collectively referred to as the microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) or centrosome.

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: A pair of centrioles are oriented at right angles to each other and they are located near the nucleus and Golgi complex (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Besides being an integral component of the MTOC, centrioles determine the location and align the mitotic spindle during cell division. They act as basal bodies for the assembly of microtubules that form cilia and flagella.

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: During cell division, centrioles are duplicated and form the mitotic spindle and so have a vital role in equal segregation of chromosomes between daughter cells. Abnormalities in the regulation of centriole duplication can lead to abnormalities of the microtubule organizing center and therefore abnormal sorting of chromosomes during cell divisions. These malfunctions are related to malignant cell transformations (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: A zone of dense centrosomal matrix or pericentriolar matrix contains numerous proteins that initiate the growth of a microtubule (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Microtubule formation begins within the pericentriolar matrix (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cytosol is the liquid medium of the cytoplasm, i.e., cytoplasm minus organelles and nonmembranous insoluble components (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The cytosol (which can occupy about 50% of the cell volume) is an aqueous gel containing solutes, inorganic ions, and organic molecules especially carbohydrates, proteins and lipids. This content is carefully regulated by the cell (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The cytosol is the aqueous medium for many of the cell’s metabolic activities and movements of materials, organelles, etc.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nuclear envelope is the structure enclosing the cell nucleus and separating it from the cytoplasm, consisting of two concentric lipid bilayers (the inner and outer membranes) separated by a 30 nm wide perinuclear space. The outer membrane is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum, and nuclear pore complexes bridging both membranes provide communication between the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The nuclear membrane (35-75 nm thick) is a double membranous envelope that surrounds the nucleus. It is not continuous as it fuses to form nuclear pores all the way around the nuclear envelope. 

The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with, and of similar structure to, the rough or granular endoplasmic reticulum and so may house ribosomes or polyribosomes.

The inner nuclear membrane has a network of intermediate protein filaments attached to the inner surface called the nuclear or fibrous lamina. This nuclear lamina is a supportive “skeleton” but is also essential for many activities including DNA replication, transcription, and gene regulation.

Between the two nuclear membranes is a perinuclear cisternal space (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus. The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nuclear envelope is a physical barrier that controls the movement of materials between the nucleus and the cell cytoplasm. The fibrous lamina stabilizes the nuclear envelope.

sections.name: Quick Facts

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The nucleoplasm occupies the nucleus (apart from the nucleolus and chromatin) and includes a very fine scaffolding network of protein filaments originating from the nuclear pores (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Molecules pass through the nucleoplasm as a consequence of the activity of the chromatin and the nucleolus (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nucleolus is a rounded, dense body, present in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells during interphase, that is the site of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) synthesis and ribosomal subunit assembly. It consists of (a) a fibrillar center, containing the rRNA genes, surrounded by (b) the pars fibrosa, a dense fibrillar component where transcription occurs, and (c) the pars granulosa, a granular component where the ribosomal subunits are assembled. Multiple nucleoli occur in some cells (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The most predominant, non-membranous structure in the nucleus is the spherical nucleolus. It surrounds rRNA genes that are transcriptionally active. The nucleolus is the site of synthesis of the ribosomal ribonucleic acid (rRNA), ribosomal production, and assembly. The size of the nucleolus is 1–2 μm but its size varies within different populations of cells. In cells that are most active in synthesizing proteins, the nucleolus is well developed and prominent. It is common for some cells to contain more than one nucleolus.

Morphologically, the nucleolus is divided into three distinct regions which are the fibrillar centers, fibrillar material, and granular material. 

The fibrillar centers contain DNA loops of chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21 and 22 which contain rRNA genes, RNA polymerase I, and transcription factors. 

The fibrillar material (also known as “pars fibrosa”) contains large amounts of rRNA and ribosomal genes that actively undergo transcription. 

The granular material (also known as “pars granulosa”) contains pre-ribosomal particles that are densely packed and is the site where ribosomes start to assemble.

Like heterochromatin, the nucleolus stains with basic dyes and hematoxylin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The nucleolus is located near the center of the nucleus.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: The nucleolus synthesizes and assembles ribosomal RNA (rRNA) (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: List of Clinical Correlates
sections.text: Nucleoli house proteins for ribosome synthesis and oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes that control cell proliferation. Structural and functional faults in nucleoli have been the basis of a number of disease processes including some types of cancers (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The nuclear pores are the small octagonal openings in the nuclear envelope at sites where the two nuclear membranes are in contact and through which transport between the nucleus and the cytoplasm occurs; the pore and the associated structures embedded in its rim form the nuclear pore complex (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: Nuclear pores occur all the way around the nuclear envelope at sites where the outer and inner membranes of the nuclear envelope fuse. They are not open pores and formed from more than 100 proteins arranged in an octagonal pore complex (Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: Nuclear pores occur all the way around the nuclear envelope.

sections.name: Function
sections.text:
Nuclear pores allow the transfer of materials in and out of the nucleus. For instance, rRNA or ribonucleic acid, travels from the nucleolus out through these pores into the cell cytoplasm. 

Normally, any molecule less than about 9 nm can pass freely through the nuclear pore. More complex molecules pass through only by a receptor-mediated, active process thereby consuming energy (ATP) (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Heterochromatin is the form of chromatin that is darkly staining and tightly coiled in interphase; it is composed of repetitive DNA, is late to replicate, and is transcriptionally inactive (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
Compact or very condensed chromatin visible with the light microscope is called heterochromatin. It's more tightly packed DNA. 

A clump of chromatin (heterochromatin) frequently seen in female cells is called sex chromatin and is one of the two X chromosomes and is generally inactive.

Heterochromatin stains with basic dyes and hematoxylin (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Heterochromatin is prominent in cells that are metabolically quiescent.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Euchromatin is the form of chromatin that is genetically active and constitutes the majority of the chromosomes; it is relatively uncoiled and stains lightly during interphase and condenses and stains more darkly during nuclear division (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text: The lighter-stained, dispersed chromatin is called euchromatin. It's less compact. When it's less compact or when there's a lot of euchromatin inside the cell nucleus, it means that the DNA is uncoiled, and more open to transcriptional enzymes.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Euchromatin is indicative of the genetic information in the DNA being read and transcribed. Therefore, euchromatin is prominent in cells that are very metabolically active particularly in the production of proteins (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Microvilli are the minute cylindrical processes on the free surface of a cell, organized around a core of cross-linked actin filaments anchored to the terminal web, which increase the surface size of the cell; found especially in cells of the proximal convolution of the renal tubules and of the intestinal epithelium (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
A microvillus is an extension of cytoplasm from the apical surface of many epithelial cells. Depending on the epithelial cell, a microvillus may be just a small, irregular-shaped projection, or a very tall projection organized as a numerous, closely packed group, over the entire apical surface of the cell. 

Each microvillus contains a core of actin filaments that extends into the apical part of the cell cytoplasm and attaches to a horizontal network of actin filaments called the terminal web. The molecule myosin binds the actin filaments to the plasmalemma of the microvillus.

On some epithelial surfaces, when microvilli are numerous and closely packed, they are often referred to as a striated or brush border (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: A microvillus is an extension of cytoplasm from the apical surface of many epithelial cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Microvilli increase the surface area of the cell and so increase the absorption capability of the epithelial surface. The contractile ability of the terminal web can cause the intermicrovillus space to widen and further increase absorptive capacity (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Exocytosis is the discharge of material from a cell by fusion of a membrane-bound vesicle with the plasma membrane and subsequent release of the vesicle's contents into the extracellular environment (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
Many substances enter and leave the cell, and move between different cytoplasmic regions or organelles, by vesicular transport. Vesicles present in the cytoplasm (although appearing structurally similar) reflect different traffic pathways and functional states. In most cases, there is a continual renewal/replacement of the plasma membrane as new vesicles are formed from the cell membrane and enter the cell (endocytosis) or fuse with the plasma membrane to excrete substances (exocytosis).

Exocytosis is the release of bulk materials from the cell, a process whereby a membrane-bound structure within the cell approaches and fuses with the plasma membrane of the cell and release its content into the extracellular environment. An example of exocytosis is the release of digestive enzymes from salivary glands and the exocrine pancreas.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cell membrane is the structure enveloping a cell, enclosing the cytoplasm and forming a selective permeability barrier; it consists of a lipid bilayer with integral and peripheral proteins and contains channels and pumps to transport substances across the membrane, as well as receptors to receive stimuli from the external environment and transduce them into intracellular signals (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The cell membrane (or plasmalemma) is a bi-layered membrane, containing primarily phospholipids, cholesterol, and protein molecules. About 7.5-10 nm in width, it can have integral proteins attached to either the internal or the external surface of the bilayer. 

The external surface of the cell membrane contains a carbohydrate-rich region termed the glycocalyx which links to cell membrane proteins and lipids (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The cell membrane is the external boundary of the cell.

sections.name: Function
Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disease and is partly due to a defect in the proteins that affect chloride ion (Cl-) channels within the cell membrane. 

Many glycoproteins and glycolipids in the cell membrane act as receptors that mediate various cell activities, cell adhesions, and responses to chemical messengers. A number of diseases are a result of defective receptors e.g., target cells of some hormones do not respond because they lack the relevant, competent receptors (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Endocytosis is the uptake by a cell of material from the environment by invagination of its plasma membrane; it includes both phagocytosis and pinocytosis (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
Many substances enter and leave the cell, and move between different cytoplasmic regions or organelles, by vesicular transport. Vesicles present in the cytoplasm (although appearing structurally similar) reflect different traffic pathways and functional states. In most cases, there is a continual renewal/replacement of the plasma membrane as new vesicles are formed from the cell membrane and enter the cell (endocytosis) or fuse with the plasma membrane to excrete substances (exocytosis).

The general term for the uptake of materials into the cell is called endocytosis. Many endocytotic processes are receptor mediated. Receptors for many substances aggregate on the cell surface as “coated pits.” They bind the ligand and enter the cell as a coated vesicle then quickly lose their clathrin coat and fuse with endosomes. Endosomes form a system of vesicles (early endosomes). These early endosomes recycle some of the plasmalemma components back to the cell surface, particularly clathrin to form new coated pits, then proceed to go deeper into the cell with other endosomes to become late endosomes. 

Some endosomes are functionally connected to the transport vesicles in the rough endoplasmic reticulum (and most likely the Golgi complex) to deliver hydrolytic enzymes to late endosomes that carry a mannose-6-phosphate (M-6-P) receptor. These are endosomes destined to be lysosomes. Early endosomes transport and sort proteins received by endocytosis and direct them to appropriate cellular compartments. Late endosomes are lysosomes.

Most cells in the body utilize a process called pinocytosis to ingest fluid and small protein molecules via small vesicles about 80–150 nm in diameter. It is a continual process, so small vesicles are continually forming at the cell surface. Most of the vesicles eventually fuse with lysosomes although they are very numerous in endothelial cells as they move materials from their surface of origin to the other side. They are also numerous at the surfaces of smooth muscle cells and their initial invaginations from the smooth muscle plasma membrane are referred to as caveolae.

During phagocytosis large particles which include bacteria and foreign materials are ingested into the cell. Pseudopodia from the plasma membrane engulf these large particles into a large vesicle about 250 nm in diameter called a phagosome. An endolysosome (or phagolysosome) forms when the phagosome enters the cell and fuses with a lysosome. The lysosomal contents include hydrolytic enzymes which digest the content within the phagosome. Some of the digested products may be used by the cell but most will be exported out of the cell by exocytosis.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Exocytosis is the discharge of material from a cell by fusion of a membrane-bound vesicle with the plasma membrane and subsequent release of the vesicle's contents into the extracellular environment (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
Many substances enter and leave the cell, and move between different cytoplasmic regions or organelles, by vesicular transport. Vesicles present in the cytoplasm (although appearing structurally similar) reflect different traffic pathways and functional states. In most cases, there is a continual renewal/replacement of the plasma membrane as new vesicles are formed from the cell membrane and enter the cell (endocytosis) or fuse with the plasma membrane to excrete substances (exocytosis).

Exocytosis is the release of bulk materials from the cell, a process whereby a membrane-bound structure within the cell approaches and fuses with the plasma membrane of the cell and release its content into the extracellular environment. An example of exocytosis is the release of digestive enzymes from salivary glands and the exocrine pancreas.

sections.name: References
sections.text: Dorland, W. (2011) Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary. 32nd edn. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders.

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: Microvilli are the minute cylindrical processes on the free surface of a cell, organized around a core of cross-linked actin filaments anchored to the terminal web, which increase the surface size of the cell; found especially in cells of the proximal convolution of the renal tubules and of the intestinal epithelium (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
A microvillus is an extension of cytoplasm from the apical surface of many epithelial cells. Depending on the epithelial cell, a microvillus may be just a small, irregular-shaped projection, or a very tall projection organized as a numerous, closely packed group, over the entire apical surface of the cell. 

Each microvillus contains a core of actin filaments that extends into the apical part of the cell cytoplasm and attaches to a horizontal network of actin filaments called the terminal web. The molecule myosin binds the actin filaments to the plasmalemma of the microvillus.

On some epithelial surfaces, when microvilli are numerous and closely packed, they are often referred to as a striated or brush border (Ross and Pawlina, 2006).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: A microvillus is an extension of cytoplasm from the apical surface of many epithelial cells.

sections.name: Function
sections.text: Microvilli increase the surface area of the cell and so increase the absorption capability of the epithelial surface. The contractile ability of the terminal web can cause the intermicrovillus space to widen and further increase absorptive capacity (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Quick Facts
sections.text: The cell membrane is the structure enveloping a cell, enclosing the cytoplasm and forming a selective permeability barrier; it consists of a lipid bilayer with integral and peripheral proteins and contains channels and pumps to transport substances across the membrane, as well as receptors to receive stimuli from the external environment and transduce them into intracellular signals (Dorland, 2011).

sections.name: Structure and/or Key Feature(s)
sections.text:
The cell membrane (or plasmalemma) is a bi-layered membrane, containing primarily phospholipids, cholesterol, and protein molecules. About 7.5-10 nm in width, it can have integral proteins attached to either the internal or the external surface of the bilayer. 

The external surface of the cell membrane contains a carbohydrate-rich region termed the glycocalyx which links to cell membrane proteins and lipids (Ross and Pawlina, 2006; Ovalle, Nahirney and Netter, 2013; McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).

sections.name: Anatomical Relations
sections.text: The cell membrane is the external boundary of the cell.

sections.name: Function
Clinical Correlates
sections.text:
Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disease and is partly due to a defect in the proteins that affect chloride ion (Cl-) channels within the cell membrane. 

Many glycoproteins and glycolipids in the cell membrane act as receptors that mediate various cell activities, cell adhesions, and responses to chemical messengers. A number of diseases are a result of defective receptors e.g., target cells of some hormones do not respond because they lack the relevant, competent receptors (McKinley, O'Loughlin and Pennefather-O'Brien, 2016).
